447|        # the "rest" of the code. The fun part is that \u00e0 is
448|        # "latin small letter a with grave", so if you type that on a French
449|        # keyboard, you _also_ get a \xe0.
450|        # E.g., consider the Up arrow. This returns \xe0 and then \x48. The
451|        # resulting Unicode string reads as "a with grave" + "capital H".
452|        # This is indistinguishable from when the user actually types
453|        # "a with grave" and then "capital H".
454|        #
455|        # When \xe0 is returned, we assume it's part of a special-key sequence
456|        # and call `getwch` again, but that means that when the user types
457|        # the \u00e0 character, `getchar` doesn't return until a second
458|        # character is typed.
459|        # The alternative is returning immediately, but that would mess up
460|        # cross-platform handling of arrow keys and others that start with
461|        # \xe0. Another option is using `getch`, but then we can't reliably
462|        # read non-ASCII characters, because return values of `getch` are
463|        # limited to the current 8-bit codepage.

46|def _unpack_args(
47|    args: Sequence[str], nargs_spec: Sequence[int]
48|) -> tuple[Sequence[str | Sequence[str | None] | None], list[str]]:
49|    """Given an iterable of arguments and an iterable of nargs specifications,
50|    it returns a tuple with all the unpacked arguments at the first index
51|    and all remaining arguments as the second.
52|
53|    The nargs specification is the number of arguments that should be consumed
54|    or `-1` to indicate that this position should eat up all the remainders.
55|    """
56|    args = deque(args)
57|    nargs_spec = deque(nargs_spec)
58|    rv: list[str | tuple[str | None, ...] | None] = []
59|    spos: int | None = None
60|
61|    def _fetch(c: deque[V]) -> V | None:
62|        try:
63|            if spos is None:
64|                return c.popleft()
65|            else:
66|                return c.pop()
67|        except IndexError:
68|            return None
69|
70|    while nargs_spec:
71|        nargs = _fetch(nargs_spec)
72|        assert nargs is not None
73|
74|        if nargs == 1:
75|            rv.append(_fetch(args))
76|        elif nargs > 1:
77|            x = [_fetch(args) for _ in range(nargs)]
78|
79|            # If we're reversed, we're pulling in the arguments in reverse,
80|            # so we need to turn them around.
81|            if spos is not None:
82|                x.reverse()
83|
84|            rv.append(tuple(x))
85|        elif nargs < 0:
86|            if spos is not None:  # pragma: no cover
87|                raise TypeError("Cannot have two nargs < 0")
88|
89|            spos = len(rv)
90|            rv.append(None)
91|
92|    # spos is the position of the wildcard (star).  If it's not `None`,
93|    # we fill it with the remainder.
94|    if spos is not None:
95|        rv[spos] = tuple(args)
96|        args = []
97|        rv[spos + 1 :] = reversed(rv[spos + 1 :])
98|
99|    return tuple(rv), list(args)

207|class _OptionParser:
208|    """The option parser is an internal class that is ultimately used to
209|    parse options and arguments.  It's modelled after optparse and brings
210|    a similar but vastly simplified API.  It should generally not be used
211|    directly as the high level Click classes wrap it for you.
212|
213|    It's not nearly as extensible as optparse or argparse as it does not
214|    implement features that are implemented on a higher level (such as
215|    types or defaults).
216|    """

218|    def __init__(self, ctx: Union["Context", None] = None) -> None:

220|        # This controls how the parser deals with interspersed arguments.
221|        # If this is set to `False`, the parser will stop on the first
222|        # non-option.  Click uses this to implement nested subcommands
223|        # safely.
224|        self.allow_interspersed_args: bool = True
225|        # This tells the parser how to deal with unknown options.  By
226|        # default it will error out (which is sensible), but there is a
227|        # second mode where it will ignore it and continue processing
228|        # after shifting all the unknown options into the resulting args.
229|        self.ignore_unknown_options: bool = False
230|
231|        if ctx is not None:
232|            self.allow_interspersed_args = ctx.allow_interspersed_args
233|            self.ignore_unknown_options = ctx.ignore_unknown_options
234|
235|        self._short_opt: dict[str, _Option] = {}
236|        self._long_opt: dict[str, _Option] = {}
237|        self._opt_prefixes = {"-", "--"}
238|        self._args: list[_Argument] = []

240|    def add_option(
241|        self,
242|        obj: "CoreOption",
243|        opts: Sequence[str],
244|        dest: str | None,
245|        action: str = "store",
246|        nargs: int = 1,
247|        const: Any | None = None,
248|    ) -> None:
249|        """Adds a new option named `dest` to the parser.  The destination
250|        is not inferred (unlike with optparse) and needs to be explicitly
251|        provided.  Action can be any of ``store``, ``store_const``,
252|        ``append``, ``append_const`` or ``count``.
253|
254|        The `obj` can be used to identify the option in the order list
255|        that is returned from the parser.
256|        """
257|        opts = [_normalize_opt(opt, self.ctx) for opt in opts]
258|        option = _Option(obj, opts, dest, action=action, nargs=nargs, const=const)
259|        self._opt_prefixes.update(option.prefixes)
260|        for opt in option._short_opts:
261|            self._short_opt[opt] = option
262|        for opt in option._long_opts:
263|            self._long_opt[opt] = option

265|    def add_argument(
266|        self, obj: "CoreArgument", dest: str | None, nargs: int = 1
267|    ) -> None:
268|        """Adds a positional argument named `dest` to the parser.
269|
270|        The `obj` can be used to identify the option in the order list
271|        that is returned from the parser.

275|    def parse_args(
276|        self, args: list[str]
277|    ) -> tuple[dict[str, Any], list[str], list["CoreParameter"]]:
278|        """Parses positional arguments and returns ``(values, args, order)``
279|        for the parsed options and arguments as well as the leftover
280|        arguments if there are any.  The order is a list of objects as they
281|        appear on the command line.  If arguments appear multiple times they
282|        will be memorized multiple times as well.

286|            self._process_args_for_options(state)

293|    def _process_args_for_args(self, state: _ParsingState) -> None:

326|        # [arg0, ..., arg(i-1)] (any options and their arguments will have

330|        # If it consumes 1 (eg. arg is an option that takes no arguments),

340|    def _match_long_opt(

352|            # explicit value, because no exception is raised in this
353|            # branch.  This means that the inserted value will be fully
354|            # consumed.

368|    def _match_short_opt(self, arg: str, state: _ParsingState) -> None:
369|        stop = False
370|        i = 1
371|        prefix = arg[0]
372|        unknown_options = []
373|
374|        for ch in arg[1:]:
375|            opt = _normalize_opt(f"{prefix}{ch}", self.ctx)
376|            option = self._short_opt.get(opt)
377|            i += 1
378|
379|            if not option:

381|                    unknown_options.append(ch)

384|            if option.takes_value:

386|                # next arg, and stop consuming characters of arg.
387|                if i < len(arg):

389|                    stop = True
390|
391|                value = self._get_value_from_state(opt, option, state)
392|
393|            else:

395|
396|            option.process(value, state)

398|            if stop:

402|        # remaining options and re-attach the prefix, then report that
403|        # to the state as new 'largs'.  This way there is basic combinatorics
404|        # that can be achieved while still ignoring unknown arguments.
405|        if self.ignore_unknown_options and unknown_options:
406|            state.largs.append(f"{prefix}{''.join(unknown_options)}")

408|    def _get_value_from_state(
409|        self, option_name: str, option: _Option, state: _ParsingState
410|    ) -> str | Sequence[str]:
411|        nargs = option.nargs
412|
413|        value: str | Sequence[str]
414|
415|        if len(state.rargs) < nargs:
416|            msg = "an argument." if nargs == 1 else f"{nargs} arguments."
417|            raise BadOptionUsage(
418|                option_name,
419|                f"Option {option_name!r} requires {msg}",
420|            )
421|        elif nargs == 1:
422|            value = state.rargs.pop(0)
423|        else:
424|            value = tuple(state.rargs[:nargs])
425|            del state.rargs[:nargs]
426|
427|        return value
428|
429|    def _process_opts(self, arg: str, state: _ParsingState) -> None:
430|        explicit_value = None
431|        # Long option handling happens in two parts.  The first part is
432|        # supporting explicitly attached values.  In any case, we will try
433|        # to long match the option first.
434|        if "=" in arg:
435|            long_opt, explicit_value = arg.split("=", 1)
436|        else:
437|            long_opt = arg
438|        norm_long_opt = _normalize_opt(long_opt, self.ctx)
439|
440|        # At this point we will match the (assumed) long option through
441|        # the long option matching code.  Note that this allows options
442|        # like "-foo" to be matched as long options.
443|        try:
444|            self._match_long_opt(norm_long_opt, explicit_value, state)
445|        except NoSuchOption:

447|            # to try with short options.  However there is a special rule
448|            # which says, that if we have a two character options prefix
449|            # (applies to "--foo" for instance), we do not dispatch to the
450|            # short option code and will instead raise the no option
451|            # error.
452|            if arg[:2] not in self._opt_prefixes:
453|                self._match_short_opt(arg, state)
454|                return
455|
456|            if not self.ignore_unknown_options:
457|                raise
458|
459|            state.largs.append(arg)

75|def prompt(
76|    text: str,
77|    default: Any | None = None,
78|    hide_input: bool = False,
79|    confirmation_prompt: bool | str = False,
80|    type: ParamType | Any | None = None,
81|    value_proc: Callable[[str], Any] | None = None,
82|    prompt_suffix: str = ": ",
83|    show_default: bool = True,
84|    err: bool = False,
85|    show_choices: bool = True,
86|) -> Any:
87|    """Prompts a user for input.  This is a convenience function that can
88|    be used to prompt a user for input later.
89|
90|    If the user aborts the input by sending an interrupt signal, this
91|    function will catch it and raise an `Abort` exception.
92|    """
93|
94|    def prompt_func(text: str) -> str:
95|        f = hidden_prompt_func if hide_input else visible_prompt_func
96|        try:
97|            # Write the prompt separately so that we get nice
98|            # coloring through colorama on Windows
99|            echo(text[:-1], nl=False, err=err)
100|            # Echo the last character to stdout to work around an issue where
101|            # readline causes backspace to clear the whole line.
102|            return f(text[-1:])
103|        except (KeyboardInterrupt, EOFError):  # pragma: no cover
104|            # getpass doesn't print a newline if the user aborts input with ^C.
105|            # Allegedly this behavior is inherited from getpass(3).
106|            # A doc bug has been filed at https://bugs.python.org/issue24711
107|            if hide_input:
108|                echo(None, err=err)
109|            raise Abort() from None
110|
111|    if value_proc is None:
112|        value_proc = convert_type(type, default)
113|
114|    prompt = _build_prompt(
115|        text, prompt_suffix, show_default, default, show_choices, type
116|    )
117|
118|    if confirmation_prompt:
119|        if confirmation_prompt is True:
120|            confirmation_prompt = "Repeat for confirmation"
121|
122|        confirmation_prompt = _build_prompt(confirmation_prompt, prompt_suffix)
123|
124|    while True:
125|        while True:
126|            value = prompt_func(prompt)
127|            if value:
128|                break
129|            elif default is not None:
130|                value = default
131|                break
132|        try:
133|            result = value_proc(value)
134|        except UsageError as e:  # pragma: no cover
135|            if hide_input:
136|                echo("Error: The value you entered was invalid.", err=err)
137|            else:

140|        if not confirmation_prompt:
141|            return result

143|            value2 = prompt_func(confirmation_prompt)
144|            is_empty = not value and not value2
145|            if value2 or is_empty:
146|                break

28|def wrap_text(
29|    text: str,
30|    width: int = 78,
31|    initial_indent: str = "",
32|    subsequent_indent: str = "",
33|    preserve_paragraphs: bool = False,
34|) -> str:
35|    """A helper function that intelligently wraps text.  By default, it
36|    assumes that it operates on a single paragraph of text but if the
37|    `preserve_paragraphs` parameter is provided it will intelligently
38|    handle paragraphs (defined by two empty lines).
39|
40|    If paragraphs are handled, a paragraph can be prefixed with an empty
41|    line containing the ``\\b`` character (``\\x08``) to indicate that
42|    no rewrapping should happen in that block.
43|    """
44|    from ._textwrap import TextWrapper
45|
46|    text = text.expandtabs()
47|    wrapper = TextWrapper(
48|        width,
49|        initial_indent=initial_indent,
50|        subsequent_indent=subsequent_indent,
51|        replace_whitespace=False,
52|    )
53|    if not preserve_paragraphs:
54|        return wrapper.fill(text)
55|
56|    p: list[tuple[int, bool, str]] = []
57|    buf: list[str] = []
58|    indent = None
59|
60|    def _flush_par() -> None:
61|        if not buf:
62|            return
63|        if buf[0].strip() == "\b":
64|            p.append((indent or 0, True, "\n".join(buf[1:])))
65|        else:
66|            p.append((indent or 0, False, " ".join(buf)))
67|        del buf[:]
68|
69|    for line in text.splitlines():
70|        if not line:
71|            _flush_par()
72|            indent = None
73|        else:
74|            if indent is None:
75|                orig_len = term_len(line)
76|                line = line.lstrip()
77|                indent = orig_len - term_len(line)
78|            buf.append(line)
79|    _flush_par()
80|
81|    rv = []
82|    for indent, raw, text in p:
83|        with wrapper.extra_indent(" " * indent):
84|            if raw:
85|                rv.append(wrapper.indent_only(text))
86|            else:
87|                rv.append(wrapper.fill(text))
88|
89|    return "\n\n".join(rv)

92|class HelpFormatter:
93|    """This class helps with formatting text-based help pages.  It's
94|    usually just needed for very special internal cases, but it's also
95|    exposed so that developers can write their own fancy outputs.
96|
97|    At present, it always writes into memory.
98|    """
99|
100|    def __init__(
101|        self,
102|        indent_increment: int = 2,
103|        width: int | None = None,
104|        max_width: int | None = None,
105|    ) -> None:
106|        self.indent_increment = indent_increment
107|        if max_width is None:
108|            max_width = 80
109|        if width is None:
110|            import shutil
111|
112|            width = FORCED_WIDTH
113|            if width is None:
114|                width = max(min(shutil.get_terminal_size().columns, max_width) - 2, 50)
115|        self.width = width
116|        self.current_indent: int = 0
117|        self.buffer: list[str] = []
118|
119|    def write(self, string: str) -> None:
120|        """Writes a unicode string into the internal buffer."""
121|        self.buffer.append(string)
122|
123|    def indent(self) -> None:
124|        """Increases the indentation."""
125|        self.current_indent += self.indent_increment
126|
127|    def dedent(self) -> None:
128|        """Decreases the indentation."""
129|        self.current_indent -= self.indent_increment
130|
131|    def write_usage(self, prog: str, args: str = "", prefix: str | None = None) -> None:
132|        """Writes a usage line into the buffer."""
133|        if prefix is None:
134|            prefix = "Usage: "
135|
136|        usage_prefix = f"{prefix:>{self.current_indent}}{prog} "
137|        text_width = self.width - self.current_indent
138|
139|        if text_width >= (term_len(usage_prefix) + 20):
140|            # The arguments will fit to the right of the prefix.
141|            indent = " " * term_len(usage_prefix)
142|            self.write(
143|                wrap_text(
144|                    args,
145|                    text_width,
146|                    initial_indent=usage_prefix,
147|                    subsequent_indent=indent,
148|                )
149|            )
150|        else:
151|            # The prefix is too long, put the arguments on the next line.
152|            self.write(usage_prefix)
153|            self.write("\n")
154|            indent = " " * (max(self.current_indent, term_len(prefix)) + 4)
155|            self.write(
156|                wrap_text(
157|                    args, text_width, initial_indent=indent, subsequent_indent=indent
158|                )
159|            )
160|
161|        self.write("\n")
162|
163|    def write_heading(self, heading: str) -> None:
164|        """Writes a heading into the buffer."""
165|        self.write(f"{'':>{self.current_indent}}{heading}:\n")
166|
167|    def write_paragraph(self) -> None:
168|        """Writes a paragraph into the buffer."""
169|        if self.buffer:
170|            self.write("\n")
171|
172|    def write_text(self, text: str) -> None:
173|        """Writes re-indented text into the buffer.  This rewraps and
174|        preserves paragraphs.
175|        """
176|        indent = " " * self.current_indent
177|        self.write(
178|            wrap_text(
179|                text,
180|                self.width,
181|                initial_indent=indent,
182|                subsequent_indent=indent,
183|                preserve_paragraphs=True,
184|            )
185|        )
186|        self.write("\n")
187|
188|    def write_dl(
189|        self,
190|        rows: Sequence[tuple[str, str]],
191|        col_max: int = 30,
192|        col_spacing: int = 2,
193|    ) -> None:
194|        """Writes a definition list into the buffer.  This is how options
195|        and commands are usually formatted.
196|        """
197|        rows = list(rows)
198|        widths = measure_table(rows)
199|        if len(widths) != 2:  # pragma: no cover
200|            raise TypeError("Expected two columns for definition list")
201|
202|        first_col = min(widths[0], col_max) + col_spacing
203|
204|        for first, second in iter_rows(rows, len(widths)):
205|            self.write(f"{'':>{self.current_indent}}{first}")
206|            if not second:
207|                self.write("\n")
208|                continue
209|            if term_len(first) <= first_col - col_spacing:
210|                self.write(" " * (first_col - term_len(first)))
211|            else:
212|                self.write("\n")
213|                self.write(" " * (first_col + self.current_indent))
214|
215|            text_width = max(self.width - first_col - 2, 10)
216|            wrapped_text = wrap_text(second, text_width, preserve_paragraphs=True)
217|            lines = wrapped_text.splitlines()
218|
219|            if lines:
220|                self.write(f"{lines[0]}\n")
221|
222|                for line in lines[1:]:
223|                    self.write(f"{'':>{first_col + self.current_indent}}{line}\n")
224|            else:  # pragma: no cover
225|                self.write("\n")

227|    @contextmanager
228|    def section(self, name: str) -> Iterator[None]:

230|        and the indents.

232|        self.write_paragraph()

244|        try:
245|            yield
246|        finally:

249|    def getvalue(self) -> str:
250|        """Returns the buffer contents."""

254|def join_options(options: Sequence[str]) -> tuple[str, bool]:
255|    """Given a list of option strings this joins them in the most appropriate
256|    way and returns them in the form ``(formatted_string,
257|    any_prefix_is_slash)`` where the second item in the tuple is a flag that
258|    indicates if any of the option prefixes was a slash.
259|    """
260|    rv = []
261|    any_prefix_is_slash = False
262|
263|    for opt in options:
264|        prefix = _split_opt(opt)[0]
265|
266|        if prefix == "/":
267|            any_prefix_is_slash = True
268|
269|        rv.append((len(prefix), opt))
270|
271|    rv.sort(key=lambda x: x[0])
272|    return ", ".join(x[1] for x in rv), any_prefix_is_slash

24|    ) -> Mapping[ParamTypeValue, str]:
25|        """

27|        the normalized values that are accepted via the command line.

32|                ctx=ctx,

41|

43|            normed_value = ctx.token_normalize_func(normed_value)
44|
45|        if not self.case_sensitive:

52|            choice_metavars = [

54|            ]
55|            choices_str = "|".join([*dict.fromkeys(choice_metavars)])
56|        else:

58|                [str(i) for i in self._normalized_mapping(ctx=ctx).values()]
59|            )

66|    ) -> str:

72|        self, value: Any, param: _click.Parameter | None, ctx: _click.Context | None

76|        matching normalized value in the list of choices. Then return the
77|        matched "original" choice.

80|        normalized_mapping = self._normalized_mapping(ctx=ctx)

6|class TextWrapper(textwrap.TextWrapper):
7|    def _handle_long_word(
8|        self,
9|        reversed_chunks: list[str],
10|        cur_line: list[str],
11|        cur_len: int,
12|        width: int,
13|    ) -> None:
14|        space_left = max(width - cur_len, 1)
15|
16|        last = reversed_chunks[-1]
17|        cut = last[:space_left]
18|        res = last[space_left:]
19|        cur_line.append(cut)
20|        reversed_chunks[-1] = res
21|
22|    @contextmanager
23|    def extra_indent(self, indent: str) -> Iterator[None]:
24|        old_initial_indent = self.initial_indent
25|        old_subsequent_indent = self.subsequent_indent
26|        self.initial_indent += indent
27|        self.subsequent_indent += indent
28|
29|        try:
30|            yield
31|        finally:
32|            self.initial_indent = old_initial_indent
33|            self.subsequent_indent = old_subsequent_indent
34|

36|        rv = []
37|

40|
41|            if idx > 0:

1|---
2|name: typer
3|description: Typer best practices and conventions. Use when working with Typer CLIs. Keeps Typer code clean and up to date with the latest features and patterns, updated with new versions. Write new code or refactor and update old code.
4|---
5|
6|# Typer
7|
8|Official Typer skill to write code with best practices, keeping up to date with new versions and features.
9|
10|## Installing typer
11|
12|In a virtual environment, `pip install typer` (with pip) or `uv pip install typer` (with uv). For your library/project, add `typer` to the dependencies in `pyproject.toml`.
13|
14|Do not install `typer-slim` or `typer-cli`, they are both deprecated and will now simply install `typer`.
15|
16|Typer supports Python 3.10 and above.
17|
18|## Use an explicit `Typer` app
19|
20|For maximum generalizability, create an explicit Typer app and register subcommand(s), instead of using `typer.run`:
21|
22|```python
23|import typer
24|
25|app = typer.Typer()
26|
27|
28|@app.command()
29|def hello():
30|    print(f"Hello World")
31|
32|
33|if __name__ == "__main__":
34|    app()
35|```
36|
37|instead of:
38|
39|```python
40|# DO NOT DO THIS: Not extensible. Use Typer() instead.
41|import typer
42|
43|
44|def main():
45|    print(f"Hello World")
46|
47|
48|if __name__ == "__main__":
49|    typer.run(main)
50|```
51|
52|## Execute the app
53|
54|To execute the app in the terminal, run
55|
56|```bash
57|python main.py
58|```
59|
60|When multiple commands are registered to the Typer app, you have to add the command name:
61|
62|```bash
63|python main.py hello
64|```
65|
66|To see the automatically generated help documentation, run
67|
68|```bash
69|python main.py --help
70|```
71|
72|or set `no_args_is_help` to `True` when creating the `Typer()` add to automatically show the help when running a command without any arguments.
73|
74|## Use `Annotated`
75|
76|Always prefer the `Annotated` style for declarations of CLI arguments and options.
77|
78|It allows us to pass additional metadata that can be used by Typer.
79|
80|```python
81|from typing import Annotated
82|
83|import typer
84|
85|app = typer.Typer()
86|
87|
88|@app.command()
89|def hello(name: Annotated[str, typer.Argument()] = "World"):
90|    # Note that name is an optional Argument, as a default is provided
91|    print(f"Hello {name}")
92|
93|
94|if __name__ == "__main__":
95|    app()
96|```
97|
98|This program can be run as-is, or can provide a specific name:
99|
100|```bash
101|python main.py
102|python main.py Rick
103|```
104|
105|An older way of setting a default value is this:
106|```python
107|# DO NOT DO THIS: old style. Use Annotated instead.
108|
109|
110|@app.command()
111|def main(name: str = typer.Argument(default="World")):
112|    # Note that name is an optional Argument, as a default is provided
113|    print(f"Hello {name}")
114|```
115|
116|Similarly, the old style could use ellipsis (...) to explicitly mark an argument as required.
117|
118|```python
119|# DO NOT DO THIS: old style. Use Annotated without a default value instead.
120|
121|
122|@app.command()
123|def main(name: str = typer.Argument(default=...)):
124|    # Note that name is now a required Argument
125|    print(f"Hello {name}")
126|```
127|
128|## CLI Options
129|
130|CLI options are declared in a similar fashion as arguments, but will be called on the CLI with a single dash (single letter) or 2 dashes (full name).
131|
132|The CLI option name is automatically generated from the variable name, so `user_name` becomes `--user-name` automatically:
133|
134|```python
135|from typing import Annotated
136|
137|import typer
138|
139|app = typer.Typer()
140|
141|
142|@app.command()
143|def main(user_name: Annotated[str, typer.Option()]):
144|    # On the CLI, the required user name can be specified with --user-name
145|    print(f"Hello {user_name}")
146|
147|
148|if __name__ == "__main__":
149|    app()
150|```
151|
152|If you want to specify a different name, or want to add a short version, declare them in the `typer.Option`:
153|
154|```python
155|from typing import Annotated
156|
157|import typer
158|
159|app = typer.Typer()
160|
161|
162|@app.command()
163|def main(user_name: Annotated[str, typer.Option("--name", "-n")]):
164|    # On the CLI, the required user name can be specified with -n or --name
165|    print(f"Hello {user_name}")
166|
167|
168|if __name__ == "__main__":
169|    app()
170|```
171|
172|You can run this program as such:
173|
174|```bash
175|python main.py -n "Rick"
176|python main.py --name "Morty"
177|```
178|
179|### CLI options with multiple values
180|
181|By declaring a CLI option as a list, it can receive multiple values:
182|
183|```python
184|from typing import Annotated
185|
186|import typer
187|
188|app = typer.Typer()
189|
190|
191|@app.command()
192|def main(user: Annotated[list[str] | None, typer.Option()] = None):
193|    if not user:
194|        print(f"No users provided!")
195|        raise typer.Abort()
196|    for u in user:
197|        print(f"Processing user: {u}")
198|
199|
200|if __name__ == "__main__":
201|    app()
202|```
203|
204|This can be executed like so:
205|
206|```bash
207|python main.py --user Rick --user Morty --user Summer
208|```
209|
210|## Rich
211|
212|By default, Rich can be used with its custom markup syntax to set colors and styles, e.g.
213|
214|```python
215|from rich import print
216|
217|print("[bold red]Alert![/bold red] [green]Portal gun[/green] shooting! :boom:")
218|```
219|
220|Typer supports using Rich formatting in the docstrings and the help messages of CLI arguments and CLI options.
221|
222|
223|```python
224|from typing import Annotated
225|
226|import typer
227|
228|app = typer.Typer(rich_markup_mode="rich")
229|
230|
231|@app.command()
232|def create(
233|    username: Annotated[
234|        str, typer.Argument(help="The username to be [green]created[/green]")
235|    ],
236|):
237|    """
238|    [bold green]Create[/bold green] a new [italic]shiny[/italic] user. :sparkles:
239|
240|    This requires a [underline]username[/underline].
241|    """
242|    print(f"Creating user: {username}")
243|
244|
245|@app.command(help="[bold red]Delete[/bold red] a user with [italic]username[/italic].")
246|def delete(
247|    username: Annotated[
248|        str, typer.Argument(help="The username to be [red]deleted[/red]")
249|    ],
250|):
251|    """
252|    Some internal utility function to delete.
253|    """
254|    print(f"Deleting user: {username}")
255|
256|
257|if __name__ == "__main__":
258|    app()
259|```
260|
261|To disable Rich formatting, set `rich_markup_mode` to `None` when creating a `Typer()` app. By default (when no value is given), Rich formatting is enabled.
262|
263|### Rich markdown
264|
265|You can also set `rich_markup_mode` to `"markdown"` to use Markdown in the docstring:
266|
267|```python
268|from typing import Annotated
269|
270|import typer
271|
272|app = typer.Typer(rich_markup_mode="markdown")
273|
274|
275|@app.command(help="**Delete** a user with *username*.")
276|def delete(
277|    username: Annotated[
278|        str, typer.Argument(help="The username to be **deleted** :boom:")
279|    ],
280|):
281|    print(f"Deleting user: {username}")
282|
283|
284|if __name__ == "__main__":
285|    app()
286|```
287|
288|## Click
289|
290|Originally, Typer was built on Click. However, since version 0.26.0, Typer has vendored Click. As such, Click extensions should not be used anymore.
291|
292|Other settings of `Option` and `Argument` that came from Click but shouldn't be used in Typer anymore, include: `expose_value`, `shell_complete`, `show_choices`, `errors`, `prompt_required`, `is_flag`, `flag_value` and `allow_from_autoenv`.
293|
294|Code bases using these should be refactored to use pure Typer functionality.

190|### Breaking Changes
191|
192|* ➖ Vendor Click and streamline Typer's functionality and code base. PR [#1774](https://github.com/fastapi/typer/pull/1774) by [@svlandeg](https://github.com/svlandeg).
193|    * Typer no longer depends on Click as a third party dependency, it vendors (includes the source code of) Click.
194|    * This simplifies the work done by both Click and Typer teams.
195|    * It allows Typer to evolve independently, and enables several new planned features.
196|    * It will solve several dependency conflict situations for projects that use some packages that depend on Click and some that depend on Typer.
197|    * This also means that Click-specific functionality is no longer supported, like extracting the Click app and adding Click-specific plug-ins, or customizing the field types with Click-specific types.

853|## 0.14.0 (2024-11-28)
854|
855|### Breaking Changes
856|
857|* 🔥 Remove auto naming of groups added via `add_typer` based on the group's callback function name. PR [#1052](https://github.com/fastapi/typer/pull/1052) by [@patrick91](https://github.com/patrick91).
858|
859|Before, it was supported to infer the name of a command group from the callback function name in the sub-app, so, in this code:
860|
861|```python
862|import typer
863|
864|app = typer.Typer()
865|users_app = typer.Typer()
866|
867|app.add_typer(users_app)
868|
869|
870|@users_app.callback()
871|def users():  # <-- This was the inferred command group name
872|    """
873|    Manage users in the app.
874|    """
875|
876|
877|@users_app.command()
878|def create(name: str):
879|    print(f"Creating user: {name}")
880|```
881|
882|...the command group would be named `users`, based on the name of the function `def users()`.
883|
884|Now you need to set it explicitly:
885|
886|```python
887|import typer
888|
889|app = typer.Typer()
890|users_app = typer.Typer()
891|
892|app.add_typer(users_app, name="users")  # <-- Explicitly set the command group name
893|
894|
895|@users_app.callback()
896|def users():
897|    """
898|    Manage users in the app.
899|    """
900|
901|
902|@users_app.command()
903|def create(name: str):
904|    print(f"Creating user: {name}")
905|```
906|
907|Updated docs [SubCommand Name and Help](https://typer.tiangolo.com/tutorial/subcommands/name-and-help/).
908|
909|**Note**: this change will enable important features in the next release. 🤩

1127|## 0.12.1 (2024-04-05)
1128|
1129|Now you don't need to install `typer[all]`. When you install `typer` it comes with the default optional dependencies and the `typer` command.
1130|
1131|If you don't want the extra optional dependencies (`rich` and `shellingham`), you can install `typer-slim` instead.
1132|
1133|You can also install `typer-slim[standard]`, which includes the default optional dependencies, but not the `typer` command.
1134|
1135|Now the package `typer-cli` doesn't add anything on top of what `typer` has, it only depends on `typer`, and is there only for backwards compatibility, so that projects that depend on `typer-cli` can get the latest features of the `typer` command while they upgrade their dependencies to require `typer` directly.

1145|This fixes a problem that would break the `typer` installation directory when upgrading from `typer <0.12.0` to `typer >=0.12.0`, see issue [#790](https://github.com/tiangolo/typer/issues/790).

1153|## 0.12.0 (2024-03-30)
1154|
1155|In version `0.12.0`, the `typer` package depends on `typer-slim[standard]` which includes the default dependencies (instead of `typer[all]`) and `typer-cli` (that provides the `typer` command).
1156|
1157|If you don't want the extra optional dependencies (`rich` and `shellingham`), you can install `typer-slim` instead.
1158|
1159|You can also install `typer-slim[standard]`, which includes the default optional dependencies, but not the `typer` command.
1160|
1161|In version `0.12.0` the `typer-cli` package only provides the `typer` command, but the code is still in the main code, so even without installing `typer-cli`, it can be called with `python -m typer`.
1162|
1163|This approach of having `typer` depend on `typer-slim[standard]` instead of including the whole code and dependencies itself caused an issue when upgrading from `typer <0.12.0` to `typer >=0.12.0`, see issue [#790](https://github.com/tiangolo/typer/issues/790). This is fixed in version `0.12.1`.

1368|## 0.6.0 (2022-07-12)
1369|
1370|This release adds deep integrations with [Rich](https://rich.readthedocs.io/en/stable/). ✨
1371|
1372|`rich` is an optional dependency, you can install it directly or it will be included when you install with:
1373|
1374|```console
1375|$ pip install "typer[all]"
1376|```
1377|
1378|If Rich is available, it will be used to show the content from `--help` options, validation errors, and even errors in your app (exception tracebacks).
1379|
1380|There are new options to group commands, *CLI arguments*, and *CLI options*, support for [Rich Console Markup](https://rich.readthedocs.io/en/stable/markup.html), and more! 🎉
1381|
1382|### Features
1383|
1384|* ✨ Richify, add integrations with Rich everywhere. PR [#419](https://github.com/tiangolo/typer/pull/419) by [@tiangolo](https://github.com/tiangolo).
1385|    * Recommend Rich as the main information displaying tool, new docs: [Printing and Colors](https://typer.tiangolo.com/tutorial/printing/).
1386|    * For most use cases not using Rich, use plain `print()` instead of `typer.echo()` in the docs, to simplify the concepts and avoid confusions. New docs: [Printing and Colors - typer Echo](https://typer.tiangolo.com/tutorial/printing/#typer-echo).
1387|    * Define help panels for *CLI arguments*, new docs: [CLI Arguments with Help - CLI Argument help panels](https://typer.tiangolo.com/tutorial/arguments/help/#cli-argument-help-panels).
1388|    * Define help panels for *CLI options*, new docs: [CLI Options with Help - CLI Options help panels](https://typer.tiangolo.com/tutorial/options/help/#cli-options-help-panels).
1389|    * New docs for deprecating commands: [Commands - Command Help - Deprecate a Command](https://typer.tiangolo.com/tutorial/commands/help/#deprecate-a-command).
1390|    * Support for Rich Markdown in docstrings, *CLI parameters* `help`, and `epilog` with the new parameter `typer.Typer(rich_markup_mode="markdown")`, new docs: [Commands - Command Help - Rich Markdown and Markup](https://typer.tiangolo.com/tutorial/commands/help/#rich-markdown-and-markup).
1391|    * Support for Rich Markup (different from Markdown) in docstrings, *CLI parameters* `help`, and `epilog` with the new parameter `typer.Typer(rich_markup_mode="rich")`, new docs: [Commands - Command Help - Rich Markdown and Markup](https://typer.tiangolo.com/tutorial/commands/help/#rich-markdown-and-markup).
1392|    * Define help panels for *commands*, new docs: [Commands - Command Help - Help Panels](https://typer.tiangolo.com/tutorial/commands/help/#help-panels).
1393|    * New docs for setting an `epilog`, with support for Rich Markdown and Console Markup, new docs: [Commands - Command Help - Epilog](https://typer.tiangolo.com/tutorial/commands/help/#epilog).
1394|* ✨ Refactor and document handling pretty exceptions. PR [#422](https://github.com/tiangolo/typer/pull/422) by [@tiangolo](https://github.com/tiangolo).
1395|    * Add support for customizing pretty short errors, new docs: [Exceptions and Errors](https://typer.tiangolo.com/tutorial/exceptions/).
1396|* ✨ Allow configuring pretty errors when creating the Typer instance. PR [#416](https://github.com/tiangolo/typer/pull/416) by [@tiangolo](https://github.com/tiangolo).

4|

185|## Suggest Commands
186|
187|As of version 0.20.0, Typer added support for suggesting mistyped command names. This feature is **enabled by default**, but you can disable it with the parameter `suggest_commands=False`:
188|
189|{* docs_src/commands/index/tutorial005_py310.py hl[3] *}
190|
191|If a user mistypes a command, they'll see a helpful suggestion:
192|
193|<div class="termy">
194|
195|```console
196|$ uv run python main.py crate
197|
198|<font color="#C4A000">Usage: </font>main.py [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...
199|<font color="#AAAAAA">Try </font><font color="#22436D">'main.py </font><font color="#4C6A8A"><b>--help</b></font><font color="#22436D">'</font><font color="#AAAAAA"> for help.</font>
200|<font color="#CC0000">╭─ Error ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮</font>
201|<font color="#CC0000">│</font> No such command 'crate'. Did you mean 'create'?                   <font color="#CC0000">│</font>
202|<font color="#CC0000">╰───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯</font>
203|```
204|
205|</div>
206|
207|If there are multiple close matches, Typer will suggest them all. This feature uses Python's built-in `difflib.get_close_matches()` to find similar command names, making your CLI more user-friendly by helping users recover from typos.

209|## Rich Markdown and Markup
210|
211|Typer installs **Rich** to allow for more formatting in the docstrings and the `help` parameter for *CLI arguments* and *CLI options*. You will see more about it below. 👇
212|
213|/// note
214|
215|You can disable rich text formatting by setting `rich_markup_mode` to `None` for your specific app.
216|Alternatively, you can disable it globally using an environmental variable `TYPER_USE_RICH` set to `False` or `0`.
217|
218|///
219|
220|### Rich Markup
221|
222|If you set `rich_markup_mode="rich"` when creating the `typer.Typer()` app (which is the default), you will be able to use [Rich Console Markup](https://rich.readthedocs.io/en/stable/markup.html) in the docstring, and even in the help for the *CLI arguments* and options:
223|
224|{* docs_src/commands/help/tutorial004_an_py310.py hl[5,11,15:17,22,25,28] *}
225|
226|With that, you can use [Rich Console Markup](https://rich.readthedocs.io/en/stable/markup.html) to format the text in the docstring for the command `create`, make the word "`create`" bold and green, and even use an [emoji](https://rich.readthedocs.io/en/stable/markup.html#emoji).
227|
228|You can also use markup in the help for the `username` CLI Argument.
229|
230|And the same as before, the help text overwritten for the command `delete` can also use Rich Markup, the same in the CLI Argument and CLI Option.
231|

349|## Help Panels
350|
351|If you have many commands or CLI parameters, you might want to show their documentation in different panels when using the `--help` option.
352|
353|If you installed [Rich](https://rich.readthedocs.io/) as described in [Printing and Colors](../printing.md), you can configure the panel to use for each command or CLI parameter.
354|
355|### Help Panels for Commands
356|
357|To set the panel for a command you can pass the argument `rich_help_panel` with the name of the panel you want to use:
358|
359|{* docs_src/commands/help/tutorial006_py310.py hl[22,30,38,46] *}
360|
361|Commands without a panel will be shown in the default panel `Commands`, and the rest will be shown in the next panels:
362|

374|<font color="#A5A5A1">│                               shell, to copy it or customize the  │</font>
375|<font color="#A5A5A1">│                               installation.                       │</font>

394|### Help Panels for CLI Parameters
395|
396|The same way, you can configure the panels for *CLI arguments* and *CLI options* with `rich_help_panel`.
397|
398|And of course, in the same application you can also set the `rich_help_panel` for commands.
399|
400|{* docs_src/commands/help/tutorial007_an_py310.py hl[14,20,26,36] *}
401|
402|Then if you run the application you will see all the *CLI parameters* in their respective panels.
403|
404|* First the ***CLI arguments*** that don't have a panel name set in a **default** one named "`Arguments`".
405|* Next the ***CLI arguments*** with a **custom panel**. In this example named "`Secondary Arguments`".
406|* After that, the ***CLI options*** that don't have a panel in a **default** one named "`Options`".
407|* And finally, the ***CLI options*** with a **custom panel** set. In this example named "`Additional Data`".
408|
409|You can check the `--help` option for the command `create`:
410|

427|<font color="#A5A5A1">╭─ Options ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮</font>
428|<font color="#A5A5A1">│ </font><font color="#A1EFE4"><b>--force</b></font>    <font color="#AE81FF"><b>--no-force</b></font>      Force the creation of the user         │

1|# Exceptions and Errors
2|
3|When your code has errors and you run it, it will show the error and an exception.
4|
5|Typer does some tricks to help you detect those errors quickly.
6|
7|## Example Broken App
8|
9|Let's take this example broken app:
10|
11|{* docs_src/exceptions/tutorial001_py310.py hl[8] *}
12|
13|This code is broken because you can't sum a string and a number (`name + 3`).
14|
15|## Exceptions with Rich
16|
17|**Typer** will automatically use Rich to automatically show you nicely printed errors.
18|
19|It will **omit** all the parts of the traceback (the chain of things that called your function) that come from the internal parts in Typer.
20|
21|So, the error you see will be **much clearer** and simpler, to help you detect the problem in your code quickly:
22|
23|<div class="termy">
24|
25|```console
26|$ uv run python main.py
27|
28|<font color="#F92672">╭──────────────── </font><font color="#F92672"><b>Traceback (most recent call last)</b></font><font color="#F92672"> ────────────────╮</font>
29|<font color="#F92672">│</font> <font color="#A37F4E">/home/user/code/superapp/</font><font color="#F4BF75"><b>main.py</b></font>:<font color="#66D9EF">8</font> in <font color="#A6E22E">main</font>                        <font color="#F92672">│</font>
30|<font color="#F92672">│</font>                                                                   <font color="#F92672">│</font>
31|<font color="#F92672">│</font>    5                                                              <font color="#F92672">│</font>
32|<font color="#F92672">│</font>    6 <font color="#FF00FF">@app</font>.command()                                               <font color="#F92672">│</font>
33|<font color="#F92672">│</font>    7 <font color="#66D9EF">def</font> <font color="#A6E22E">main</font>(name: <font color="#A1EFE4">str</font> = <font color="#F4BF75">"morty"</font>):                               <font color="#F92672">│</font>
34|<font color="#F92672">│</font> <font color="#F92672">❱ </font> 8 │   <font color="#A1EFE4">print</font>(name + <font color="#66D9EF">3</font>)                                          <font color="#F92672">│</font>
35|<font color="#F92672">│</font>    9                                                              <font color="#F92672">│</font>
36|<font color="#F92672">│</font>    10                                                             <font color="#F92672">│</font>
37|<font color="#F92672">│</font>    11 <font color="#66D9EF">if</font> <font color="#F92672">__name__</font> == <font color="#F4BF75">"__main__"</font>:                                  <font color="#F92672">│</font>
38|<font color="#F92672">╰───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯</font>
39|<font color="#F92672"><b>TypeError: </b></font>can only concatenate str <b>(</b>not <font color="#A6E22E">"int"</font><b>)</b> to str
40|```
41|
42|</div>
43|
44|## Exceptions without Rich
45|
46|You can disable Rich globally using the environmental variable `TYPER_USE_RICH`.
47|
48|In this case, Typer will still do some tricks to show you the information **as clearly as possible**:
49|
50|<div class="termy">
51|
52|```console
53|$ uv run python main.py
54|
55|Traceback (most recent call last):
56|
57|  File "main.py", line 12, in <module>
58|    app()
59|
60|  File "main.py", line 8, in main
61|    print(name + 3)
62|
63|TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str
64|```
65|
66|</div>
67|
68|## Show Local Variables for Detailed Debugging
69|
70|When using Rich, you can get more verbose output by printing the values of the <abbr title="a variable that lives only inside a function, its value is only visible inside of it">local variables</abbr> as part of the error message.
71|
72|By default, this setting is disabled (since Typer 0.23.0) to avoid showing **delicate information**, for example a **password**, a **key** or a **token**.
73|
74|In these cases, it could be problematic if the automatic errors show the value in those local variables.
75|
76|This would be relevant in particular if your CLI application is being run on some CI (continuous integration) system that is recording the logs.
77|
78|However, if you do want to enable the setting, you can set the parameter `pretty_exceptions_show_locals=True` when creating the `typer.Typer()` application:
79|
80|{* docs_src/exceptions/tutorial002_py310.py hl[3] *}
81|
82|Now, when using Rich, you will see the error with the local variables:
83|
84|<div class="termy">
85|
86|```console
87|$ uv run python main.py
88|
89|<font color="#F92672">╭──────────────── </font><font color="#F92672"><b>Traceback (most recent call last)</b></font><font color="#F92672"> ────────────────╮</font>
90|<font color="#F92672">│</font> <font color="#A37F4E">/home/user/code/superapp/</font><font color="#F4BF75"><b>main.py</b></font>:<font color="#66D9EF">5</font> in <font color="#A6E22E">main</font>                        <font color="#F92672">│</font>
91|<font color="#F92672">│</font>                                                                   <font color="#F92672">│</font>
92|<font color="#F92672">│</font>    2                                                              <font color="#F92672">│</font>
93|<font color="#F92672">│</font>    3                                                              <font color="#F92672">│</font>
94|<font color="#F92672">│</font>    4 <font color="#66D9EF">def</font> <font color="#A6E22E">main</font>(name: <font color="#A1EFE4">str</font> = <font color="#F4BF75">"morty"</font>):                               <font color="#F92672">│</font>
95|<font color="#F92672">│</font> <font color="#F92672">❱ </font> 5 │   <font color="#A1EFE4">print</font>(name + <font color="#66D9EF">3</font>)                                          <font color="#F92672">│</font>
96|<font color="#F92672">│</font>    6                                                              <font color="#F92672">│</font>
97|<font color="#F92672">│</font>    7                                                              <font color="#F92672">│</font>
98|<font color="#F92672">│</font>    8 <font color="#66D9EF">if</font> <font color="#F92672">__name__</font> == <font color="#F4BF75">"__main__"</font>:                                   <font color="#F92672">│</font>
99|<font color="#F92672">│</font>                                                                   <font color="#F92672">│</font>
100|<font color="#F92672">│</font> <font color="#F4BF75">╭──── locals ────╮</font>                                                <font color="#F92672">│</font>
101|<font color="#F92672">│</font> <font color="#F4BF75">│</font> name = <font color="#F4BF75">'morty'</font> <font color="#F4BF75">│</font>                                                <font color="#F92672">│</font>
102|<font color="#F92672">│</font> <font color="#F4BF75">╰────────────────╯</font>                                                <font color="#F92672">│</font>
103|<font color="#F92672">╰───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯</font>
104|<font color="#F92672"><b>TypeError: </b></font>can only concatenate str <b>(</b>not <font color="#A6E22E">"int"</font><b>)</b> to str
105|```
106|
107|</div>
108|
109|Being able to see the values of local variables is very **helpful** to diagnose, **debug**, and fix problems.
110|
111|But you should only enable it if you're not dealing with delicate information.
112|
113|## Disable Short Output
114|
115|If you want to show the full exception, including the internal parts in Typer, you can use the parameter `pretty_exceptions_short=False`:
116|

36|
37|## What is a **CLI argument**
38|
39|Here we will use the word **CLI argument** to refer to **CLI parameters** passed in some specific order to the CLI application. By default, they are *required*.
40|
41|If you go to your terminal and type:
42|
43|<div class="termy">
44|
45|```bash
46|$ ls ./myproject
47|
48|first-steps.md  intro.md
49|```
50|
51|</div>
52|
53|`ls` will show the contents of the directory `./myproject`.
54|
55|* `ls` is the *program* (or "command", "CLI app").
56|* `./myproject` is a *CLI argument*, in this case it refers to the path of a directory.
57|
58|They are a bit different from **CLI options** that you will see later below.
59|
60|## Add a CLI argument
61|
62|Update the previous example with an argument `name`:
63|
64|{* docs_src/first_steps/tutorial002_py310.py hl[4,5] *}

66|<div class="termy">

68|```console

144|/// tip
145|
146|Notice that the order is important. The last name has to go after the first name.

149|

155|
156|///
157|
158|## What is a **CLI option**
159|
160|Here we will use the word **CLI option** to refer to *CLI parameters* passed to the CLI application with a specific name. For example, if you go to your terminal and type:
161|
162|<div class="termy">
163|
164|```console
165|$ ls ./myproject --size
166|
167|12 first-steps.md   4 intro.md
168|```
169|
170|</div>
171|
172|`ls` will show the contents of the directory `./myproject` with their `size`.
173|
174|* `ls` is the *program* (or "command", "CLI app").
175|* `./myproject` is a *CLI argument*.
176|* `--size` is an optional *CLI option*.
177|
178|The program knows it has to show the size because it sees `--size`, not because of the order.
179|
180|A *CLI option* like `--size` doesn't depend on the order like a *CLI argument*.
181|
182|So, if you put the `--size` *before* the *CLI argument*, it still works (in fact, that's the most common way of doing it):
183|
184|<div class="termy">
185|
186|```console
187|$ ls --size ./myproject
188|
189|12 first-steps.md   4 intro.md
190|```
191|
192|</div>
193|
194|The main visual difference between a *CLI option* and a *CLI argument* is that the *CLI option* has `--` prepended to the name, like in "`--size`".
195|
196|A *CLI option* doesn't depend on the order because it has a predefined name (here it's `--size`). This is because the CLI app is looking specifically for a literal `--size` parameter (also known as "flag" or "switch"), with that specific "name" (here the specific name is "`--size`"). The CLI app will check if you typed it or not, it will be actively looking for `--size` even if you didn't type it (to check if it's there or not).
197|
198|In contrast, the CLI app is not actively looking for the *CLI argument* with a text "`./myproject`", it has no way to know if you would type `./myproject` or `./my-super-awesome-project` or anything else. It's just waiting to get whatever you give it. The only way to know that you refer to a specific *CLI argument* is because of the order. The same way that it knows that the first *CLI argument* was the `name` and the second was the `lastname`, but if you mixed the order, it wouldn't be able to handle it.
199|
200|Instead, with a *CLI option*, the order doesn't matter.
201|
202|Also, by default, a *CLI option* is *optional* (not *required*).
203|
204|So, by default:
205|
206|* A *CLI argument* is **required**
207|* A *CLI option* is **optional**
208|
209|But the *required* and *optional* defaults can be changed.
210|
211|So, the main and **most important** difference is that:
212|
213|* *CLI options* **start with `--`** and don't depend on the order
214|* *CLI arguments* depend on the **sequence order**
215|
216|/// tip
217|
218|In this example above the *CLI option* `--size` is just a "flag" or "switch" that will contain a boolean value, `True` or `False`, depending on if it was added to the command or not.
219|
220|This one doesn't receive any values. But *CLI options* can also receive values like *CLI arguments*. You'll see how later.
221|

392|
393|## Arguments, options, parameters, optional, required
394|
395|Be aware that these terms refer to multiple things depending on the context, and sadly, those "contexts" mix frequently, so it's easy to get confused.
396|
397|### In Python
398|
399|In Python, the names of the variables in a function, like `name` and `lastname`:
400|
401|```Python
402|def main(name: str, lastname: str = ""):
403|    pass
404|```
405|
406|are called "Python function parameters" or "Python function arguments".
407|
408|/// note | Technical Details
409|
410|There's actually a very small distinction in Python between "parameter" and "argument".
411|
412|It's quite technical... and somewhat pedantic.
413|
414|*Parameter* refers to the variable name in a function *declaration*. Like:
415|
416|```
417|def bring_person(name: str, lastname: str = ""):
418|    pass
419|```
420|
421|*Argument* refers to the value passed when *calling* a function. Like:
422|
423|```
424|person = bring_person("Camila", lastname="Gutiérrez")
425|```
426|
427|...but you will probably see them used interchangeably in most of the places (including here).
428|
429|///
430|
431|#### Python default values
432|
433|In Python, in a function, a parameter with a *default value* like `lastname` in:
434|
435|```Python
436|def main(name: str, lastname: str = ""):
437|    pass
438|```
439|
440|is considered an "optional parameter" (or "optional argument").
441|
442|The default value can be anything, like `""` or `None`.
443|
444|And a parameter like `name`, that doesn't have a default value, is considered *required*.
445|
446|### In CLIs
447|
448|When talking about command line interface applications, the words **"argument"** and **"parameter"** are commonly used to refer to that data passed to a CLI app, those parameters.
449|
450|But those words **don't imply** anything about the data being required, needing to be passed in a certain order, nor having a flag like `--lastname`.
451|
452|The parameters that come with a name like `--lastname` (and optionally a value) are commonly optional, not required. So, when talking about CLIs it's common to call them **optional arguments** or **optional parameters**. Sometimes these *optional parameters* that start with `--` are also called a **flag** or a **switch**.
453|
454|In reality, the parameters that require an order can be made *optional* too. And the ones that come with a flag (like `--lastname`) can be *required* too.
455|
456|### In **Typer**
457|
458|To try and make it a bit easier, we'll normally use the words "parameter" or "argument" to refer to "Python functions parameters" or "Python functions arguments".
459|
460|We'll use ***CLI argument*** to refer to those *CLI parameters* that depend on the specific order. That are **required** by default.
461|
462|And we'll use ***CLI option*** to refer to those *CLI parameters* that depend on a name that starts with `--` (like `--lastname`). That are **optional** by default.
463|
464|We will use ***CLI parameter*** to refer to both, *CLI arguments* and *CLI options*.
465|
466|## The `typer` Command
467|
468|When you [activate the project's virtual environment](install.md#activate-the-virtual-environment), the `typer` command installed in that project becomes available directly in your shell.
469|
470|After you install completion for it, this `typer` command allows you to run your scripts with ✨ auto completion ✨ in your terminal.
471|
472|As an alternative to running with Python:
473|
474|<div class="termy">
475|
476|```console
477|$ uv run python main.py
478|
479|Hello World
480|```
481|
482|</div>
483|
484|You can run with the `typer` command:
485|
486|<div class="termy">
487|
488|```console
489|$ typer main.py run
490|
491|Hello World
492|```
493|
494|</div>
495|
496|...and it will give you auto completion in your terminal when you hit <kbd>TAB</kbd> for all your code.
497|
498|So you can use it to have auto completion for your own scripts as you continue with the tutorial.
499|
500|/// tip
501|
502|Your CLI application built with **Typer** won't need the `typer` command to have auto completion once you create a Python package.
503|
504|But for short scripts and for learning, before creating a Python package, it might be useful.

33|---
34|
35|Typer is a library for building <abbr title="command line interface, programs executed from a terminal">CLI</abbr> applications that users will **love using** and developers will **love creating**. Based on Python type hints.
36|
37|It's also a command line tool to run scripts, automatically converting them to CLI applications.
38|
39|The key features are:
40|
41|* **Intuitive to write**: Great editor support. <abbr title="also known as auto-complete, autocompletion, IntelliSense">Completion</abbr> everywhere. Less time debugging. Designed to be easy to use and learn. Less time reading docs.
42|* **Easy to use**: It's easy to use for the final users. Automatic help, and automatic completion for all shells.
43|* **Short**: Minimize code duplication. Multiple features from each parameter declaration. Fewer bugs.
44|* **Start simple**: The simplest example adds only 2 lines of code to your app: **1 import, 1 function call**.
45|* **Grow large**: Grow in complexity as much as you want, create arbitrarily complex trees of commands and groups of subcommands, with options and arguments.
46|* **Run scripts**: Typer includes a `typer` command/program that you can use to run scripts, automatically converting them to CLIs, even if they don't use Typer internally.
47|
48|## FastAPI of CLIs
49|
50|**Typer** is [FastAPI](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com)'s little sibling, it's the FastAPI of CLIs.
51|

53|
54|First, [install `uv`](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/), and then add **Typer** to your project:

57|

59|$ uv add typer
60|---> 100%
61|```
62|
63|</div>

65|This installs both the Typer library and the `typer` command in the project's virtual environment. To use `typer` directly with shell completion, [activate the project environment and install completion](tutorial/install.md#activate-the-virtual-environment).

67|If you prefer to use `pip`, install `typer` inside a virtual environment. See the [installation guide](tutorial/install.md) for the alternative steps.

184|## Example upgrade

186|This was the simplest example possible.

190|### An example with two subcommands
191|
192|Modify the file `main.py`.
193|
194|Create a `typer.Typer()` app, and create two subcommands with their parameters.
195|
196|```Python hl_lines="3  6  11  20"
197|import typer
198|
199|app = typer.Typer()
200|
201|
202|@app.command()
203|def hello(name: str):
204|    print(f"Hello {name}")
205|
206|
207|@app.command()
208|def goodbye(name: str, formal: bool = False):
209|    if formal:
210|        print(f"Goodbye Ms. {name}. Have a good day.")
211|    else:
212|        print(f"Bye {name}!")
213|
214|
215|if __name__ == "__main__":
216|    app()
217|```

219|And that will:
220|
221|* Explicitly create a `typer.Typer` app.
222|    * The previous `typer.run` actually creates one implicitly for you.
223|* Add two subcommands with `@app.command()`.
224|* Execute the `app()` itself, as if it was a function (instead of `typer.run`).

296|╰───────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
297|
298|// Automatic --formal and --no-formal for the bool option 🎉
299|```
300|
301|</div>
302|
303|Now you can try out the new command line application:
304|
305|<div class="termy">
306|
307|```console
308|// Use it with the hello command
309|
310|$ uv run python main.py hello Camila
311|
312|Hello Camila
313|
314|// And with the goodbye command
315|
316|$ uv run python main.py goodbye Camila
317|
318|Bye Camila!
319|
320|// And with --formal
321|
322|$ uv run python main.py goodbye --formal Camila
323|
324|Goodbye Ms. Camila. Have a good day.
325|```
326|
327|</div>
328|
329|**Note**: If your app only has one command, by default the command name is **omitted** in usage: `python main.py Camila`. However, when there are multiple commands, you must **explicitly include the command name**: `python main.py hello Camila`. See [One or Multiple Commands](https://typer.tiangolo.com/tutorial/commands/one-or-multiple/) for more details.
330|
331|### Recap
332|
333|In summary, you declare **once** the types of parameters (*CLI arguments* and *CLI options*) as function parameters.
334|
335|You do that with standard modern Python types.
336|
337|You don't have to learn a new syntax, the methods or classes of a specific library, etc.
338|
339|Just standard **Python**.
340|
341|For example, for an `int`:
342|
343|```Python
344|total: int
345|```
346|
347|or for a `bool` flag:
348|
349|```Python
350|force: bool
351|```
352|
353|And similarly for **files**, **paths**, **enums** (choices), etc. And there are tools to create **groups of subcommands**, add metadata, extra **validation**, etc.
354|
355|**You get**: great editor support, including **completion** and **type checks** everywhere.
356|
357|**Your users get**: automatic **`--help`**, **auto-completion** in their terminal (Bash, Zsh, Fish, PowerShell) when they install your package or when using the `typer` command.
358|
359|For a more complete example including more features, see the <a href="https://typer.tiangolo.com/tutorial/">Tutorial - User Guide</a>.
360|
361|## Dependencies
362|
363|**Typer** requires only a few dependencies (most are tiny):
364|
365|* [`rich`](https://rich.readthedocs.io/en/stable/index.html): to show nicely formatted errors automatically.
366|* [`shellingham`](https://github.com/sarugaku/shellingham): to automatically detect the current shell when installing completion.
367|* [`annotated-doc`](https://github.com/fastapi/annotated-doc): to generate documentation from Python type annotations.
368|* [`colorama`](https://github.com/tartley/colorama) (only on Windows): for producing colored terminal text on Windows.
369|
370|### Click code
371|
372|Typer used to depend on [Click](https://click.palletsprojects.com/) as well, a popular tool for building CLIs in Python.
373|
374|Since version 0.26.0, Typer has vendored Click (included Click's source code internally, instead of installing it as a third party package) and has unified the code interactions between Typer and the embedded Click source code for easier maintainability in the future.
375|
376|Note that some Click functionality will not be available anymore in the future, as we continue to improve and extend Typer's codebase.
377|
378|### `typer-slim`
379|
380|There used to be a slimmed-down version of Typer called `typer-slim`, which didn't include the dependencies `rich` and `shellingham`, nor the `typer` command.
381|
382|However, since version 0.22.0, we have stopped supporting this, and `typer-slim` now simply installs (all of) Typer.
383|
384|If you want to disable Rich globally, you can set an environmental variable `TYPER_USE_RICH` to `False` or `0`.
385|
