1|# Building a Package
2|
3|When you create a CLI program with **Typer** you probably want to create your own Python package.
4|
5|That's what allows your users to install it and have it as an independent program that they can use in their terminal.
6|
7|And that's also required for shell auto completion to work (unless you use your program through the `typer` command).
8|
9|Nowadays, there are several ways and tools to create Python packages (what you install with `pip install something` or `uv add something`).
10|
11|You might even have your favorite already.
12|
13|Here's a very opinionated, short guide, showing one of the alternative ways of creating a Python package with a **Typer** app, from scratch.
14|
15|/// tip
16|
17|If you already have a favorite way of creating Python packages, feel free to skip this.
18|
19|///
20|
21|## Prerequisites
22|
23|For this guide we'll use [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/).
24|
25|uv's docs are great, so go ahead, check them and install it.
26|
27|## Create a project
28|
29|Let's say we want to create a CLI application called `portal-gun`.
30|
31|To make sure your package doesn't collide with the package created by someone else, we'll name it with a prefix of your name.
32|
33|So, if your name is Rick, we'll call it `rick-portal-gun`.
34|
35|Create a project with uv:
36|
37|<div class="termy">
38|
39|```console
40|$ uv init --package rick-portal-gun
41|
42|Initialized project `rick-portal-gun` at `/home/rick-portal-gun`
43|
44|// Enter the new project directory
45|cd ./rick-portal-gun
46|```
47|
48|</div>
49|
50|## Dependencies and environment
51|
52|Add `typer` to your dependencies:
53|
54|<div class="termy">
55|
56|```console
57|$ uv add typer
58|
59|// It creates a virtual environment for your project
60|Using CPython 3.14.0 interpreter at: /location/of/python/
61|Creating virtual environment at: .venv
62|
63|Resolved 9 packages in 21ms
64|      Built rick-portal-gun @ file:/home/rick-portal-gun
65|Prepared 1 package in 19ms
66|Installed 9 packages in 34ms
67| + colorama==0.4.6
68| + markdown-it-py==4.0.0
69| + mdurl==0.1.2
70| + pygments==2.19.2
71| + rich==14.2.0
72| + rick-portal-gun==0.1.0 (from file:/home/rick-portal-gun)
73| + shellingham==1.5.4
74| + typer==0.21.0
75| + typing-extensions==4.15.0
76|
77|
78|// Activate that new virtual environment
79|$ source .venv/bin/activate
80|
81|// Open an editor using this new environment, for example VS Code
82|$ code ./
83|```
84|
85|</div>
86|
87|You can see that you have a generated project structure that looks like:
88|
89|```
90|.
91|├── pyproject.toml
92|├── README.md
93|├── src
94|│   └── rick_portal_gun
95|│     └── __init__.py
96|└── uv.lock
97|```
98|
99|## Create your app
100|
101|Now let's create an extremely simple **Typer** app.
102|
103|Create a file `src/rick_portal_gun/main.py` with:
104|
105|```Python
106|import typer
107|
108|
109|app = typer.Typer()
110|
111|
112|@app.callback()
113|def callback():
114|    """
115|    Awesome Portal Gun
116|    """
117|
118|
119|@app.command()
120|def shoot():
121|    """
122|    Shoot the portal gun
123|    """
124|    typer.echo("Shooting portal gun")
125|
126|
127|@app.command()
128|def load():
129|    """
130|    Load the portal gun
131|    """
132|    typer.echo("Loading portal gun")
133|```
134|
135|/// tip
136|
137|As we are creating an installable Python package, there's no need to add a section with `if __name__ == "__main__":`.
138|
139|///
140|
141|## Modify the README
142|
143|Let's change the README to have something like:
144|
145|```Markdown
146|# Portal Gun
147|
148|The awesome Portal Gun
149|```
150|
151|## Add a "script"
152|
153|We are creating a Python package that can be installed with `uv add` or `pip install`.
154|
155|But we want it to provide a CLI program that can be executed in the shell.
156|
157|To do that, we add a configuration to the `pyproject.toml` in the section `[project.scripts]`:
158|
159|```TOML hl_lines="12 13"
160|[project]
161|name = "rick-portal-gun"
162|version = "0.1.0"
163|description = "Add your description here"
164|readme = "README.md"
165|authors = ["Rick Sanchez <rick@example.com>"]
166|requires-python = ">=3.14"
167|dependencies = [
168|    "typer>=0.21.0",
169|]
170|
171|[project.scripts]
172|rick-portal-gun = "rick_portal_gun.main:app"
173|
174|[build-system]
175|requires = ["uv_build>=0.8.14,<0.9.0"]
176|build-backend = "uv_build"
177|```
178|
179|Here's what that line means:
180|
181|`rick-portal-gun`: will be the name of the CLI program. That's how we will call it in the terminal once it is installed. Like:
182|
183|<div class="termy">
184|
185|```console
186|$ rick-portal-gun
187|
188|// Something happens here ✨
189|```
190|
191|</div>
192|
193|`rick_portal_gun.main`, in the part `"rick_portal_gun.main:app"`, with underscores, refers to the Python module to import. That's what someone would use in a section like:
194|
195|```Python
196|from rick_portal_gun.main import # something goes here
197|```
198|
199|The `app` in `"rick_portal_gun.main:app"` is the thing to import from the module, and to call as a function, like:
200|
201|```Python
202|from rick_portal_gun.main import app
203|
204|app()
205|```
206|
207|That config section tells uv that when this package is installed, we want it to create a command line program called `rick-portal-gun`.
208|
209|And that the object to call (like a function) is the one in the variable `app` inside of the module `rick_portal_gun.main`.
210|
211|## Install your package
212|
213|That's what we need to create a package.
214|
215|You can now install it:
216|
217|<div class="termy">
218|
219|```console
220|$ uv sync
221|
222|Resolved 10 packages in 1ms
223|      Built rick-portal-gun @ file:/home/rick-portal-gun
224|Prepared 1 package in 18ms
225|Uninstalled 1 package in 1ms
226|Installed 1 package in 13ms
227| ~ rick-portal-gun==0.1.0 (from file:/home/rick-portal-gun)
228|
229|```
230|
231|</div>
232|
233|## Try your CLI program
234|
235|Your package is installed in the environment created by uv, but you can already use it.
236|
237|<div class="termy">
238|
239|```console
240|// You can use the which program to check which rick-portal-gun program is available (if any)
241|$ which rick-portal-gun
242|
243|// You get the one from your environment
244|/home/rick-portal-gun/.venv/bin/rick-portal-gun
245|
246|// Try it
247|$ rick-portal-gun --help
248|
249|// You get all the standard help
250|Usage: rick-portal-gun [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...
251|
252|  Awesome Portal Gun
253|
254|Options:
255|  --install-completion  Install completion for the current shell.
256|  --show-completion     Show completion for the current shell, to copy it or customize the installation.
257|
258|  --help                Show this message and exit.
259|
260|Commands:
261|  shoot  Shoot the portal gun
262|  load   Load the portal gun
263|```
264|
265|</div>
266|
267|## Create a wheel package
268|
269|Python packages have a standard format called a "wheel". It's a file that ends in `.whl`.
270|
271|You can create a wheel with uv:
272|
273|<div class="termy">
274|
275|```console
276|$ uv build
277|
278|Building source distribution (uv build backend)...
279|Building wheel from source distribution (uv build backend)...
280|Successfully built dist/rick_portal_gun-0.1.0.tar.gz
281|Successfully built dist/rick_portal_gun-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl
282|```
283|
284|</div>
285|
286|After that, if you check in your project directory, you should now have a couple of extra files at `./dist/`:
287|
288|``` hl_lines="3 4"
289|.
290|├── dist
291|│   ├── rick_portal_gun-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl
292|│   └── rick-portal-gun-0.1.0.tar.gz
293|├── pyproject.toml
294|├── README.md
295|├── ...
296|```
297|
298|The `.whl` is the wheel file. You can send that wheel file to anyone and they can use it to install your program (we'll see how to upload it to PyPI in a bit).
299|
300|## Test your wheel package
301|
302|Now you can open another terminal and install that package as an isolated command-line tool with:
303|
304|<div class="termy">
305|
306|```console
307|$ uv tool install /home/rick/rick-portal-gun/dist/rick_portal_gun-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl
308|
309|---> 100%
310|```
311|
312|</div>
313|
314|/// tip
315|
316|`uv` installs the tool in its own isolated environment, avoiding conflicts with your projects and system Python.
317|
318|///
319|
320|Now you have your CLI program installed. And you can use it freely:
321|
322|<div class="termy">
323|
324|```console
325|$ rick-portal-gun shoot
326|
327|// It works 🎉
328|Shooting portal gun
329|```
330|
331|</div>
332|
333|Having it installed globally (and not in a single environment), you can now install completion globally for it:
334|
335|<div class="termy">
336|
337|```console
338|$ rick-portal-gun --install-completion
339|
340|zsh completion installed in /home/rick/.zshrc.
341|Completion will take effect once you restart the terminal.
342|```
343|
344|</div>
345|
346|/// tip
347|
348|If you want to remove completion you can just delete the added line in that file.
349|
350|///
351|
352|And after you restart the terminal you will get completion for your new CLI program:
353|
354|<div class="termy">
355|
356|```console
357|$ rick-portal-gun [TAB][TAB]
358|
359|// You get completion for your CLI program ✨
360|load   -- Load the portal gun
361|shoot  -- Shoot the portal gun
362|```
363|
364|</div>
365|
366|## Support `python -m` (optional)
367|
368|You may have seen that you can call many Python modules as scripts with `python -m some-module`.
369|
370|For example, one way to call `pip` is:
371|
372|<div class="termy">
373|
374|```console
375|$ pip install fastapi
376|```
377|
378|</div>
379|
380|But you can also call Python with the `-m` *CLI Option* and pass a module for it to execute as if it was a script, like:
381|
382|<div class="termy">
383|
384|```console
385|$ python -m pip install fastapi
386|```
387|
388|</div>
389|
390|Here we pass `pip` as the value for `-m`, so, Python will execute the module `pip` as if it was a script. And then it will pass the rest of the *CLI Parameters* (`install fastapi`) to it.
391|
392|These two are more or less equivalent, the `install fastapi` will be passed to `pip`.
393|
394|/// tip
395|
396|In the case of `pip`, in many occasions it's actually recommended that you run it with `python -m`, because if you create a virtual environment with its own `python`, that will ensure that you use the `pip` from *that* environment.
397|
398|///
399|
400|### Add a `__main__.py`
401|
402|You can support that same style of calling the package/module for your own package, simply by adding a file `__main__.py`.
403|
404|Python will look for that file and execute it.
405|
406|The file would live right beside `__init__.py` and `main.py`:
407|
408|``` hl_lines="7"
409|.
410|├── pyproject.toml
411|├── README.md
412|├── src
413|│   └── rick_portal_gun
414|│     ├── __init__.py
415|│     ├── __main__.py
416|│     └── main.py
417|└── uv.lock
418|```
419|
420|No other file has to import it, you don't have to reference it in your `pyproject.toml` or anything else, it just works by default, as it is standard Python behavior.
421|
422|Then in that file you can execute your **Typer** program:
423|
424|```Python
425|from .main import app
426|
427|app()
428|```
429|
430|Now, after installing your package, if you call it with `python -m` it will work:
431|
432|<div class="termy">
433|
434|```console
435|$ python -m rick_portal_gun --help
436|
437|Usage: python -m rick_portal_gun [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...
438|
439|  Awesome Portal Gun
440|
441|Options:
442|  --install-completion  Install completion for the current shell.
443|  --show-completion     Show completion for the current shell, to copy it or customize the installation.
444|
445|  --help                Show this message and exit.
446|
447|Commands:
448|  shoot  Shoot the portal gun
449|  load   Load the portal gun
450|```
451|
452|</div>
453|
454|/// tip
455|
456|Notice that you have to pass the importable version of the package name, so `rick_portal_gun` instead of `rick-portal-gun`.
457|
458|///
459|
460|That works! 🚀
461|
462|### Autocompletion and `python -m`
463|
464|Have in mind that TAB completion (shell auto-completion) won't work when using `python -m`.
465|
466|Auto-completion depends on the name of the program called, it's tied to each specific program name.
467|
468|So, to have shell completion for `rick-portal-gun` you would have to call it directly:
469|
470|<div class="termy">
471|
472|```console
473|$ rick-portal-gun [TAB][TAB]
474|```
475|
476|</div>
477|
478|But you can still support `python -m` for the cases where it's useful.
479|
480|## Publish to PyPI (optional)
481|
482|You can publish that new package to [PyPI](https://pypi.org/) to make it public, so others can install it easily.
483|
484|So, go ahead and create an account there (it's free).
485|
486|### PyPI API token
487|
488|To do it, you first need to configure a PyPI auth token.
489|
490|Login to [PyPI](https://pypi.org/).
491|
492|And then go to [https://pypi.org/manage/account/token/](https://pypi.org/manage/account/token/) to create a new token.
493|
494|Let's say your new API token is:
495|
496|```
497|pypi-wubalubadubdub-deadbeef1234
498|```
499|
500|Now configure uv to use this token by setting an environment variable:
501|
502|<div class="termy">
503|
504|```console
505|$ export UV_PUBLISH_TOKEN=pypi-wubalubadubdub-deadbeef1234
506|// It won't show any output, but it's already configured
507|```
508|
509|</div>
510|
511|### Publish to PyPI
512|
513|Now you can publish your package.
514|
515|<div class="termy">
516|
517|```console
518|$ uv publish
519|
520|Publishing 2 files https://upload.pypi.org/legacy/
521|Uploading rick_portal_gun-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl (2.3KiB)
522|Uploading rick_portal_gun-0.1.0.tar.gz (841.0B)
523|```
524|
525|</div>
526|
527|Now you can go to PyPI and check your projects at [https://pypi.org/manage/projects/](https://pypi.org/manage/projects/).
528|
529|You should now see your new "rick-portal-gun" package.
530|
531|### Install from PyPI
532|
533|Now to see that we can install it from PyPI, open another terminal, and uninstall the currently installed package.
534|
535|<div class="termy">
536|
537|```console
538|$ uv tool uninstall rick-portal-gun
539|```
540|
541|</div>
542|
543|And now install it again, but this time using just the name, so that `uv` pulls it from PyPI:
544|
545|<div class="termy">
546|
547|```console
548|$ uv tool install rick-portal-gun
549|```
550|
551|</div>
552|
553|And now test the newly installed package from PyPI:
554|
555|<div class="termy">
556|
557|```console
558|$ rick-portal-gun load
559|
560|// It works! 🎉
561|Loading portal gun
562|```
563|
564|</div>
565|
566|## Generate docs
567|
568|You can use the `typer` command to generate docs for your package that you can put in your `README.md`:
569|
570|<div class="termy">
571|
572|```console
573|$ typer rick_portal_gun.main utils docs --output README.md --name rick-portal-gun
574|
575|Docs saved to: README.md
576|```
577|
578|</div>
579|
580|You just have to pass it the module to import (`rick_portal_gun.main`) and it will detect the `typer.Typer` app automatically.
581|
582|By specifying the `--name` of the program it will be able to use it while generating the docs.
583|
584|### Publish a new version with the docs
585|
586|Now you can publish a new version with the updated docs.
587|
588|For that you need to first increase the version in `pyproject.toml`:
589|
590|```TOML hl_lines="3"
591|[project]
592|name = "rick-portal-gun"
593|version = "0.2.0"
594|description = "Add your description here"
595|readme = "README.md"
596|authors = ["Rick Sanchez <rick@example.com>"]
597|requires-python = ">=3.14"
598|dependencies = [
599|    "typer>=0.21.0",
600|]
601|
602|[project.scripts]
603|rick-portal-gun = "rick_portal_gun.main:app"
604|
605|[build-system]
606|requires = ["uv_build>=0.8.14,<0.9.0"]
607|build-backend = "uv_build"
608|```
609|
610|And then build and publish again:
611|
612|<div class="termy">
613|
614|```console
615|$ uv build
616|$ uv publish
617|
618|Publishing 2 files https://upload.pypi.org/legacy/
619|Uploading rick_portal_gun-0.2.0-py3-none-any.whl (2.3KiB)
620|Uploading rick_portal_gun-0.2.0.tar.gz (840.0B)
621|```
622|
623|</div>
624|
625|And now you can go to PyPI, to the project page, and reload it, and it will now have your new generated docs.
626|
627|## What's next
628|
629|This is a very simple guide. You could add many more steps.
630|
631|For example, you should use [Git](https://git-scm.com/), the version control system, to save your code.
632|
633|You could use [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) to manage your installed CLI Python programs in isolated environments.
634|
635|Maybe use automatic formatting with [Ruff](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/).
636|
637|You'll probably want to publish your code as open source to [GitHub](https://github.com/).
638|
639|And then you could integrate a <abbr title="Continuous Integration">CI</abbr> tool to run your tests and deploy your package automatically.
640|
641|And there's a long etc. But now you have the basics and you can continue on your own. 🚀

25|---
26|
27|Typer is a library for building <abbr title="command line interface, programs executed from a terminal">CLI</abbr> applications that users will **love using** and developers will **love creating**. Based on Python type hints.
28|
29|It's also a command line tool to run scripts, automatically converting them to CLI applications.
30|
31|The key features are:
32|
33|* **Intuitive to write**: Great editor support. <abbr title="also known as auto-complete, autocompletion, IntelliSense">Completion</abbr> everywhere. Less time debugging. Designed to be easy to use and learn. Less time reading docs.
34|* **Easy to use**: It's easy to use for the final users. Automatic help, and automatic completion for all shells.
35|* **Short**: Minimize code duplication. Multiple features from each parameter declaration. Fewer bugs.
36|* **Start simple**: The simplest example adds only 2 lines of code to your app: **1 import, 1 function call**.
37|* **Grow large**: Grow in complexity as much as you want, create arbitrarily complex trees of commands and groups of subcommands, with options and arguments.
38|* **Run scripts**: Typer includes a `typer` command/program that you can use to run scripts, automatically converting them to CLIs, even if they don't use Typer internally.
39|
40|## FastAPI of CLIs
41|
42|**Typer** is [FastAPI](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com)'s little sibling, it's the FastAPI of CLIs.
43|
44|## Installation
45|
46|First, [install `uv`](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/), and then add **Typer** to your project:
47|
48|<div class="termy">
49|
50|```console
51|$ uv add typer
52|---> 100%
53|```
54|
55|</div>
56|
57|This installs both the Typer library and the `typer` command in the project's virtual environment. To use `typer` directly with shell completion, [activate the project environment and install completion](tutorial/install.md#activate-the-virtual-environment).
58|
59|If you prefer to use `pip`, install `typer` inside a virtual environment. See the [installation guide](tutorial/install.md) for the alternative steps.
60|
61|## Example
62|
63|### The absolute minimum
64|
65|* Create a file `main.py` with:
66|
67|```Python
68|def main(name: str):
69|    print(f"Hello {name}")
70|```
71|
72|This script doesn't even use Typer internally. But you can use the `typer` command to run it as a CLI application.
73|
74|### Run it
75|
76|Run your application with the `typer` command:
77|
78|<div class="termy">
79|
80|```console
81|// Run your application
82|$ typer main.py run
83|
84|// You get a nice error, you are missing 'name'
85|Usage: typer [PATH_OR_MODULE] run [OPTIONS] {name}
86|Try 'typer [PATH_OR_MODULE] run --help' for help.
87|╭─ Error ───────────────────────────────────────────╮
88|│ Missing argument 'name'.                          │
89|╰───────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
90|
91|
92|// You get a --help for free
93|$ typer main.py run --help
94|
95|Usage: typer [PATH_OR_MODULE] run [OPTIONS] {name}
96|
97|Run the provided Typer app.
98|
99|╭─ Arguments ───────────────────────────────────────╮
100|│ *    name      <str>  [required]                  │
101|╰───────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
102|╭─ Options ─────────────────────────────────────────╮
103|│ --help          Show this message and exit.       │
104|╰───────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
105|
106|// Now pass the 'name' argument
107|$ typer main.py run Camila
108|
109|Hello Camila
110|
111|// It works! 🎉
112|```
113|
114|</div>
115|
116|This is the simplest use case, not even using Typer internally, but it can already be quite useful for simple scripts.
117|
118|**Note**: auto-completion works when you create a Python package and run it with `--install-completion` or when you use the `typer` command.
119|
120|## Use Typer in your code
121|
122|Now let's start using Typer in your own code, update `main.py` with:
123|
124|```Python
125|import typer
126|
127|
128|def main(name: str):
129|    print(f"Hello {name}")
130|
131|
132|if __name__ == "__main__":
133|    typer.run(main)
134|```
135|
136|Now you could run it with Python directly:
137|
138|<div class="termy">
139|
140|```console
141|// Run your application
142|$ uv run python main.py
143|
144|// You get a nice error, you are missing 'name'
145|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS] {name}
146|Try 'main.py --help' for help.
147|╭─ Error ───────────────────────────────────────────╮
148|│ Missing argument 'name'.                          │
149|╰───────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
150|
151|
152|// You get a --help for free
153|$ uv run python main.py --help
154|
155|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS] {name}
156|
157|╭─ Arguments ───────────────────────────────────────╮
158|│ *    name      <str>  [required]                  │
159|╰───────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
160|╭─ Options ─────────────────────────────────────────╮
161|│ --help          Show this message and exit.       │
162|╰───────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
163|
164|// Now pass the 'name' argument
165|$ uv run python main.py Camila
166|
167|Hello Camila
168|
169|// It works! 🎉
170|```
171|
172|</div>
173|
174|**Note**: you can also call this same script with the `typer` command, but you don't need to.
175|
176|## Example upgrade
177|
178|This was the simplest example possible.
179|
180|Now let's see one a bit more complex.
181|
182|### An example with two subcommands
183|
184|Modify the file `main.py`.
185|
186|Create a `typer.Typer()` app, and create two subcommands with their parameters.
187|
188|```Python hl_lines="3  6  11  20"
189|import typer
190|
191|app = typer.Typer()
192|
193|
194|@app.command()
195|def hello(name: str):
196|    print(f"Hello {name}")
197|
198|
199|@app.command()
200|def goodbye(name: str, formal: bool = False):
201|    if formal:
202|        print(f"Goodbye Ms. {name}. Have a good day.")
203|    else:
204|        print(f"Bye {name}!")
205|
206|
207|if __name__ == "__main__":
208|    app()
209|```
210|
211|And that will:
212|
213|* Explicitly create a `typer.Typer` app.
214|    * The previous `typer.run` actually creates one implicitly for you.
215|* Add two subcommands with `@app.command()`.
216|* Execute the `app()` itself, as if it was a function (instead of `typer.run`).
217|
218|### Run the upgraded example
219|
220|Check the new help:
221|
222|<div class="termy">
223|
224|```console
225|$ uv run python main.py --help
226|
227| Usage: main.py [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...
228|
229|╭─ Options ─────────────────────────────────────────╮
230|│ --install-completion          Install completion  │
231|│                               for the current     │
232|│                               shell.              │
233|│ --show-completion             Show completion for │
234|│                               the current shell,  │
235|│                               to copy it or       │
236|│                               customize the       │
237|│                               installation.       │
238|│ --help                        Show this message   │
239|│                               and exit.           │
240|╰───────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
241|╭─ Commands ────────────────────────────────────────╮
242|│ hello                                             │
243|│ goodbye                                           │
244|╰───────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
245|
246|// When you create a package you get ✨ auto-completion ✨ for free, installed with --install-completion
247|
248|// You have 2 subcommands (the 2 functions): hello and goodbye
249|```
250|
251|</div>
252|
253|Now check the help for the `hello` command:
254|
255|<div class="termy">
256|
257|```console
258|$ uv run python main.py hello --help
259|
260| Usage: main.py hello [OPTIONS] {name}
261|
262|╭─ Arguments ───────────────────────────────────────╮
263|│ *    name      <str>  [required]                  │
264|╰───────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
265|╭─ Options ─────────────────────────────────────────╮
266|│ --help          Show this message and exit.       │
267|╰───────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
268|```
269|
270|</div>
271|
272|And now check the help for the `goodbye` command:
273|
274|<div class="termy">
275|
276|```console
277|$ uv run python main.py goodbye --help
278|
279| Usage: main.py goodbye [OPTIONS] {name}
280|
281|╭─ Arguments ───────────────────────────────────────╮
282|│ *    name      <str>  [required]                  │
283|╰───────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
284|╭─ Options ─────────────────────────────────────────╮
285|│ --formal    --no-formal      [default: no-formal] │
286|│ --help                       Show this message    │
287|│                              and exit.            │
288|╰───────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
289|
290|// Automatic --formal and --no-formal for the bool option 🎉
291|```
292|
293|</div>
294|
295|Now you can try out the new command line application:
296|
297|<div class="termy">
298|
299|```console
300|// Use it with the hello command
301|
302|$ uv run python main.py hello Camila
303|
304|Hello Camila
305|
306|// And with the goodbye command
307|
308|$ uv run python main.py goodbye Camila
309|
310|Bye Camila!
311|
312|// And with --formal
313|
314|$ uv run python main.py goodbye --formal Camila
315|
316|Goodbye Ms. Camila. Have a good day.
317|```
318|
319|</div>
320|
321|**Note**: If your app only has one command, by default the command name is **omitted** in usage: `python main.py Camila`. However, when there are multiple commands, you must **explicitly include the command name**: `python main.py hello Camila`. See [One or Multiple Commands](https://typer.tiangolo.com/tutorial/commands/one-or-multiple/) for more details.
322|
323|### Recap
324|
325|In summary, you declare **once** the types of parameters (*CLI arguments* and *CLI options*) as function parameters.
326|
327|You do that with standard modern Python types.
328|
329|You don't have to learn a new syntax, the methods or classes of a specific library, etc.
330|
331|Just standard **Python**.
332|
333|For example, for an `int`:
334|
335|```Python
336|total: int
337|```
338|
339|or for a `bool` flag:
340|
341|```Python
342|force: bool
343|```
344|
345|And similarly for **files**, **paths**, **enums** (choices), etc. And there are tools to create **groups of subcommands**, add metadata, extra **validation**, etc.
346|
347|**You get**: great editor support, including **completion** and **type checks** everywhere.
348|
349|**Your users get**: automatic **`--help`**, **auto-completion** in their terminal (Bash, Zsh, Fish, PowerShell) when they install your package or when using the `typer` command.
350|
351|For a more complete example including more features, see the <a href="https://typer.tiangolo.com/tutorial/">Tutorial - User Guide</a>.
352|
353|## Dependencies
354|
355|**Typer** requires only a few dependencies (most are tiny):
356|
357|* [`rich`](https://rich.readthedocs.io/en/stable/index.html): to show nicely formatted errors automatically.
358|* [`shellingham`](https://github.com/sarugaku/shellingham): to automatically detect the current shell when installing completion.
359|* [`annotated-doc`](https://github.com/fastapi/annotated-doc): to generate documentation from Python type annotations.
360|* [`colorama`](https://github.com/tartley/colorama) (only on Windows): for producing colored terminal text on Windows.
361|
362|### Click code
363|
364|Typer used to depend on [Click](https://click.palletsprojects.com/) as well, a popular tool for building CLIs in Python.
365|
366|Since version 0.26.0, Typer has vendored Click (included Click's source code internally, instead of installing it as a third party package) and has unified the code interactions between Typer and the embedded Click source code for easier maintainability in the future.
367|
368|Note that some Click functionality will not be available anymore in the future, as we continue to improve and extend Typer's codebase.
369|
370|### `typer-slim`
371|
372|There used to be a slimmed-down version of Typer called `typer-slim`, which didn't include the dependencies `rich` and `shellingham`, nor the `typer` command.
373|
374|However, since version 0.22.0, we have stopped supporting this, and `typer-slim` now simply installs (all of) Typer.
375|
376|If you want to disable Rich globally, you can set an environmental variable `TYPER_USE_RICH` to `False` or `0`.
377|

1|# CLI Option autocompletion
2|
3|As you have seen, apps built with **Typer** have completion in your shell that works when you create a Python package or using the `typer` command.
4|
5|It normally completes *CLI options*, *CLI arguments*, and subcommands (that you will learn about later).
6|
7|But you can also provide auto completion for the **values** of *CLI options* and *CLI arguments*. We will learn about that here.
8|
9|## Review completion
10|
11|Before checking how to provide custom completions, let's check again how it works.
12|
13|After installing completion for your own Python package (or using the `typer` command), when you use your CLI program and start adding a *CLI option* with `--` and then hit <kbd>TAB</kbd>, your shell will show you the available *CLI options* (the same for *CLI arguments*, etc).
14|
15|To check it quickly without creating a new Python package, use the `typer` command.
16|
17|Then let's create a small example program:
18|
19|{* docs_src/options_autocompletion/tutorial001_an_py310.py *}
20|
21|And let's try it with the `typer` command to get completion:
22|
23|<div class="termy">
24|
25|```console
26|// Hit the TAB key in your keyboard below where you see the: [TAB]
27|$ typer ./main.py [TAB][TAB]
28|
29|// Depending on your terminal/shell you will get some completion like this ✨
30|run    -- Run the provided Typer app.
31|utils  -- Extra utility commands for Typer apps.
32|
33|// Then try with "run" and --
34|$ typer ./main.py run --[TAB][TAB]
35|
36|// You will get completion for --name, depending on your terminal it will look something like this
37|--name  -- The name to say hi to.
38|
39|// And you can run it as if it was with Python directly
40|$ typer ./main.py run --name Camila
41|
42|Hello Camila
43|```
44|
45|</div>
46|
47|## Custom completion for values
48|
49|Right now we get completion for the *CLI option* names, but not for the values.
50|
51|We can provide completion for the values creating an `autocompletion` function, similar to the `callback` functions from [CLI Option Callback and Context](./options/callback-and-context.md):
52|
53|{* docs_src/options_autocompletion/tutorial002_an_py310.py hl[6:7,16] *}
54|
55|We return a `list` of strings from the `complete_name()` function.
56|
57|And then we get those values when using completion:
58|
59|<div class="termy">
60|
61|```console
62|$ typer ./main.py run --name [TAB][TAB]
63|
64|// We get the values returned from the function 🎉
65|Camila     Carlos     Sebastian
66|```
67|
68|</div>
69|
70|We got the basics working. Now let's improve it.
71|
72|## Check the incomplete value
73|
74|Right now, we always return those values, even if users start typing `Sebast` and then hit <kbd>TAB</kbd>, they will also get the completion for `Camila` and `Carlos` (depending on the shell), while we should only get completion for `Sebastian`.
75|
76|But we can fix that so that it always works correctly.
77|
78|Modify the `complete_name()` function to receive a parameter of type `str`, it will contain the incomplete value.
79|
80|Then we can check and return only the values that start with the incomplete value from the command line:
81|
82|{* docs_src/options_autocompletion/tutorial003_an_py310.py hl[8:13] *}
83|
84|Now let's try it:
85|
86|<div class="termy">
87|
88|```console
89|$ typer ./main.py run --name Ca[TAB][TAB]
90|
91|// We get the values returned from the function that start with Ca 🎉
92|Camila     Carlos
93|```
94|
95|</div>
96|
97|Now we are only returning the valid values, that start with `Ca`, we are no longer returning `Sebastian` as a completion option.
98|
99|/// tip
100|
101|You have to declare the incomplete value of type `str` and that's what you will receive in the function.
102|
103|No matter if the actual value will be an `int`, or something else, when doing completion, you will only get a `str` as the incomplete value.
104|
105|And the same way, you can only return `str`, not `int`, etc.
106|
107|///
108|
109|## Add help to completions
110|
111|Right now we are returning a `list` of `str`.
112|
113|But some shells (Zsh, Fish, PowerShell) are capable of showing extra help text for completion.
114|
115|We can provide that extra help text so that those shells can show it.
116|
117|In the `complete_name()` function, instead of providing one `str` per completion element, we provide a `tuple` with 2 items. The first item is the actual completion string, and the second item is the help text.
118|
119|So, in the end, we return a `list` of `tuples` of `str`:
120|
121|{* docs_src/options_autocompletion/tutorial004_an_py310.py hl[5:9,12:18] *}
122|
123|/// tip
124|
125|If you want to have help text for each item, make sure each item in the list is a `tuple`. Not a `list`.
126|
127|In the end, the return will be a `list` (or other iterable) of `tuples` of 2 `str`.
128|
129|///
130|
131|/// note
132|
133|The help text will be visible in Zsh, Fish, and PowerShell.
134|
135|Bash doesn't support showing the help text, but completion will still work the same.
136|
137|///
138|
139|If you have a shell like Zsh, it would look like:
140|
141|<div class="termy">
142|
143|```console
144|$ typer ./main.py run --name [TAB][TAB]
145|
146|// We get the completion items with their help text 🎉
147|Camila     -- The reader of books.
148|Carlos     -- The writer of scripts.
149|Sebastian  -- The type hints guy.
150|```
151|
152|</div>
153|
154|## Simplify with `yield`
155|
156|Instead of creating and returning a list with values (`str` or `tuple`), we can use `yield` with each value that we want in the completion.
157|
158|That way our function will be a [generator](https://docs.python.org/3.8/glossary.html#index-19) that **Typer** can iterate:
159|
160|{* docs_src/options_autocompletion/tutorial005_an_py310.py hl[12:15] *}
161|
162|That simplifies our code a bit and works the same.
163|
164|/// tip
165|
166|If the `yield` part seems complex for you, don't worry, you can just use the version with the `list` above.
167|
168|In the end, that's just to save us a couple of lines of code.
169|
170|///
171|
172|/// note
173|
174|The function can use `yield`, so it doesn't have to return strictly a `list`, it just has to be [iterable](https://docs.python.org/3.8/glossary.html#term-iterable).
175|
176|But each of the elements for completion has to be a `str` or a `tuple` (when containing a help text).
177|
178|///
179|
180|## Access other *CLI parameters* with the Context
181|
182|Let's say that now we want to modify the program to be able to "say hi" to multiple people at the same time.
183|
184|So, we will allow multiple `--name` *CLI options*.
185|
186|/// tip
187|
188|You will learn more about *CLI parameters* with multiple values later in the tutorial.
189|
190|So, for now, take this as a sneak peek 😉.
191|
192|///
193|
194|For this we use a `list` of `str`:
195|
196|{* docs_src/options_autocompletion/tutorial006_an_py310.py hl[8:13] *}
197|
198|And then we can use it like:
199|
200|<div class="termy">
201|
202|```console
203|$ typer ./main.py run --name Camila --name Sebastian
204|
205|Hello Camila
206|Hello Sebastian
207|```
208|
209|</div>
210|
211|### Getting completion for multiple values
212|
213|And the same way as before, we want to provide **completion** for those names. But we don't want to provide the **same names** for completion if they were already given in previous parameters.
214|
215|For that, we will access and use the "Context". Every Typer application has a special object called a "Context" that is normally hidden.
216|
217|But you can access the context by declaring a function parameter of type `typer.Context`.
218|
219|And from that context you can get the current values for each parameter.
220|
221|{* docs_src/options_autocompletion/tutorial007_an_py310.py hl[12:13,15] *}
222|
223|We are getting the `names` already provided with `--name` in the command line before this completion was triggered.
224|
225|If there's no `--name` in the command line, it will be `None`, so we use `or []` to make sure we have a `list` (even if empty) to check its contents later.
226|
227|Then, when we have a completion candidate, we check if each `name` was already provided with `--name` by checking if it's in that list of `names` with `name not in names`.
228|
229|And then we `yield` each item that has not been used yet.
230|
231|Check it:
232|
233|<div class="termy">
234|
235|```console
236|$ typer ./main.py run --name [TAB][TAB]
237|
238|// The first time we trigger completion, we get all the names
239|Camila     -- The reader of books.
240|Carlos     -- The writer of scripts.
241|Sebastian  -- The type hints guy.
242|
243|// Add a name and trigger completion again
244|$ typer ./main.py run --name Sebastian --name Ca[TAB][TAB]
245|
246|// Now we get completion only for the names we haven't used 🎉
247|Camila  -- The reader of books.
248|Carlos  -- The writer of scripts.
249|
250|// And if we add another of the available names:
251|$ typer ./main.py run --name Sebastian --name Camila --name [TAB][TAB]
252|
253|// We get completion for the only available one
254|Carlos  -- The writer of scripts.
255|```
256|
257|</div>
258|
259|/// tip
260|
261|It's quite possible that if there's only one option left, your shell will complete it right away instead of showing the option with the help text, to save you more typing.
262|
263|///
264|
265|## Getting the raw *CLI parameters*
266|
267|You can also get the raw *CLI parameters*, just a `list` of `str` with everything passed in the command line before the incomplete value.
268|
269|For example, something like `["typer", "main.py", "run", "--name"]`.
270|
271|/// tip
272|
273|This would be for advanced scenarios, in most use cases you would be better off using the context.
274|
275|But it's still possible if you need it.
276|
277|///
278|
279|As a simple example, let's show it on the screen before completion.
280|
281|Because completion is based on the output printed by your program (handled internally by **Typer**), during completion we can't just print something else as we normally do.
282|
283|### Printing to "standard error"
284|
285|/// tip
286|
287|If you need a refresher about what is "standard output" and "standard error" check the section in [Printing and Colors: "Standard Output" and "Standard Error"](./printing.md#standard-output-and-standard-error).
288|
289|///
290|
291|The completion system only reads from "standard output", so, printing to "standard error" won't break completion. 🚀
292|
293|You can print to "standard error" with a **Rich** `Console(stderr=True)`.
294|
295|Using `stderr=True` tells **Rich** that the output should be shown in "standard error".
296|
297|{* docs_src/options_autocompletion/tutorial008_an_py310.py hl[12,15:16] *}
298|
299|/// note
300|
301|If you have disabled Rich, you can also use `print(lastname, file=sys.stderr)` or `typer.echo("some text", err=True)` instead.
302|
303|///
304|
305|We get all the *CLI parameters* as a raw `list` of `str` by declaring a parameter with type `list[str]`, here it's named `args`.
306|
307|/// tip
308|
309|Here we name the list of all the raw *CLI parameters* `args` because that's the usual convention.
310|
311|But it doesn't contain only *CLI arguments*, it has everything, including *CLI options* and values, as a raw `list` of `str`.
312|
313|///
314|
315|And then we just print it to "standard error".
316|
317|<div class="termy">
318|
319|```console
320|$ typer ./main.py run --name [TAB][TAB]
321|
322|// First we see the raw CLI parameters
323|['./main.py', 'run', '--name']
324|
325|// And then we see the actual completion
326|Camila     -- The reader of books.
327|Carlos     -- The writer of scripts.
328|Sebastian  -- The type hints guy.
329|```
330|
331|</div>
332|
333|/// tip
334|
335|This is a very simple (and quite useless) example, just so you know how it works and that you can use it.
336|
337|But it's probably useful only in very advanced use cases.
338|
339|///
340|
341|## Getting the Context and the raw *CLI parameters*
342|
343|Of course, you can declare everything if you need it, the context, the raw *CLI parameters*, and the incomplete `str`:
344|
345|{* docs_src/options_autocompletion/tutorial009_an_py310.py hl[15] *}
346|
347|Check it:
348|
349|<div class="termy">
350|
351|```console
352|$ typer ./main.py run --name [TAB][TAB]
353|
354|// First we see the raw CLI parameters
355|['./main.py', 'run', '--name']
356|
357|// And then we see the actual completion
358|Camila     -- The reader of books.
359|Carlos     -- The writer of scripts.
360|Sebastian  -- The type hints guy.
361|
362|$ typer ./main.py run --name Sebastian --name Ca[TAB][TAB]
363|
364|// Again, we see the raw CLI parameters
365|['./main.py', 'run', '--name', 'Sebastian', '--name']
366|
367|// And then we see the rest of the valid completion items
368|Camila     -- The reader of books.
369|Carlos     -- The writer of scripts.
370|```
371|
372|</div>
373|
374|## Types, types everywhere
375|
376|**Typer** uses the type declarations to detect what it has to provide to your `autocompletion` function.
377|
378|You can declare function parameters of these types:
379|
380|* `str`: for the incomplete value.
381|* `typer.Context`: for the current context.
382|* `list[str]`: for the raw *CLI parameters*.
383|
384|It doesn't matter how you name them, in which order, or which ones of the 3 options you declare. It will all "**just work**" ✨

7|```Python
8|app.add_typer(users.app, name="users")
9|```
10|
11|## Add a help text
12|
13|We can also set the `help` text while adding a Typer:
14|
15|{* docs_src/subcommands/name_help/tutorial001_py310.py hl[6] *}
16|
17|And then we get that help text for that command in the *CLI program*:
18|
19|<div class="termy">
20|
21|```console
22|// Check the main help
23|$ uv run python main.py --help
24|
25|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...
26|
27|Options:
28|  --install-completion  Install completion for the current shell.
29|  --show-completion     Show completion for the current shell, to copy it or customize the installation.
30|  --help                Show this message and exit.
31|
32|Commands:
33|  users  Manage users in the app.
34|
35|// Check the help for the users command
36|$ uv run python main.py users --help
37|
38|Usage: main.py users [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...
39|
40|  Manage users in the app.
41|
42|Options:
43|  --help  Show this message and exit.
44|
45|Commands:
46|  create
47|```
48|
49|</div>
50|
51|We can set the `help` in several places, each one taking precedence over the other, overriding the previous value.
52|
53|Let's see those locations.
54|
55|/// tip
56|
57|There are other attributes that can be set in that same way in the same places we'll see next.
58|
59|But those are documented later in another section.
60|
61|///
62|
63|## Inferring help text from callback
64|
65|### Inferring a command's help text
66|
67|When you create a command with `@app.command()`, by default, it generates the name from the function name.
68|
69|And by default, the help text is extracted from the function's docstring.
70|
71|For example:
72|
73|```Python
74|@app.command()
75|def create(item: str):
76|    """
77|    Create an item.
78|    """
79|    typer.echo(f"Creating item: {item}")
80|```
81|
82|...will create a command `create` with a help text of `Create an item`.
83|
84|### Inferring the help text from `@app.callback()`
85|
86|The same way, if you define a callback in a `typer.Typer()`, the help text is extracted from the callback function's docstring.
87|
88|Here's an example:
89|
90|{* docs_src/subcommands/name_help/tutorial002_py310.py hl[9,10,11,12,13] *}
91|
92|The help text for that command will be the callback function's docstring: `Manage users in the app.`.
93|
94|Check it:
95|
96|<div class="termy">
97|
98|```console
99|// Check the main help
100|$ uv run python main.py --help
101|
102|// Notice the help text "Manage users in the app."
103|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...
104|
105|Options:
106|  --install-completion  Install completion for the current shell.
107|  --show-completion     Show completion for the current shell, to copy it or customize the installation.
108|  --help                Show this message and exit.
109|
110|Commands:
111|  users  Manage users in the app.
112|
113|// Check the help for the users command
114|$ uv run python main.py users --help
115|
116|// Notice the main description: "Manage users in the app."
117|Usage: main.py users [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...
118|
119|  Manage users in the app.
120|
121|Options:
122|  --help  Show this message and exit.
123|
124|Commands:
125|  create
126|```
127|
128|</div>
129|
130|/// note
131|
132|Before Typer 0.14.0, in addition to the help text, the command name was also inferred from the callback function name, this is no longer the case.
133|
134|///

136|### Help from callback parameter in `typer.Typer()`
137|
138|If you pass a `callback` parameter while creating a `typer.Typer(callback=some_function)` it will be used to infer the help text.
139|
140|This has the lowest priority, we'll see later what has a higher priority and can override it.
141|

169|

171|Usage: main.py users [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...

184|### Override a callback set in `typer.Typer()` with `@app.callback()`
185|
186|The same as with normal **Typer** apps, if you pass a `callback` to `typer.Typer(callback=some_function)` and then override it with `@app.callback()`, the help text will be inferred from the new callback:
187|

192|Check it:
193|
194|<div class="termy">
195|
196|```console
197|// Check the main help
198|$ uv run python main.py --help
199|

204|  --install-completion  Install completion for the current shell.
205|  --show-completion     Show completion for the current shell, to copy it or customize the installation.

212|$ uv run python main.py users --help
213|
214|// Notice the main description: "Manage users in the app."
215|Usage: main.py users [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...
216|
217|  Manage users in the app.
218|
219|Options:
220|  --help  Show this message and exit.
221|
222|Commands:

226|</div>

228|### Help from callback in `app.add_typer()`
229|
230|If you override the callback in `app.add_typer()` when including a sub-app, the help will be inferred from this callback function.
231|
232|This takes precedence over inferring the help from a callback set in `@sub_app.callback()` and `typer.Typer(callback=sub_app_callback)`.
233|
234|Check the code:
235|
236|{* docs_src/subcommands/name_help/tutorial005_py310.py hl[15,16,17,18,21] *}
237|
238|The help text will be `I have the highland! Create some users.` instead of the previous ones.
239|
240|Check it:
241|
242|<div class="termy">
243|
244|```console
245|// Check the main help
246|$ uv run python main.py --help
247|
248|// Check the command new-users and its help text
249|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...
250|
251|Options:
252|  --install-completion  Install completion for the current shell.
253|  --show-completion     Show completion for the current shell, to copy it or customize the installation.
254|  --help                Show this message and exit.
255|
256|Commands:
257|  new-users  I have the highland! Create some users.
258|
259|// Now check the help for the new-users command
260|$ uv run python main.py new-users --help
261|
262|// Notice the help text
263|Usage: main.py new-users [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...
264|
265|  I have the highland! Create some users.
266|
267|Options:
268|  --help  Show this message and exit.
269|
270|Commands:
271|  create
272|```

274|</div>
275|
276|### Enough inferring
277|
278|So, when inferring help text, the precedence order from lowest priority to highest is:
279|
280|* `sub_app = typer.Typer(callback=some_function)`
281|* `@sub_app.callback()`
282|* `app.add_typer(sub_app, callback=new_function)`
283|
284|That's for inferring the help text from functions.
285|
286|But if you set the help text explicitly, that has a higher priority than these.
287|
288|## Set the name and help
289|
290|Let's now see the places where you can set the command name and help text, from lowest priority to highest.
291|
292|/// tip

295|
296|///

298|### Name and help in `typer.Typer()`

307|

310|The rest of the callbacks and overrides are there only to show you that they don't affect the name and help text when you set it explicitly.

312|///
313|
314|We set an explicit help `Explicit help.`.

319|

354|### Help text in `@app.callback()`
355|
356|Many parameters that you use when creating a `typer.Typer()` app can be overridden in the parameters of `@app.callback()`.
357|
358|Continuing with the previous example, we now override the `help` in `@user_app.callback()`:

365|

368|```console

400|### Name and help in `app.add_typer()`
401|
402|And finally, with the highest priority, you can override all that by explicitly setting the `name` and `help` in `app.add_typer()`, just like we did on the first example above:
403|

405|
406|And now, with the highest priorities of them all, the command name will now be `cake-sith-users` and the help text will be `Unlimited powder! Eh, users.`.

411|

414|$ uv run python main.py --help

418|

421|  --show-completion     Show completion for the current shell, to copy it or customize the installation.
422|  --help                Show this message and exit.
423|
424|Commands:
425|  cake-sith-users  Unlimited powder! Eh, users.
426|
427|// And check the help for the command cake-sith-users
428|$ uv run python main.py cake-sith-users --help
429|
430|// Notice the main help text
431|Usage: main.py cake-sith-users [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...
432|
433|  Unlimited powder! Eh, users.
434|
435|Options:
436|  --help  Show this message and exit.
437|
438|Commands:
439|  create
440|```
441|
442|</div>
443|
444|## Recap
445|
446|The precedence to generate a command's **help**, from lowest priority to highest, is:
447|
448|* Implicitly inferred from `sub_app = typer.Typer(callback=some_function)`
449|* Implicitly inferred from the callback function under `@sub_app.callback()`
450|* Implicitly inferred from `app.add_typer(sub_app, callback=some_function)`
451|* Explicitly set on `sub_app = typer.Typer(help="Some help.")`
452|* Explicitly set on `app.add_typer(sub_app, help="Some help.")`
453|
454|And the priority to set the command's **name**, from lowest priority to highest, is:
455|
456|* Explicitly set on `sub_app = typer.Typer(name="some-name")`
457|* Explicitly set on `app.add_typer(sub_app, name="some-name")`
458|
459|So, `app.add_typer(sub_app, name="some-name", help="Some help.")` always wins.

1|# Printing and Colors
2|
3|You can use the normal `print()` to show information on the screen:
4|
5|{* docs_src/typer_app/tutorial001_py310.py hl[8] *}
6|

17|</div>
18|
19|## Use Rich
20|
21|You can also display beautiful and more complex information using [Rich](https://rich.readthedocs.io/). It comes by default when you install `typer`.
22|
23|### Use Rich `print`
24|
25|For the simplest cases, you can just import `print` from `rich` and use it instead of the standard `print`:

27|{* docs_src/printing/tutorial001_py310.py hl[2,18] *}

30|
31|<div class="termy">
32|
33|```console
34|$ uv run python main.py

40|    <font color="#A6E22E">'items'</font>: <b>[</b>
41|        <b>{</b><font color="#A6E22E">'name'</font>: <font color="#A6E22E">'Portal Gun'</font><b>}</b>,
42|        <b>{</b><font color="#A6E22E">'name'</font>: <font color="#A6E22E">'Plumbus'</font><b>}</b>
43|    <b>]</b>,
44|    <font color="#A6E22E">'active'</font>: <font color="#A6E22E"><i>True</i></font>,
45|    <font color="#A6E22E">'affiliation'</font>: <font color="#AE81FF"><i>None</i></font>
46|<b>}</b>
47|```

49|</div>
50|
51|### Rich Markup
52|
53|Rich also supports a [custom markup syntax](https://rich.readthedocs.io/en/stable/markup.html) to set colors and styles, for example:
54|
55|{* docs_src/printing/tutorial002_py310.py hl[9] *}
56|
57|<div class="termy">
58|
59|```console
60|$ uv run python main.py
61|
62|<font color="#F92672"><b>Alert!</b></font> <font color="#A6E22E">Portal gun</font> shooting! 💥
63|```
64|
65|</div>
66|
67|In this example you can see how to use font styles, colors, and even emojis.
68|
69|To learn more check out the [Rich docs](https://rich.readthedocs.io/en/stable/markup.html).
70|
71|### Rich Tables
72|
73|The way Rich works internally is that it uses a `Console` object to display the information.
74|
75|When you call Rich's `print`, it automatically creates this object and uses it.
76|
77|But for advanced use cases, you could create a `Console` yourself.
78|
79|{* docs_src/printing/tutorial003_py310.py hl[2:3,5,12:15] *}
80|
81|In this example, we create a `Console`, and a `Table`. And then we can add some rows to the table, and print it.
82|
83|If you run it, you will see a nicely formatted table:
84|
85|<div class="termy">
86|
87|```console
88|$ uv run python main.py
89|
90|┏━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━━┓
91|┃<b> Name  </b>┃<b> Item       </b>┃
92|┡━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━━━┩
93|│ Rick  │ Portal Gun │
94|│ Morty │ Plumbus    │
95|└───────┴────────────┘
96|```
97|
98|</div>
99|
100|Rich has many other features, as an example, you can check the docs for:
101|
102|* [Prompt](https://rich.readthedocs.io/en/stable/prompt.html)
103|* [Markdown](https://rich.readthedocs.io/en/stable/markdown.html)
104|* [Panel](https://rich.readthedocs.io/en/stable/panel.html)
105|* ...and more.
106|
107|### Typer and Rich
108|
109|If you are wondering what tool should be used for what, **Typer** is useful for structuring the command line application, with options, arguments, subcommands, data validation, etc.
110|
111|In general, **Typer** tends to be the entry point to your program, taking the first input from the user.
112|
113|**Rich** is useful for the parts that need to *display* information. Showing beautiful content on the screen.
114|
115|The best results for your command line application are achieved combining both **Typer** and **Rich**.
116|
117|## "Standard Output" and "Standard Error"
118|
119|The way printing works underneath is that the **operating system** (Linux, Windows, macOS) treats what we print as if our CLI program was **writing text** to a "**virtual file**" called "**standard output**".
120|
121|When our code "prints" things it is actually "writing" to this "virtual file" of "standard output".
122|
123|This might seem strange, but that's how the CLI program and the operating system interact with each other.
124|
125|And then the operating system **shows on the screen** whatever our CLI program "**wrote**" to that "**virtual file**" called "**standard output**".
126|
127|### Standard Error
128|
129|And there's another "**virtual file**" called "**standard error**" that is normally only used for errors.
130|
131|But we can also "print" to "standard error". And both are shown on the terminal to the users.
132|
133|/// note
134|
135|If you use PowerShell it's quite possible that what you print to "standard error" won't be shown in the terminal.
136|
137|In PowerShell, to see "standard error" you would have to check the variable `$Error`.
138|
139|But it will work normally in Bash, Zsh, and Fish.
140|
141|///
142|
143|### Printing to "standard error"
144|
145|You can print to "standard error" creating a Rich `Console` with `stderr=True`.
146|
147|/// tip
148|
149|`stderr` is short for "standard error".
150|
151|///
152|
153|Using `stderr=True` tells **Rich** that the output should be shown in "standard error".
154|
155|{* docs_src/printing/tutorial004_py310.py hl[4,11] *}
156|
157|When you try it in the terminal, it will probably just look the same:
158|
159|<div class="termy">
160|
161|```console
162|$ uv run python main.py
163|
164|Here is something written to standard error
165|```
166|
167|</div>
168|
169|## "Standard Input"
170|
171|As a final detail, when you type text in your keyboard to your terminal, the operating system also considers it another "**virtual file**" that you are writing text to.
172|
173|This virtual file is called "**standard input**".
174|
175|### What is this for
176|
177|Right now this probably seems quite useless 🤷‍♂.
178|
179|But understanding that will come handy in the future, for example for autocompletion and testing.
180|
181|## Typer Echo
182|
183|/// warning
184|
185|In most of the cases, for displaying advanced information, it is recommended to use [Rich](https://rich.readthedocs.io/).
186|
187|You can probably skip the rest of this section. 🎉😎
188|
189|///
190|
191|**Typer** also has a small utility `typer.echo()` to print information on the screen. But normally you shouldn't need it.
192|
193|For the simplest cases, you can use the standard Python `print()`.
194|
195|And for the cases where you want to display data more beautifully, or more advanced content, you should use **Rich** instead.
196|
197|### Why `typer.echo`
198|
199|`typer.echo()` applies some checks to try and convert binary data to strings, and other similar things.
200|
201|But in most of the cases you wouldn't need it, as in modern Python strings (`str`) already support and use Unicode, and you would rarely deal with pure `bytes` that you want to print on the screen.
202|
203|If you have some `bytes` objects, you would probably want to decode them intentionally and directly before trying to print them.
204|
205|And if you want to print data with colors and other features, you are much better off with the more advanced tools in **Rich**.
206|
207|### Untrusted Text
208|
209|`typer.echo()` preserves terminal control sequences, including those used for colors. When displaying text from an untrusted source, escape control characters first. For a diagnostic representation of a string, you can use `typer.echo(repr(value))`.
210|
211|Setting `color=False` disables styling, but does not sanitize all terminal control sequences.
212|
213|### Color
214|
215|/// note | Technical Details
216|
217|The way color works in terminals is by using some codes (ANSI escape sequences) as part of the text.
218|
219|So, a colored text is still just a `str`.
220|
221|///
222|
223|/// tip
224|
225|Again, you are much better off using [Rich](https://rich.readthedocs.io/) for this. 😎
226|
227|///
228|
229|You can create colored strings to output to the terminal with `typer.style()`, that gives you `str`s that you can then pass to `typer.echo()`:
230|
231|{* docs_src/printing/tutorial005_py310.py hl[10,12] *}
232|
233|/// tip
234|
235|The parameters `fg` and `bg` receive strings with the color names for the "<strong>f</strong>ore<strong>g</strong>round" and "<strong>b</strong>ack<strong>g</strong>round" colors. You could simply pass `fg="green"` and `bg="red"`.
236|
237|But **Typer** provides them all as variables like `typer.colors.GREEN` just so you can use autocompletion while selecting them.
238|
239|///
240|
241|Check it:
242|
243|<div class="use-termynal" data-termynal>
244|<span data-ty="input">python main.py</span>
245|<span data-ty>everything is <span style="color: green; font-weight: bold;">good</span></span>
246|<span data-ty="input">python main.py --no-good</span>
247|<span data-ty>everything is <span style="color: white; background-color: red;">bad</span></span>
248|</div>
249|
250|You can pass these function arguments to `typer.style()`:
251|
252|* `fg`: the foreground color.
253|* `bg`: the background color.
254|* `bold`: enable or disable bold mode.
255|* `dim`: enable or disable dim mode. This is badly supported.
256|* `underline`: enable or disable underline.
257|* `blink`: enable or disable blinking.
258|* `reverse`: enable or disable inverse rendering (foreground becomes background and the other way round).
259|* `reset`: by default a reset-all code is added at the end of the string which means that styles do not carry over.  This can be disabled to compose styles.
260|
261|### `typer.secho()` - style and print
262|
263|/// tip
264|
265|In case you didn't see above, you are much better off using [Rich](https://rich.readthedocs.io/) for this. 😎
266|
267|///
268|
269|There's a shorter form to style and print at the same time with `typer.secho()` it's like `typer.echo()` but also adds style like `typer.style()`:
270|
271|{* docs_src/printing/tutorial006_py310.py hl[8] *}
272|
273|Check it:
274|
275|<div class="use-termynal" data-termynal>
276|<span data-ty="input">python main.py Camila</span>
277|<span style="color: magenta;" data-ty>Welcome here Camila</span>
278|</div>
--- END FILE: docs/tutorial/printing.md ---

1|# CLI Arguments with Help
2|
3|In the *First Steps* section you saw how to add help for a CLI app/command by adding it to a function's <abbr title="a multi-line string as the first expression inside a function (not assigned to any variable) used for documentation">docstring</abbr>.
4|
5|Here's how that last example looked like:
6|
7|{* docs_src/first_steps/tutorial006_py310.py *}
8|
9|Now that you also know how to use `typer.Argument()`, let's use it to add documentation specific for a *CLI argument*.
10|
11|## Add a `help` text for a *CLI argument*
12|
13|You can use the `help` parameter to add a help text for a *CLI argument*:
14|
15|{* docs_src/arguments/help/tutorial001_an_py310.py hl[9] *}
16|
17|And it will be used in the automatic `--help` option:
18|
19|<div class="termy">
20|
21|```console
22|$ uv run python main.py --help
23|
24|// Check the section with Arguments below 🚀
25|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS] {name}
26|
27|Arguments:
28|  name  The name of the user to greet  [required]
29|
30|Options:
31|  --help                Show this message and exit.
32|```
33|
34|</div>
35|
36|## Combine help text and docstrings
37|
38|And of course, you can also combine that `help` with the <abbr title="a multi-line string as the first expression inside a function (not assigned to any variable) used for documentation">docstring</abbr>:
39|
40|{* docs_src/arguments/help/tutorial002_an_py310.py hl[9:12] *}
41|
42|And the `--help` option will combine all the information:
43|
44|<div class="termy">
45|
46|```console
47|$ uv run python main.py --help
48|
49|// Notice that we have the help text from the docstring and also the Arguments 📝
50|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS] {name}
51|
52|  Say hi to 'name' very gently, like Dirk.
53|
54|Arguments:
55|  name  The name of the user to greet  [required]
56|
57|Options:
58|  --help                Show this message and exit.
59|```
60|
61|</div>
62|
63|## Help with defaults
64|
65|If you have a *CLI argument* with a default value, like `"World"`:
66|
67|{* docs_src/arguments/help/tutorial003_an_py310.py hl[9] *}
68|
69|It will show that default value in the help text:
70|
71|<div class="termy">
72|
73|```console
74|$ uv run python main.py --help
75|
76|// Notice the [default: World] 🔍
77|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS] [name]
78|
79|  Say hi to 'name' very gently, like Dirk.
80|
81|Arguments:
82|  name  Who to greet  [default: World]
83|
84|Options:
85|  --help                Show this message and exit.
86|```
87|
88|</div>
89|
90|But you can disable that if you want to, with `show_default=False`:
91|
92|{* docs_src/arguments/help/tutorial004_an_py310.py hl[11] *}
93|
94|And then it won't show the default value:
95|
96|<div class="termy">
97|
98|```console
99|$ uv run python main.py --help
100|
101|// Notice the there's no [default: World] now 🔥
102|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS] [name]
103|
104|  Say hi to 'name' very gently, like Dirk.
105|
106|Arguments:
107|  name  Who to greet
108|
109|Options:
110|  --help                Show this message and exit.
111|```
112|
113|</div>
114|
115|## Custom default string
116|
117|You can use the same `show_default` to pass a custom string (instead of a `bool`) to customize the default value to be shown in the help text:
118|
119|{* docs_src/arguments/help/tutorial005_an_py310.py hl[13] *}
120|
121|And it will be used in the help text:
122|
123|<div class="termy">
124|
125|```console
126|$ uv run python main.py --help
127|
128|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS] [name]
129|
130|Arguments:
131|  name  Who to greet  [default: (Deadpoolio the amazing's name)]
132|
133|
134|Options:
135|  --help                Show this message and exit.
136|
137|// See it shows "(Deadpoolio the amazing's name)" instead of the actual default of "Wade Wilson"
138|```
139|
140|</div>
141|
142|## Custom help name (`metavar`)
143|
144|You can also customize the text used in the generated help text to represent a *CLI argument*.
145|
146|By default, it will be the same name you declared, with casing preserved.
147|
148|So, if you declare it as:
149|
150|```Python
151|name: str
152|```
153|
154|It will be shown as:
155|
156|```
157|name
158|```
159|
160|But you can customize it with the `metavar` parameter for `typer.Argument()`.
161|
162|For example, let's say you don't want to have the default of `name`, you want to have `username`, and you really want ✨ emojis ✨ everywhere:
163|
164|{* docs_src/arguments/help/tutorial006_an_py310.py hl[9] *}
165|
166|Now the generated help text will have `✨username✨` instead of `name`:
167|
168|<div class="termy">
169|
170|```console
171|$ uv run python main.py --help
172|
173|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS] [✨username✨]
174|
175|Arguments:
176|  ✨username✨  [default: World]
177|
178|Options:
179|  --help                Show this message and exit.
180|```
181|
182|</div>
183|
184|## *CLI Argument* help panels
185|
186|You might want to show the help information for *CLI arguments* in different panels when using the `--help` option.
187|
188|If you have installed Rich as described in the docs for [Printing and Colors](../printing.md), you can set the `rich_help_panel` parameter to the name of the panel where you want this *CLI argument* to be shown:
189|
190|{* docs_src/arguments/help/tutorial007_an_py310.py hl[12,16] *}
191|
192|Then, if you check the `--help` option, you will see a default panel named "`Arguments`" for the *CLI arguments* that don't have a custom `rich_help_panel`.
193|
194|And next you will see other panels for the *CLI arguments* that have a custom panel set in the `rich_help_panel` parameter:
195|
196|<div class="termy">
197|
198|```console
199|$ uv run python main.py --help
200|
201|<b> </b><font color="#F4BF75"><b>Usage: </b></font><b>main.py [OPTIONS] {name} [lastname] [age]               </b>
202|<b>                                                                     </b>
203| Say hi to 'name' very gently, like Dirk.
204|
205|<font color="#A5A5A1">╭─ Arguments ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮</font>
206|<font color="#A5A5A1">│ </font><font color="#F92672">*</font>    name      <font color="#F4BF75"><b>str</b></font>  Who to greet [default: None] <font color="#A6194C">[required]</font>       │
207|<font color="#A5A5A1">╰───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯</font>
208|<font color="#A5A5A1">╭─ Secondary Arguments ─────────────────────────────────────────────╮</font>
209|<font color="#A5A5A1">│   lastname      </font><font color="#A37F4E"><b>lastname</b></font>  The last name                           │
210|<font color="#A5A5A1">│   age           </font><font color="#A37F4E"><b>age     </b></font>  The user's age                          │
211|<font color="#A5A5A1">╰───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯</font>
212|<font color="#A5A5A1">╭─ Options ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮</font>
213|<font color="#A5A5A1">│ </font><font color="#A1EFE4"><b>--help</b></font>                        Show this message and exit.         │
214|<font color="#A5A5A1">╰───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯</font>
215|```
216|
217|</div>
218|
219|In this example we have a custom *CLI arguments* panel named "`Secondary Arguments`".
220|
221|## Help with style using Rich
222|
223|In a future section you will see how to use custom markup in the `help` for *CLI arguments* when reading about [Commands - Command Help](../commands/help.md#rich-markdown-and-markup).
224|
225|If you are in a hurry you can jump there, but otherwise, it would be better to continue reading here and following the tutorial in order.
226|
227|## Hide a *CLI argument* from the help text
228|
229|If you want, you can make a *CLI argument* **not** show up in the `Arguments` section in the help text.
230|
231|You will probably not want to do this normally, but it's possible:
232|
233|{* docs_src/arguments/help/tutorial008_an_py310.py hl[9] *}
234|
235|Check it:
236|
237|<div class="termy">
238|
239|```console
240|$ uv run python main.py --help
241|
242|// Notice there's no Arguments section at all 🔥
243|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS] [name]
244|
245|  Say hi to 'name' very gently, like Dirk.
246|
247|Options:
248|  --help                Show this message and exit.
249|```
250|
251|</div>
252|
253|/// note
254|
255|Have in mind that the *CLI argument* will still show up in the first line with `Usage`.
256|
257|But it won't show up in the main help text under the `Arguments` section.
258|
259|///
260|
261|### Help text for *CLI arguments*
262|
263|**Typer supports `help` for *CLI arguments*** to make it easier to have consistent help texts with a consistent format for your CLI programs. 🎨
264|
265|This is also to help you create CLI programs that are ✨ awesome ✨ *by default*. With very little code.
266|
267|If you don't want the CLI Argument to be shown in help outputs, you can set the `hidden` parameter to `True`.

1|# `typer` command
2|
3|The `typer` command provides ✨ completion ✨ in the Terminal for your own small scripts. Even if they don't use Typer internally. Of course, it works better if you use **Typer** in your script.
4|
5|It's probably most useful if you have a small custom Python script using **Typer** (maybe as part of some project), for some small tasks, and it's not complex/important enough to create a whole installable Python package.
6|
7|In that case, you can run your program with the `typer` command in your Terminal, and it will provide completion for your script.
8|
9|The `typer` command also has functionality to generate Markdown documentation for your own **Typer** programs 📝.
10|
11|## Install
12|
13|Add Typer to your project:
14|
15|```console
16|$ uv add typer
17|```
18|
19|This installs both the Typer library and the `typer` command in the project's `.venv`.
20|
21|Activate that environment to make `typer` available as a first-class command in your terminal:
22|
23|//// tab | Linux, macOS
24|
25|```console
26|$ source .venv/bin/activate
27|```
28|
29|////
30|
31|//// tab | Windows PowerShell
32|
33|```console
34|$ .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
35|```
36|
37|////
38|
39|//// tab | Windows Bash
40|
41|```console
42|$ source .venv/Scripts/activate
43|```
44|
45|////
46|
47|Using the `typer` command from the project environment ensures it uses the same Typer version and dependencies as the project.
48|
49|If you don't want to use the `typer` command, you can call the Typer library as a module with:
50|
51|```console
52|$ uv run python -m typer
53|```
54|
55|## Install completion
56|
57|You can then install completion for the `typer` command with:
58|
59|<div class="termy">
60|
61|```console
62|$ typer --install-completion
63|
64|bash completion installed in /home/user/.bashrc.
65|Completion will take effect once you restart the terminal.
66|```
67|
68|</div>
69|
70|### Sample script
71|
72|Let's say you have a script that uses **Typer** in `my_custom_script.py`:
73|
74|```Python
75|from typing import Optional
76|
77|import typer
78|
79|app = typer.Typer()
80|
81|
82|@app.command()
83|def hello(name: Optional[str] = None):
84|    if name:
85|        typer.echo(f"Hello {name}")
86|    else:
87|        typer.echo("Hello World!")
88|
89|
90|@app.command()
91|def bye(name: Optional[str] = None):
92|    if name:
93|        typer.echo(f"Bye {name}")
94|    else:
95|        typer.echo("Goodbye!")
96|
97|
98|if __name__ == "__main__":
99|    app()
100|```
101|
102|For it to work, you would also install **Typer**:
103|
104|<div class="termy">
105|
106|```console
107|$ uv add typer
108|---> 100%
109|```
110|
111|</div>
112|
113|### Run with Python
114|
115|Then you could run your script with normal Python:
116|
117|<div class="termy">
118|
119|```console
120|$ uv run python my_custom_script.py hello
121|
122|Hello World!
123|
124|$ uv run python my_custom_script.py hello --name Camila
125|
126|Hello Camila!
127|
128|$ uv run python my_custom_script.py bye --name Camila
129|
130|Bye Camila
131|```
132|
133|</div>
134|
135|There's nothing wrong with using Python directly to run it. And, in fact, if some other code or program uses your script, that would probably be the best way to do it.
136|
137|⛔️ But in your terminal, you won't get completion when hitting <kbd>TAB</kbd> for any of the subcommands or options, like `hello`, `bye`, and `--name`.
138|
139|### Run with the `typer` command.
140|
141|You can also run the same script with the `typer` command:
142|
143|<div class="termy">
144|
145|```console
146|$ typer my_custom_script.py run hello
147|
148|Hello World!
149|
150|$ typer my_custom_script.py run hello --name Camila
151|
152|Hello Camila!
153|
154|$ typer my_custom_script.py run bye --name Camila
155|
156|Bye Camila
157|```
158|
159|</div>
160|
161|* Instead of using `python` directly you use the `typer` command.
162|* After the name of the file, add the subcommand `run`.
163|
164|✔️ If you installed completion for the `typer` command as described above, when you hit <kbd>TAB</kbd> you will have ✨ completion for everything ✨, including all the subcommands and options of your script, like `hello`, `bye`, and `--name` 🚀.
165|
166|## If main
167|
168|Because the `typer` command won't use the block with:
169|
170|```Python
171|if __name__ == "__main__":
172|    app()
173|```
174|
175|...you can also remove it if you are calling that script only with the `typer` command.
176|
177|## Run other files
178|
179|The `typer` command can run any script with **Typer**, but the script doesn't even have to use **Typer** at all.
180|
181|You could even run a file with a function that could be used with `typer.run()`, even if the script doesn't use `typer.run()` or anything else.
182|
183|For example, a file `main.py` like this will still work:
184|
185|```Python
186|def main(name: str = "World"):
187|    """
188|    Say hi to someone, by default to the World.
189|    """
190|    print(f"Hello {name}")
191|```
192|
193|Then you can call it with:
194|
195|<div class="termy">
196|
197|```console
198|$ typer main.py run --help
199|Usage: typer [PATH_OR_MODULE] run [OPTIONS]
200|
201|  Say hi to someone, by default to the World.
202|
203|Options:
204|  --name <str>  [default: World]
205|  --help        Show this message and exit.
206|
207|$ typer main.py run --name Camila
208|
209|Hello Camila
210|```
211|
212|</div>
213|
214|And it will also have completion for things like the `--name` *CLI Option*.
215|
216|## Run a package or module
217|
218|Instead of a file path you can pass a module (possibly in a package) to import.
219|
220|For example:
221|
222|<div class="termy">
223|
224|```console
225|$ typer my_package.main run --help
226|Usage: typer [PATH_OR_MODULE] run [OPTIONS]
227|
228|Options:
229|  --name <str>
230|  --help       Show this message and exit.
231|
232|$ typer my_package.main run --name Camila
233|
234|Hello Camila
235|```
236|
237|</div>
238|
239|## Options
240|
241|You can specify one of the following **CLI options**:
242|
243|* `--app`: the name of the variable with a `Typer()` object to run as the main app.
244|* `--func`: the name of the variable with a function that would be used with `typer.run()`.
245|
246|### Defaults
247|
248|When your run a script with the `typer` command it will use the app from the following priority:
249|
250|* An app object from the `--app` *CLI Option*.
251|* A function to convert to a **Typer** app from `--func` *CLI Option* (like when using `typer.run()`).
252|* A **Typer** app in a variable with a name of `app`, `cli`, or `main`.
253|* The first **Typer** app available in the file, with any name.
254|* A function in a variable with a name of `main`, `cli`, or `app`.
255|* The first function in the file, with any name.
256|
257|## Generate docs
258|
259|You can also use the `typer` command to generate Markdown documentation for your **Typer** application.
260|
261|### Sample script with docs
262|
263|For example, you could have a script like:
264|
265|{* docs_src/commands/help/tutorial001_an_py310.py *}
266|
267|### Generate docs with the `typer` command
268|
269|Then you could generate docs for it with the `typer` command.
270|
271|You can use the subcommand `utils`.
272|
273|And then the subcommand `docs`.
274|
275|<div class="termy">
276|
277|```console
278|$ typer some_script.py utils docs
279|```
280|
281|</div>
282|
283|/// tip
284|
285|If you don't want to use the `typer` command, you can still generate docs with:
286|
287|```console
288|$ uv run python -m typer some_script.py utils docs
289|```
290|
291|///
292|
293|**Options**:
294|
295|* `--name <str>`: The name of the CLI program to use in docs.
296|* `--output <file>`: An output file to write docs to, like README.md.
297|* `--title <str>`: A title to use in the docs, by default the name of the command.
298|
299|For example:
300|
301|<div class="termy">
302|
303|```console
304|$ typer my_package.main utils docs --name awesome-cli --output README.md
305|
306|Docs saved to: README.md
307|```
308|
309|</div>
310|
311|### Sample docs output
312|
313|For example, for the previous script, the generated docs would look like:
314|
315|---
316|
317|## `awesome-cli`
318|
319|Awesome CLI user manager.
320|
321|**Usage**:
322|
323|```console
324|$ awesome-cli [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...
325|```
326|
327|**Options**:
328|
329|* `--install-completion`: Install completion for the current shell.
330|* `--show-completion`: Show completion for the current shell, to copy it or customize the installation.
331|* `--help`: Show this message and exit.
332|
333|**Commands**:
334|
335|* `create`: Create a new user with username.
336|* `delete`: Delete a user with username.
337|* `delete-all`: Delete ALL users in the database.
338|* `init`: Initialize the users database.
339|
