1|# CLI Option Name
2|
3|By default **Typer** will create a *CLI option* name from the function parameter.
4|
5|So, if you have a function with:
6|
7|```Python
8|def main(user_name: Optional[str] = None):
9|    pass
10|```
11|
12|or
13|
14|```Python
15|def main(user_name: Annotated[Optional[str], typer.Option()] = None):
16|    pass
17|```
18|
19|**Typer** will create a *CLI option*:
20|
21|```
22|--user-name
23|```
24|
25|But you can customize it if you want to.
26|
27|Let's say the function parameter name is `user_name` as above, but you want the *CLI option* to be just `--name`.
28|
29|You can pass the *CLI option* name that you want to have in the following positional argument passed to `typer.Option()`:
30|
31|{* docs_src/options/name/tutorial001_an_py310.py hl[9] *}
32|
33|/// note
34|
35|"[Positional](https://docs.python.org/3.8/glossary.html#term-argument)" means that it's not a function argument with a keyword name.
36|
37|For example `show_default=True` is a keyword argument. "`show_default`" is the keyword.
38|
39|But in `"--name"` there's no `option_name="--name"` or something similar, it's just the string value `"--name"` that goes in `typer.Option()`.
40|
41|That's a "positional argument" in a function.
42|
43|///
44|
45|Check it:
46|
47|<div class="termy">
48|
49|```console
50|$ uv run python main.py --help
51|
52|// Notice the --name instead of --user-name
53|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS]
54|
55|Options:
56|  --name <str>          [required]
57|  --help                Show this message and exit.
58|
59|// Try it
60|$ uv run python main.py --name Camila
61|
62|Hello Camila
63|```
64|
65|</div>
66|
67|## *CLI option* short names
68|
69|A short name is a *CLI option* name with a single dash (`-`) instead of 2 (`--`) and a single letter, like `-n` instead of `--name`.
70|
71|For example, the `ls` program has a *CLI option* named `--size`, and the same *CLI option* also has a short name `-s`:
72|
73|<div class="termy">
74|
75|```console
76|// With the long name --size
77|$ ls ./myproject --size
78|
79|12 first-steps.md   4 intro.md
80|
81|// With the short name -s
82|$ ls ./myproject -s
83|
84|12 first-steps.md   4 intro.md
85|
86|// Both CLI option names do the same
87|```
88|
89|</div>
90|
91|### *CLI option* short names together
92|
93|Short names have another feature, when they have a single letter, as in `-s`, you can put several of these *CLI options* together, with a single dash.
94|
95|For example, the `ls` program has these 2 *CLI options* (among others):
96|
97|* `--size`: show the sizes of the listed files.
98|* `--human`: show a human-readable format, like `1MB` instead of just `1024`.
99|
100|And these 2 *CLI options* have short versions too:
101|
102|* `--size`: short version `-s`.
103|* `--human`: short version `-h`.
104|
105|So, you can put them together with `-sh` or `-hs`:
106|
107|<div class="termy">
108|
109|```console
110|// Call ls with long CLI options
111|$ ls --size --human
112|
113|12K first-steps.md   4.0K intro.md
114|
115|// Now with short versions
116|$ ls -s -h
117|
118|12K first-steps.md   4.0K intro.md
119|
120|// And with short versions together
121|$ ls -sh
122|
123|12K first-steps.md   4.0K intro.md
124|
125|// Order in short versions doesn't matter
126|$ ls -hs
127|
128|12K first-steps.md   4.0K intro.md
129|
130|// They all work the same 🎉
131|```
132|
133|</div>
134|
135|### *CLI option* short names with values
136|
137|When you use *CLI options* with short names, you can put them together if they are just boolean flags, like `--size` or `--human`.
138|
139|But if you have a *CLI option* `--file` with a short name `-f` that takes a value, if you put it with other short names for *CLI options*, you have to put it as the last letter, so that it can receive the value that comes right after.
140|
141|For example, let's say you are decompressing/extracting a file `myproject.tar.gz` with the program `tar`.
142|
143|You can pass these *CLI option* short names to `tar`:
144|
145|* `-x`: means "e`X`tract", to decompress and extract the contents.
146|* `-v`: means "`V`erbose", to print on the screen what it is doing, so you can know that it's decompressing each file and can entertain yourself while you wait.
147|* `-f`: means "`F`ile", this one requires a value, the compressed file to extract (in our example, this is `myproject.tar.gz`).
148|    * So if you use all the short names together, this `-f` has to come last, to receive the value that comes next to it.
149|
150|For example:
151|
152|<div class="termy">
153|
154|```console
155|$ tar -xvf myproject.tar.gz
156|
157|myproject/
158|myproject/first-steps.md
159|myproject/intro.md
160|
161|// But if you put the -f before
162|$ tar -fxv myproject.tar.gz
163|
164|// You get an ugly error
165|tar: You must specify one of the blah, blah, error, error
166|```
167|
168|</div>
169|
170|### Defining *CLI option* short names
171|
172|In **Typer** you can also define *CLI option* short names the same way you can customize the long names.
173|
174|You can pass *positional* arguments to `typer.Option()` to define the *CLI option* name(s).
175|
176|/// tip
177|
178|Remember the *positional* function arguments are those that don't have a keyword.
179|
180|All the other function arguments/parameters you pass to `typer.Option()` like `prompt=True` and `help="This option blah, blah"` require the keyword.
181|
182|///
183|
184|You can overwrite the *CLI option* name to use as in the previous example, but you can also declare extra alternatives, including short names.
185|
186|For example, extending the previous example, let's add a *CLI option* short name `-n`:
187|
188|{* docs_src/options/name/tutorial002_an_py310.py hl[9] *}
189|
190|Here we are overwriting the *CLI option* name that by default would be `--user-name`, and we are defining it to be `--name`. And we are also declaring a *CLI option* short name of `-n`.
191|
192|Check it:
193|
194|<div class="termy">
195|
196|```console
197|// Check the help
198|$ uv run python main.py --help
199|
200|// Notice the two CLI option names -n and --name
201|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS]
202|
203|Options:
204|  -n, --name <str>      [required]
205|  --help                Show this message and exit.
206|
207|// Try the short version
208|$ uv run python main.py -n Camila
209|
210|Hello Camila
211|```
212|
213|</div>
214|
215|### *CLI option* only short name
216|
217|If you only declare a short name like `-n` then that will be the only *CLI option* name. And neither `--name` nor `--user-name` will be available.
218|
219|{* docs_src/options/name/tutorial003_an_py310.py hl[9] *}
220|
221|Check it:
222|
223|<div class="termy">
224|
225|```console
226|$ uv run python main.py --help
227|
228|// Notice there's no --name nor --user-name, only -n
229|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS]
230|
231|Options:
232|  -n <str>              [required]
233|  --help                Show this message and exit.
234|
235|// Try it
236|$ uv run python main.py -n Camila
237|
238|Hello Camila
239|```
240|
241|</div>
242|
243|### *CLI option* short name and default
244|
245|Continuing with the example above, as **Typer** allows you to declare a *CLI option* as having only a short name, if you want to have the default long name plus a short name, you have to declare both explicitly:
246|
247|{* docs_src/options/name/tutorial004_an_py310.py hl[9] *}
248|
249|Check it:
250|
251|<div class="termy">
252|
253|```console
254|$ uv run python main.py --help
255|
256|// Notice that we have the long version --user-name back
257|// and we also have the short version -n
258|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS]
259|
260|Options:
261|  -n, --user-name <str> [required]
262|  --help                Show this message and exit.
263|
264|// Try it
265|$ uv run python main.py --user-name Camila
266|
267|Hello Camila
268|
269|// And try the short version
270|$ uv run python main.py -n Camila
271|```
272|
273|</div>
274|
275|### *CLI option* short names together
276|
277|You can create multiple short names and use them together.
278|
279|You don't have to do anything special for it to work (apart from declaring those short versions):
280|
281|{* docs_src/options/name/tutorial005_an_py310.py hl[10:11] *}
282|
283|/// tip
284|
285|Notice that, again, we are declaring the long and short version of the *CLI option* names.
286|
287|///
288|
289|Check it:
290|
291|<div class="termy">
292|
293|```console
294|$ uv run python main.py --help
295|
296|// We now have short versions -n and -f
297|// And also long versions --name and --formal
298|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS]
299|
300|Options:
301|  -n, --name <str>      [required]
302|  -f, --formal
303|  --help                Show this message and exit.
304|
305|// Try the short versions
306|$ uv run python main.py -n Camila -f
307|
308|Good day Ms. Camila.
309|
310|// And try the 2 short versions together
311|// See how -n has to go last, to be able to get the value
312|$ uv run python main.py -fn Camila
313|
314|Good day Ms. Camila.
315|```
316|
317|</div>

1|# Optional CLI Arguments
2|
3|We said before that *by default*:
4|
5|* *CLI options* are **optional**
6|* *CLI arguments* are **required**
7|
8|Again, that's how they work *by default*, and that's the convention in many CLI programs and systems.
9|
10|But you can change that.
11|
12|In fact, it's very common to have **optional** *CLI arguments*, it's way more common than having **required** *CLI options*.
13|
14|As an example of how it could be useful, let's see how the `ls` CLI program works.
15|
16|<div class="termy">
17|
18|```console
19|// If you just type
20|$ ls
21|
22|// ls will "list" the files and directories in the current directory
23|typer  tests  README.md  LICENSE
24|
25|// But it also receives an optional CLI argument
26|$ ls ./tests/
27|
28|// And then ls will list the files and directories inside of that directory from the CLI argument
29|__init__.py  test_tutorial
30|```
31|
32|</div>
33|
34|## An alternative *CLI argument* declaration
35|
36|In the [First Steps](../first-steps.md#add-a-cli-argument) you saw how to add a *CLI argument*:
37|
38|{* docs_src/first_steps/tutorial002_py310.py hl[4] *}
39|
40|Now let's see an alternative way to create the same *CLI argument*:
41|
42|{* docs_src/arguments/optional/tutorial000_an_py310.py hl[6] *}
43|
44|Or, using an explicit `Typer()` instance creation:
45|
46|{* docs_src/arguments/optional/tutorial001_an_py310.py hl[9] *}
47|
48|/// note
49|
50|Typer added support for `Annotated` (and started recommending it) in version 0.9.0.
51|
52|If you have an older version, you would get errors when trying to use `Annotated`.
53|
54|Make sure you upgrade the Typer version to at least 0.9.0 before using `Annotated`.
55|
56|///
57|
58|Before, you had this function parameter:
59|
60|```Python
61|name: str
62|```
63|
64|And now we wrap it with `Annotated`:
65|
66|```Python
67|name: Annotated[str]
68|```
69|
70|Both of these versions mean the same thing, `Annotated` is part of standard Python and is there for this.
71|
72|But the second version using `Annotated` allows us to pass additional metadata that can be used by **Typer**:
73|
74|```Python
75|name: Annotated[str, typer.Argument()]
76|```
77|
78|Now we are being explicit that `name` is a *CLI argument*. It's still a `str` and it's still required (it doesn't have a default value).
79|
80|All we did there achieves the same thing as before, a **required** *CLI argument*:
81|
82|<div class="termy">
83|
84|```console
85|$ uv run python main.py
86|
87|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS] {name}
88|Try "main.py --help" for help.
89|
90|Error: Missing argument 'name'.
91|```
92|
93|</div>
94|
95|It's still not very useful, but it works correctly.
96|
97|And being able to declare a **required** *CLI argument* using
98|
99|```Python
100|name: Annotated[str, typer.Argument()]
101|```
102|
103|...that works exactly the same as
104|
105|```Python
106|name: str
107|```
108|
109|...will come handy later.
110|
111|## Make an optional *CLI argument*
112|
113|Now, finally what we came for, an optional *CLI argument*.
114|
115|To make a *CLI argument* optional, use `typer.Argument()` and make sure to provide a "default" value, for example `"World"`:
116|
117|{* docs_src/arguments/optional/tutorial002_an_py310.py hl[9] *}
118|
119|Now we have:
120|
121|```Python
122|name: Annotated[str, typer.Argument()] = "World"
123|```
124|
125|Because we are using `typer.Argument()` **Typer** will know that this is a *CLI argument* (no matter if *required* or *optional*).
126|
127|Check the help:
128|
129|<div class="termy">
130|
131|```console
132|// First check the help
133|$ uv run python main.py --help
134|
135|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS] [name]
136|
137|Arguments:
138|  name  [default: World]
139|
140|Options:
141|  --help                Show this message and exit.
142|```
143|
144|</div>
145|
146|/// tip
147|
148|Notice that `name` is still a *CLI argument*, it's shown up there in the "`Usage: main.py` ...".
149|
150|Also notice that now `[name]` has rectangular brackets ("`[`" and "`]`") around it to denote that it's **optional**, not **required**. If it would have been required, curly brackets ("`{`" and "`}`") would be used instead.
151|
152|///
153|
154|Now run it and test it:
155|
156|<div class="termy">
157|
158|```console
159|// With no CLI argument
160|$ uv run python main.py
161|
162|Hello World!
163|
164|// With one optional CLI argument
165|$ uv run python main.py Camila
166|
167|Hello Camila
168|```
169|
170|</div>
171|
172|/// tip
173|
174|Notice that "`Camila`" here is an optional *CLI argument*, not a *CLI option*, because we didn't use something like "`--name Camila`", we just passed "`Camila`" directly to the program.
175|
176|///
177|
178|## Alternative (old) `typer.Argument()` as the default value
179|
180|**Typer** also supports another older alternative syntax for declaring *CLI arguments* with additional metadata.
181|
182|Instead of using `Annotated`, you can use `typer.Argument()` as the default value:
183|
184|{* docs_src/arguments/optional/tutorial001_py310.py hl[7] *}
185|
186|/// tip
187|
188|Prefer to use the `Annotated` version if possible.
189|
190|///
191|
192|Before, because `name` didn't have any default value it would be a **required parameter** for the Python function, in Python terms.
193|
194|When using `typer.Argument()` as the default value **Typer** does the same and makes it a **required** *CLI argument*.
195|
196|We changed it to:
197|
198|```Python
199|name: str = typer.Argument()
200|```
201|
202|But now as `typer.Argument()` is the "default value" of the function's parameter, it would mean that "it is no longer required" (in Python terms).
203|
204|As we no longer have the Python function default value (or its absence) to tell if something is required or not and what is the default value, `typer.Argument()` receives a first parameter `default` that serves the same purpose of defining that default value, or making it required.
205|
206|Not passing any value to the `default` argument is the same as marking it as required. But you can also explicitly mark it as *required* by passing `...` as the `default` argument, passed to `typer.Argument(default=...)`.
207|
208|```Python
209|name: str = typer.Argument(default=...)
210|```
211|
212|/// note
213|
214|If you hadn't seen that `...` before: it is a special single value, it is [part of Python and is called "Ellipsis"](https://docs.python.org/3/library/constants.html#Ellipsis).
215|
216|///
217|
218|{* docs_src/arguments/optional/tutorial003_py310.py hl[7] *}
219|
220|And the same way, you can make it optional by passing a different `default` value, for example `"World"`:
221|
222|{* docs_src/arguments/optional/tutorial002_py310.py hl[7] *}
223|
224|Because the first parameter passed to `typer.Argument(default="World")` (the new "default" value) is `"World"`, **Typer** knows that this is an **optional** *CLI argument*, if no value is provided when calling it in the command line, it will have that default value of `"World"`.
225|
226|The `default` argument is the first one, so it's possible that you see code that passes the value without explicitly using `default=`, like:
227|
228|```Python
229|name: str = typer.Argument(...)
230|```
231|
232|...or like:
233|
234|```Python
235|name: str = typer.Argument("World")
236|```
237|
238|...but again, try to use `Annotated` if possible, that way your code in terms of Python will mean the same thing as with **Typer** and you won't have to remember any of these details.
--- END FILE: docs/tutorial/arguments/optional.md ---

1|# CLI Option Callback and Context
2|
3|In some occasions you might want to have some custom logic for a specific *CLI parameter* (for a *CLI option*  or *CLI argument*) that is executed with the value received from the terminal.
4|
5|In those cases you can use a *CLI parameter* callback function.
6|
7|## Validate *CLI parameters*
8|
9|For example, you could do some validation before the rest of the code is executed.
10|
11|{* docs_src/options/callback/tutorial001_an_py310.py hl[8:11,15] *}
12|
13|Here you pass a function to `typer.Option()` or `typer.Argument()` with the keyword argument `callback`.
14|
15|The function receives the value from the command line. It can do anything with it, and then return the value.
16|
17|In this case, if the `--name` is not `Camila` we raise a `typer.BadParameter()` exception.
18|
19|The `BadParameter` exception is special, it shows the error with the parameter that generated it.
20|
21|Check it:
22|
23|<div class="termy">
24|
25|```console
26|$ uv run python main.py --name Camila
27|
28|Hello Camila
29|
30|$ uv run python main.py --name Rick
31|
32|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS]
33|
34|// We get the error from the callback
35|Error: Invalid value for '--name': Only Camila is allowed
36|```
37|
38|</div>
39|
40|## Handling completion
41|
42|There's something to be aware of with callbacks and completion that requires some small special handling.
43|
44|But first let's just use completion in your shell (Bash, Zsh, Fish, or PowerShell).
45|
46|After installing completion (for your own Python package), when you use your CLI program and start adding a *CLI option* with `--` and then hit <kbd>TAB</kbd>, your shell will show you the available *CLI options* (the same for *CLI arguments*, etc).
47|
48|To check it quickly with the previous script use the `typer` command:
49|
50|<div class="termy">
51|
52|```console
53|// Hit the TAB key in your keyboard below where you see the: [TAB]
54|$ typer ./main.py [TAB][TAB]
55|
56|// Depending on your terminal/shell you will get some completion like this ✨
57|run    -- Run the provided Typer app.
58|utils  -- Extra utility commands for Typer apps.
59|
60|// Then try with "run" and --help
61|$ typer ./main.py run --help
62|
63|// You get a help text with your CLI options as you normally would
64|Usage: typer [PATH_OR_MODULE] run [OPTIONS]
65|
66|  Run the provided Typer app.
67|
68|Options:
69|  --name <str>
70|  --help       Show this message and exit.
71|
72|// Then try completion with your program
73|$ typer ./main.py run --[TAB][TAB]
74|
75|// You get completion for CLI options
76|--help  -- Show this message and exit.
77|--name
78|
79|// And you can run it as if it was with Python directly
80|$ typer ./main.py run --name Camila
81|
82|Hello Camila
83|```
84|
85|</div>
86|
87|### How shell completion works
88|
89|The way it works internally is that the shell/terminal will call your CLI program with some special environment variables (that hold the current *CLI parameters*, etc) and your CLI program will print some special values that the shell will use to present completion. All this is handled for you by **Typer** behind the scenes.
90|
91|But the main **important point** is that it is all based on values printed by your program that the shell reads.
92|
93|### Breaking completion in a callback
94|
95|Let's say that when the callback is running, we want to show a message saying that it's validating the name:
96|
97|{* docs_src/options/callback/tutorial002_an_py310.py hl[9] *}
98|
99|And because the callback will be called when the shell calls your program asking for completion, that message `"Validating name"` will be printed and it will break completion.
100|
101|It will look something like:
102|
103|<div class="termy">
104|
105|```console
106|// Run it normally
107|$ typer ./main.py run --name Camila
108|
109|// See the extra message "Validating name"
110|Validating name
111|Hello Camila
112|
113|$ typer ./main.py run --[TAB][TAB]
114|
115|// Some weird broken error message ⛔️
116|(eval):1: command not found: Validating
117|rutyper ./main.pyed Typer app.
118|```
119|
120|</div>
121|
122|### Fix completion - using the `Context`
123|
124|Every Typer application has a special object called a "Context" that is normally hidden.
125|
126|But you can access the context by declaring a function parameter of type `typer.Context`.
127|
128|The "context" has some additional data about the current execution of your program:
129|
130|{* docs_src/options/callback/tutorial003_an_py310.py hl[8:10] *}
131|
132|The `ctx.resilient_parsing` will be `True` when handling completion, so you can just return without printing anything else.
133|
134|But it will be `False` when calling the program normally. So you can continue the execution of your previous code.
135|
136|That's all is needed to fix completion. 🚀
137|
138|Check it:
139|
140|<div class="termy">
141|
142|```console
143|$ typer ./main.py run --[TAB][TAB]
144|
145|// Now it works correctly 🎉
146|--help  -- Show this message and exit.
147|--name
148|
149|// And you can call it normally
150|$ typer ./main.py run --name Camila
151|
152|Validating name
153|Hello Camila
154|```
155|
156|</div>
157|
158|## Using the `CallbackParam` object
159|
160|The same way you can access the `typer.Context` by declaring a function parameter with its value, you can declare another function parameter with type `typer.CallbackParam` to get the specific `Parameter` object.
161|
162|{* docs_src/options/callback/tutorial004_an_py310.py hl[8,11] *}
163|
164|It's probably not very common, but you could do it if you need it.
165|
166|For example if you had a callback that could be used by several *CLI parameters*, that way the callback could know which parameter is each time.
167|
168|Check it:
169|
170|<div class="termy">
171|
172|```console
173|$ uv run python main.py --name Camila
174|
175|Validating param: name
176|Hello Camila
177|```
178|
179|</div>
180|
181|## Technical Details
182|
183|Because you get the relevant data in the callback function based on standard Python type annotations, you get type checks and autocompletion in your editor for free.
184|
185|And **Typer** will make sure you get the function parameters you want.
186|
187|You don't have to worry about their names, their order, etc.
188|
189|As it's based on standard Python types, it "**just works**". ✨
190|
191|### Callback with type annotations
192|
193|You can get the `typer.Context` and the `typer.CallbackParam` simply by declaring a function parameter of each type.
194|
195|The order doesn't matter, the name of the function parameters doesn't matter.
196|
197|You could also get only the `typer.CallbackParam` and not the `typer.Context`, or vice versa, it will still work.
198|
199|### `value` function parameter
200|
201|The `value` function parameter in the callback can also have any name (e.g. `lastname`) and any type, but it should have the same type annotation as in the main function, because that's what it will receive.
202|
203|It's also possible to not declare its type. It will still work.
204|
205|And it's possible to not declare the `value` parameter at all, and, for example, only get the `typer.Context`. That will also work.
--- END FILE: docs/tutorial/options/callback-and-context.md ---

1|# CLI Options with Help
2|
3|You already saw how to add a help text for *CLI arguments* with the `help` parameter.
4|
5|Let's now do the same for *CLI options*:
6|
7|{* docs_src/options/help/tutorial001_an_py310.py hl[11:12] *}
8|
9|The same way as with `typer.Argument()`, we can put `typer.Option()` inside of `Annotated`.
10|
11|We can then pass the `help` keyword parameter:
12|
13|```Python
14|lastname: Annotated[str, typer.Option(help="this option does this and that")] = ""
15|```
16|
17|...to create the help for that *CLI option*.
18|
19|The same way as with `typer.Argument()`, **Typer** also supports the old style using the function parameter default value:
20|
21|```Python
22|lastname: str = typer.Option(default="", help="this option does this and that")
23|```
24|
25|Copy that example from above to a file `main.py`.
26|
27|Test it:
28|
29|<div class="termy">
30|
31|```console
32|$ uv run python main.py --help
33|
34|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS] {name}
35|
36|  Say hi to 'name', optionally with a --lastname.
37|
38|  If --formal is used, say hi very formally.
39|
40|Arguments:
41|  name  [required]
42|
43|Options:
44|  --lastname <str>        Last name of person to greet.
45|  --formal / --no-formal  Say hi formally.  [default: no-formal]
46|  --help                  Show this message and exit.
47|
48|// Now you have a help text for the --lastname and --formal CLI options 🎉
49|```
50|
51|</div>
52|
53|## *CLI Options* help panels
54|
55|The same as with *CLI arguments*, you can put the help for some *CLI options* in different panels to be shown with the `--help` option.
56|
57|Using Rich, you can set the `rich_help_panel` parameter to the name of the panel you want for each *CLI option*:
58|
59|{* docs_src/options/help/tutorial002_an_py310.py hl[15,21] *}
60|
61|Now, when you check the `--help` option, you will see a default panel named "`Options`" for the *CLI options* that don't have a custom `rich_help_panel`.
62|
63|And below you will see other panels for the *CLI options* that have a custom panel set in the `rich_help_panel` parameter:
64|
65|<div class="termy">
66|
67|```console
68|$ uv run python main.py --help
69|
70|<b> </b><font color="#F4BF75"><b>Usage: </b></font><b>main.py [OPTIONS] {name}                                </b>
71|<b>                                                                     </b>
72| Say hi to 'name', optionally with a <font color="#A1EFE4"><b>--lastname</b></font>.
73| If <font color="#6B9F98"><b>--formal</b></font><font color="#A5A5A1"> is used, say hi very formally.                          </font>
74|
75|<font color="#A5A5A1">╭─ Arguments ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮</font>
76|<font color="#A5A5A1">│ </font><font color="#F92672">*</font>    name      <font color="#F4BF75"><b><str></b></font>  <font color="#A6194C">[required]</font>                                  │
77|<font color="#A5A5A1">╰───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯</font>
78|<font color="#A5A5A1">╭─ Options ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮</font>
79|<font color="#A5A5A1">│ </font><font color="#A1EFE4"><b>--lastname</b></font>                  <font color="#F4BF75"><b><str></b></font>  Last name of person to greet.  │
80|<font color="#A5A5A1">│ </font><font color="#A1EFE4"><b>--help</b></font>                      <font color="#F4BF75"><b>    </b></font>  Show this message and exit.     │
81|<font color="#A5A5A1">╰───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯</font>
82|<font color="#A5A5A1">╭─ Customization and Utils ─────────────────────────────────────────╮</font>
83|<font color="#A5A5A1">│ </font><font color="#A1EFE4"><b>--formal</b></font>    <font color="#AE81FF"><b>--no-formal</b></font>      Say hi formally.                     │
84|<font color="#A5A5A1">│                              [default: no-formal]                 │</font>
85|<font color="#A5A5A1">│ </font><font color="#A1EFE4"><b>--debug</b></font>     <font color="#AE81FF"><b>--no-debug</b></font>       Enable debugging.                    │
86|<font color="#A5A5A1">│                              [default: no-debug]                  │</font>
87|<font color="#A5A5A1">╰───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯</font>
88|```
89|
90|</div>
91|
92|Here we have a custom *CLI options* panel named "`Customization and Utils`".
93|
94|## Help with style using Rich
95|
96|In a future section you will see how to use custom markup in the `help` for *CLI options* when reading about [Commands - Command Help](../commands/help.md#rich-markdown-and-markup).
97|
98|If you are in a hurry you can jump there, but otherwise, it would be better to continue reading here and following the tutorial in order.
99|
100|
101|## Hide default from help
102|
103|You can tell Typer to not show the default value in the help text with `show_default=False`:
104|
105|{* docs_src/options/help/tutorial003_an_py310.py hl[9] *}
106|
107|And it will no longer show the default value in the help text:
108|
109|<div class="termy">
110|
111|```console
112|$ uv run python main.py
113|
114|Hello Wade Wilson
115|
116|// Show the help
117|$ uv run python main.py --help
118|
119|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS]
120|
121|Options:
122|  --fullname <str>
123|  --help                Show this message and exit.
124|
125|// Notice there's no [default: Wade Wilson] 🔥
126|```
127|
128|</div>
129|
130|## Custom default string
131|
132|You can use the same `show_default` to pass a custom string (instead of a `bool`) to customize the default value to be shown in the help text:
133|
134|{* docs_src/options/help/tutorial004_an_py310.py hl[11] *}
135|
136|And it will be used in the help text:
137|
138|<div class="termy">
139|
140|```console
141|$ uv run python main.py
142|
143|Hello Wade Wilson
144|
145|// Show the help
146|$ uv run python main.py --help
147|
148|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS]
149|
150|Options:
151|  --fullname <str>      [default: (Deadpoolio the amazing's name)]
152|  --help                Show this message and exit.
153|
154|// Notice how it shows "(Deadpoolio the amazing's name)" instead of the actual default of "Wade Wilson"
155|```
156|
157|</div>
--- END FILE: docs/tutorial/options/help.md ---

1|# File
2|
3|Apart from `Path` *CLI parameters* you can also declare some types of "files".
4|
5|/// tip
6|
7|In most of the cases you are probably fine just using `Path`.
8|
9|You can read and write data with `Path` the same way.
10|
11|///
12|
13|The difference is that these types will give you a Python [file-like object](https://docs.python.org/3/glossary.html#term-file-object) instead of a Python [Path](https://docs.python.org/3/library/pathlib.html#basic-use).
14|
15|A "file-like object" is the same type of object returned by `open()` as in:
16|
17|```Python
18|with open("file.txt") as f:
19|    # Here f is the file-like object
20|    read_data = f.read()
21|    print(read_data)
22|```
23|
24|But in some special use cases you might want to use these special types. For example if you are migrating an existing application.
25|
26|## `FileText` reading
27|
28|`typer.FileText` gives you a file-like object for reading text, you will get `str` data from it.
29|
30|This means that even if your file has text written in a non-english language, e.g. a `text.txt` file with:
31|
32|```
33|la cigüeña trae al niño
34|```
35|
36|You will have a `str` with the text inside, e.g.:
37|
38|```Python
39|content = "la cigüeña trae al niño"
40|```
41|
42|instead of having `bytes`, e.g.:
43|
44|```Python
45|content = b"la cig\xc3\xbce\xc3\xb1a trae al ni\xc3\xb1o"
46|```
47|
48|You will get all the correct editor support, attributes, methods, etc for the file-like object:`
49|
50|{* docs_src/parameter_types/file/tutorial001_an_py310.py hl[9] *}
51|
52|Check it:
53|
54|<div class="termy">
55|
56|```console
57|// Create a quick text config
58|$ echo "some settings" > config.txt
59|
60|// Add another line to the config to test it
61|$ echo "some more settings" >> config.txt
62|
63|// Now run your program
64|$ uv run python main.py --config config.txt
65|
66|Config line: some settings
67|
68|Config line: some more settings
69|```
70|
71|</div>
72|
73|## `FileTextWrite`
74|
75|For writing text, you can use `typer.FileTextWrite`:
76|
77|{* docs_src/parameter_types/file/tutorial002_an_py310.py hl[9:10] *}
78|
79|This would be for writing human text, like:
80|
81|```
82|some settings
83|la cigüeña trae al niño
84|```
85|
86|...not to write binary `bytes`.
87|
88|Check it:
89|
90|<div class="termy">
91|
92|```console
93|$ uv run python main.py --config text.txt
94|
95|Config written
96|
97|// Check the contents of the file
98|$ cat text.txt
99|
100|Some config written by the app
101|```
102|
103|</div>
104|
105|/// note | Technical Details
106|
107|`typer.FileTextWrite` is a just a convenience class.
108|
109|It's the same as using `typer.FileText` and setting `mode="w"`. You will learn about `mode` later below.
110|
111|///
112|
113|## `FileBinaryRead`
114|
115|To read binary data you can use `typer.FileBinaryRead`.
116|
117|You will receive `bytes` from it.
118|
119|It's useful for reading binary files like images:
120|
121|{* docs_src/parameter_types/file/tutorial003_an_py310.py hl[9] *}
122|
123|Check it:
124|
125|<div class="termy">
126|
127|```console
128|$ uv run python main.py --file lena.jpg
129|
130|Processed bytes total: 512
131|Processed bytes total: 1024
132|Processed bytes total: 1536
133|Processed bytes total: 2048
134|```
135|
136|</div>
137|
138|## `FileBinaryWrite`
139|
140|To write binary data you can use `typer.FileBinaryWrite`.
141|
142|You would write `bytes` to it.
143|
144|It's useful for writing binary files like images.
145|
146|Have in mind that you have to pass `bytes` to its `.write()` method, not `str`.
147|
148|If you have a `str`, you have to encode it first to get `bytes`.
149|
150|{* docs_src/parameter_types/file/tutorial004_an_py310.py hl[9] *}
151|
152|<div class="termy">
153|
154|```console
155|$ uv run python main.py --file binary.dat
156|
157|Binary file written
158|
159|// Check the binary file was created
160|$ ls ./binary.dat
161|
162|./binary.dat
163|```
164|
165|</div>
166|
167|## File *CLI parameter* configurations
168|
169|You can use several configuration parameters for these types (classes) in `typer.Option()` and `typer.Argument()`:
170|
171|* `mode`: controls the "[mode](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#open)" to open the file with.
172|    * It's automatically set for you by using the classes above.
173|    * Read more about it below.
174|* `encoding`: to force a specific encoding, e.g. `"utf-8"`.
175|* `lazy`: delay <abbr title="input and output, reading and writing files">I/O</abbr> operations. Automatic by default.
176|    * By default, when writing files, Typer will generate a file-like object that is not yet the actual file. Once you start writing, it will go, open the file and start writing to it, but not before. This is mainly useful to avoid creating the file until you start writing to it. It's normally safe to leave this automatic. But you can overwrite it setting `lazy=False`. By default, it's `lazy=True` for writing and `lazy=False` for reading.
177|* `atomic`: if true, all writes will actually go to a temporal file and then moved to the final destination after completing. This is useful with files modified frequently by several users/programs.
178|
179|## Advanced `mode`
180|
181|By default, **Typer** will configure the [`mode`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#open) for you:
182|
183|* `typer.FileText`: `mode="r"`, to read text.
184|* `typer.FileTextWrite`: `mode="w"`, to write text.
185|* `typer.FileBinaryRead`: `mode="rb"`, to read binary data.
186|* `typer.FileBinaryWrite`: `mode="wb"`, to write binary data.
187|
188|### Note about `FileTextWrite`
189|
190|`typer.FileTextWrite` is actually just a convenience class. It's the same as using `typer.FileText` with `mode="w"`.
191|
192|But it's probably shorter and more intuitive as you can get it with autocompletion in your editor by just starting to type `typer.File`... just like the other classes.
193|
194|### Customize `mode`
195|
196|You can override the `mode` from the defaults above.
197|
198|For example, you could use `mode="a"` to write "appending" to the same file:
199|
200|{* docs_src/parameter_types/file/tutorial005_an_py310.py hl[9] *}
201|
202|/// tip
203|
204|As you are manually setting `mode="a"`, you can use `typer.FileText` or `typer.FileTextWrite`, both will work.
205|
206|///
207|
208|Check it:
209|
210|<div class="termy">
211|
212|```console
213|$ uv run python main.py --config config.txt
214|
215|Config line written
216|
217|// Run your program a couple more times to see how it appends instead of overwriting
218|$ uv run python main.py --config config.txt

223|

228|
229|This is a single line

1|# Testing
2|
3|Testing **Typer** applications is very easy with [pytest](https://docs.pytest.org/en/latest/).
4|
5|Let's say you have an application `app/main.py` with:
6|
7|{* docs_src/testing/app01_py310/main.py *}
8|
9|So, you would use it like:
10|
11|<div class="termy">
12|
13|```console
14|$ uv run python main.py Camila --city Berlin
15|
16|Hello Camila
17|Let's have a coffee in Berlin
18|```
19|
20|</div>
21|
22|And the directory also has an empty `app/__init__.py` file.
23|
24|So, the `app` is a "Python package".
25|
26|## Test the app
27|
28|### Import and create a `CliRunner`
29|
30|Create another file/module `app/test_main.py`.
31|
32|Import `CliRunner` and create a `runner` object.
33|
34|This runner is what will "invoke" or "call" your command line application.
35|
36|{* docs_src/testing/app01_py310/test_main.py hl[1,5] *}
37|
38|/// tip
39|
40|It's important that the name of the file starts with `test_`, that way pytest will be able to detect it and use it automatically.
41|
42|///
43|
44|### Call the app
45|
46|Then create a function `test_app()`.
47|
48|And inside of the function, use the `runner` to `invoke` the application.
49|
50|The first parameter to `runner.invoke()` is a `Typer` app.
51|
52|The second parameter is a `list` of `str`, with all the text you would pass in the command line, right as you would pass it:
53|
54|{* docs_src/testing/app01_py310/test_main.py hl[8,9] *}
55|
56|/// tip
57|
58|The name of the function has to start with `test_`, that way pytest can detect it and use it automatically.
59|
60|///
61|
62|### Check the result
63|
64|Then, inside of the test function, add `assert` statements to ensure that everything in the result of the call is as it should be.
65|
66|{* docs_src/testing/app01_py310/test_main.py hl[10,11,12] *}
67|
68|Here we are checking that the exit code is 0, as it is for programs that exit without errors.
69|
70|Then we check that the text printed to "standard output" contains the text that our CLI program prints.
71|
72|/// tip
73|
74|You could also check the output sent to "standard error" (`stderr`) or "standard output" (`stdout`) independently by accessing `result.stdout` and `result.stderr` in your tests.
75|
76|///
77|
78|/// note
79|
80|If you need a refresher about what is "standard output" and "standard error" check the section in [Printing and Colors: "Standard Output" and "Standard Error"](printing.md#standard-output-and-standard-error).
81|
82|///
83|
84|### Call `pytest`
85|
86|Then you can call `pytest` in your directory and it will run your tests:
87|
88|<div class="termy">
89|
90|```console
91|$ uv run pytest
92|
93|================ test session starts ================
94|platform linux -- Python 3.10, pytest-5.3.5, py-1.8.1, pluggy-0.13.1
95|rootdir: /home/user/code/superawesome-cli/app
96|plugins: forked-1.1.3, xdist-1.31.0, cov-2.8.1
97|collected 1 item
98|
99|---> 100%
100|
101|test_main.py <span style="color: green; white-space: pre;">.                                 [100%]</span>
102|
103|<span style="color: green;">================= 1 passed in 0.03s =================</span>
104|```
105|
106|</div>
107|
108|## Testing input
109|
110|If you have a CLI with prompts, like:
111|
112|{* docs_src/testing/app02_an_py310/main.py hl[9] *}
113|
114|That you would use like:
115|
116|<div class="termy">
117|
118|```console
119|$ uv run python main.py Camila
120|
121|# Email: $ camila@example.com
122|
123|Hello Camila, your email is: camila@example.com
124|```
125|
126|</div>
127|
128|You can test the input typed in the terminal using `input="camila@example.com\n"`.
129|
130|This is because what you type in the terminal goes to "**standard input**" and is handled by the operating system as if it was a "virtual file".
131|
132|/// note
133|
134|If you need a refresher about what is "standard output", "standard error", and "standard input" check the section in [Printing and Colors: "Standard Output" and "Standard Error"](printing.md#standard-output-and-standard-error).
135|
136|///
137|
138|When you hit the <kbd>ENTER</kbd> key after typing the email, that is just a "new line character". And in Python that is represented with `"\n"`.
139|
140|So, if you use `input="camila@example.com\n"` it means: "type `camila@example.com` in the terminal, then hit the <kbd>ENTER</kbd> key":
141|
142|{* docs_src/testing/app02_py310/test_main.py hl[9] *}
143|
144|## Test a function
145|
146|If you have a script and you never created an explicit `typer.Typer` app, like:
147|
148|{* docs_src/testing/app03_py310/main.py hl[9] *}
149|
150|...you can still test it, by creating an app during testing:
151|
152|{* docs_src/testing/app03_py310/test_main.py hl[6,7,13] *}
153|
154|Of course, if you are testing that script, it's probably easier/cleaner to just create the explicit `typer.Typer` app in `main.py` instead of creating it just during the test.
155|
156|But if you want to keep it that way, e.g. because it's a simple example in documentation, then you can use that trick.
157|
158|### About the `app.command` decorator
159|
160|Notice the `app.command()(main)`.
161|
162|If it's not obvious what it's doing, continue reading...
163|
164|You would normally write something like:
165|
166|```Python
167|@app.command()
168|def main(name: str = "World"):
169|    # Some code here
170|```
171|
172|But `@app.command()` is just a decorator.
173|
174|That's equivalent to:
175|
176|```Python
177|def main(name: str = "World"):
178|    # Some code here
179|
180|decorator = app.command()
181|
182|new_main = decorator(main)
183|main = new_main
184|```
185|
186|`app.command()` returns a function (`decorator`) that takes another function as it's only parameter (`main`).
187|
188|And by using the `@something` you normally tell Python to replace the thing below (the function `main`) with the return of the `decorator` function (`new_main`).
189|
190|Now, in the specific case of **Typer**, the decorator doesn't change the original function. It registers it internally and returns it unmodified.
191|
192|So, `new_main` is actually the same original `main`.
193|
194|So, in the case of **Typer**, as it doesn't really modify the decorated function, that would be equivalent to:
195|
196|```Python
197|def main(name: str = "World"):
198|    # Some code here
199|
200|decorator = app.command()
201|
202|decorator(main)
203|```
204|
205|But then we don't need to create the variable `decorator` to use it below, we can just use it directly:
206|
207|```Python
208|def main(name: str = "World"):
209|    # Some code here
210|
211|app.command()(main)
212|```
213|
214|...that's it. It's still probably simpler to just create the explicit `typer.Typer` in the `main.py` file 😅.
--- END FILE: docs/tutorial/testing.md ---

1|# Progress Bar
2|
3|If you are executing an operation that can take some time, you can inform it to the user. 🤓
4|
5|## Progress Bar
6|
7|You can use [Rich's Progress Display](https://rich.readthedocs.io/en/stable/progress.html) to show a progress bar, for example:
8|
9|{* docs_src/progressbar/tutorial001_py310.py hl[4,12] *}
10|
11|You put the thing that you want to iterate over inside of Rich's `track()`, and then iterate over that.
12|
13|Check it:
14|
15|<div class="termy">
16|
17|```console
18|$ uv run python main.py
19|
20|---> 100%
21|
22|Processed 100 things.
23|```
24|
25|</div>
26|
27|...actually, it will look a lot prettier. ✨ But I can't show you the animation here in the docs. 😅
28|
29|The colors and information will look something like this:
30|
31|<div class="termy">
32|
33|```console
34|$ uv run python main.py
35|
36|Processing... <font color="#F92672">━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━╸</font><font color="#3A3A3A">━━━━━━━━━━</font> <font color="#AE81FF"> 74%</font> <font color="#A1EFE4">0:00:01</font>
37|```
38|
39|</div>
40|
41|## Spinner
42|
43|When you don't know how long the operation will take, you can use a spinner instead.
44|
45|Rich allows you to display many things in complex and advanced ways.
46|
47|For example, this will show two spinners:
48|
49|{* docs_src/progressbar/tutorial002_py310.py hl[4,11:18] *}
50|
51|I can't show you the beautiful animation here in the docs. 😅
52|
53|But at some point in time it will look like this (imagine it's spinning). 🤓
54|
55|<div class="termy">
56|
57|```console
58|$ uv run python main.py
59|
60|<font color="#A6E22E">⠹</font> Processing...
61|<font color="#A6E22E">⠹</font> Preparing...
62|```
63|
64|</div>
65|
66|You can learn more about it in the [Rich docs for Progress Display](https://rich.readthedocs.io/en/stable/progress.html).
67|
68|## Typer `progressbar`
69|
70|If you can, you should use **Rich** as explained above, it has more features, it's more advanced, and can display information more beautifully. ✨
71|
72|/// tip
73|
74|If you can use Rich, use the information above, the Rich docs, and skip the rest of this page. 😎
75|
76|///
77|
78|But if you can't use Rich and have it disabled, Typer comes with a simple utility to show progress bars.
79|
80|### Use `typer.progressbar`
81|
82|/// tip
83|
84|Remember, you are much better off using [Rich](https://rich.readthedocs.io/) for this. 😎
85|
86|///
87|
88|You can use `typer.progressbar()` with a `with` statement, as in:
89|
90|```Python
91|with typer.progressbar(something) as progress:
92|    pass
93|```
94|
95|And you pass as function argument to `typer.progressbar()` the thing that you would normally iterate over.
96|
97|{* docs_src/progressbar/tutorial003_py310.py hl[11] *}
98|
99|So, if you have a list of users, this could be:
100|
101|```Python
102|users = ["Camila", "Rick", "Morty"]
103|
104|with typer.progressbar(users) as progress:
105|    pass
106|```
107|
108|And the `with` statement using `typer.progressbar()` gives you an object that you can iterate over, just like if it was the same thing that you would iterate over normally.
109|
110|But by iterating over this object **Typer** will know to update the progress bar:
111|
112|```Python
113|users = ["Camila", "Rick", "Morty"]
114|
115|with typer.progressbar(users) as progress:
116|    for user in progress:
117|        typer.echo(user)
118|```
119|
120|/// tip
121|
122|Notice that there are 2 levels of code blocks. One for the `with` statement and one for the `for` statement.
123|
124|///
125|
126|/// note
127|
128|This is mostly useful for operations that take some time.
129|
130|In the example above we are faking it with `time.sleep()`.
131|
132|///
133|
134|Check it:
135|
136|<div class="termy">
137|
138|```console
139|$ uv run python main.py
140|
141|---> 100%
142|
143|Processed 100 things.
144|```
145|
146|</div>
147|
148|### Setting a Progress Bar `length`
149|
150|/// tip
151|
152|Remember, you are much better off using [Rich](https://rich.readthedocs.io/) for this. 😎
153|
154|///
155|
156|The progress bar is generated from the length of the iterable (e.g. the list of users).
157|
158|But if the length is not available (for example, with something that fetches a new user from a web API each time) you can pass an explicit `length` to `typer.progressbar()`.
159|
160|{* docs_src/progressbar/tutorial004_py310.py hl[18] *}
161|
162|Check it:
163|
164|<div class="termy">
165|
166|```console
167|$ uv run python main.py
168|
169|---> 100%
170|
171|Processed 100 user IDs.
172|```
173|
174|</div>
175|
176|#### About the function with `yield`
177|
178|If you hadn't seen something like that `yield` above, that's a "[generator](https://docs.python.org/3/glossary.html#term-generator)".
179|
180|You can iterate over that function with a `for` and at each iteration it will give you the value at `yield`.
181|
182|`yield` is like a `return` that gives values multiple times and let's you use the function in a `for` loop.
183|
184|For example:
185|
186|```Python
187|def iterate_user_ids():
188|    # Let's imagine this is a web API, not a range()
189|    for i in range(100):
190|        yield i
191|
192|
193|for i in iterate_user_ids():
194|    print(i)
195|```
196|
197|would print each of the "user IDs" (here it's just the numbers from `0` to `99`).
198|
199|### Add a `label`
200|
201|/// tip
202|
203|Remember, you are much better off using [Rich](https://rich.readthedocs.io/) for this. 😎
204|
205|///
206|
207|You can also set a `label`:
208|
209|{* docs_src/progressbar/tutorial005_py310.py hl[11] *}
210|
211|Check it:
212|
213|<div class="use-termynal">
214|<span data-ty="input">python main.py</span>
215|<span data-ty="progress" data-ty-prompt="Processing"></span>
216|<span data-ty>Processed 100 things.</span>
217|</div>
218|
219|## Iterate manually
220|
221|If you need to manually iterate over something and update the progress bar irregularly, you can do it by not passing an iterable but just a `length` to `typer.progressbar()`.
222|
223|And then calling the `.update()` method in the object from the `with` statement:
224|
225|{* docs_src/progressbar/tutorial006_py310.py hl[11,17] *}
226|
227|Check it:
228|
229|<div class="use-termynal">
230|<span data-ty="input">python main.py</span>
231|<span data-ty="progress" data-ty-prompt="Batches"></span>
232|<span data-ty>Processed 1000 things in batches.</span>
233|</div>

1|# One File Per Command
2|
3|When your CLI application grows, you can split it into multiple files and modules. This pattern helps maintain a clean and organized code structure. ✨
4|
5|This tutorial will show you how to use `add_typer` to create sub commands and organize your commands in multiple files.
6|
7|We will create a simple CLI with the following commands:
8|
9|- `version`
10|- `users add 'name'`
11|- `users delete 'name'`
12|
13|## CLI structure
14|
15|Here is the structure we'll be working with:
16|
17|```text
18|mycli/
19|├── __init__.py
20|├── main.py
21|├── users/
22|│   ├── __init__.py
23|│   ├── add.py
24|│   └── delete.py
25|└── version.py
26|```
27|
28|`mycli` will be our <abbr title="a directory with an __init__.py file, it can be imported">package</abbr>, and it will contain the following modules:
29|
30|- `main.py`: The main <abbr title="a Python file that can be imported">module</abbr> that will import the `version` and `users` modules.
31|- `version.py`: A <abbr title="a Python file that can be imported">module</abbr> that will contain the `version` command.
32|- `users/`: A <abbr title="another directory with an __init__.py file, it can also be imported">package</abbr> (inside of our `mycli` package) that will contain the `add` and `delete` commands.
33|
34|## Implementation
35|
36|Let's start implementing our CLI! 🚀
37|
38|We'll create the `version` module, the `main` module, and the `users` package.
39|
40|### Version Module (`version.py`)
41|
42|Let's start by creating the `version` module. This module will contain the `version` command.
43|
44|{* docs_src/one_file_per_command/app_py310/version.py *}
45|
46|In this file we are creating a new Typer app instance for the `version` command.
47|
48|This is not required in single-file applications, but in the case of multi-file applications it will allow us to include this command in the main application using `app.add_typer()`.
49|
50|Let's see that next!
51|
52|### Main Module (`main.py`)
53|
54|The main module will be the entry point of the application. It will import the version module and the users module.
55|
56|/// tip
57|
58|We'll see how to implement the users module in the next section.
59|
60|///
61|
62|{* docs_src/one_file_per_command/app_py310/main.py hl[8,9] *}
63|
64|In this module, we import the `version` and `users` modules and add them to the main app using `app.add_typer()`.
65|
66|For the `users` module, we specify the name as `"users"` to group the commands under the `users` sub-command.
67|
68|Notice that we didn't add a name for the `version_app` Typer app. Because of this, Typer will add the commands (just one in this case) declared in the `version_app` directly at the top level. So, there will be a top-level `version` sub-command.
69|
70|But for `users`, we add a name `"users"`, this way those commands will be under the sub-command `users` instead of at the top level. So, there will be a `users add` and `users delete` sub-sub-commands. 😅
71|
72|/// tip
73|
74|If you want a command to group the included commands in a sub-app, add a name.
75|
76|If you want to include the commands from a sub-app directly at the top level, don't add a name, or set it to `None`. 🤓
77|
78|///
79|
80|Let's now create the `users` module with the `add` and `delete` commands.
81|
82|### Users Add Command (`users/add.py`)
83|
84|{* docs_src/one_file_per_command/app_py310/users/add.py *}
85|
86|Like the `version` module, we create a new Typer app instance for the `users/add` command. This allows us to include the `add` command in the users app.
87|
88|### Users Delete Command (`users/delete.py`)
89|
90|{* docs_src/one_file_per_command/app_py310/users/delete.py *}
91|
92|And once again, we create a new Typer app instance for the `users/delete` command. This allows us to include the `delete` command in the users app.
93|
94|### Users' app (`users/__init__.py`)
95|
96|Finally, we need to create an `__init__.py` file in the `users` directory to define the `users` app.
97|
98|{* docs_src/one_file_per_command/app_py310/users/__init__.py *}
99|
100|Similarly to the `version` module, we create a new `Typer` app instance for the `users` module. This allows us to include the `add` and `delete` commands in the users app.
101|
102|## Running the Application
103|
104|Now we are ready to run the application! 😎
105|
106|To run the application, you can execute it as a Python module:
107|
108|<div class="termy">
109|
110|```console
111|$ uv run python -m mycli.main version
112|
113|My CLI Version 1.0
114|
115|$ uv run python -m mycli.main users add Camila
116|
117|Adding user: Camila
118|```
119|
120|</div>
121|
122|And if you built a package and installed your app, you can then use the `mycli` command:
123|
124|<div class="termy">
125|
126|```console
127|$ mycli version
128|
129|My CLI Version 1.0
130|
131|$ mycli users add Camila
132|
133|Adding user: Camila
134|```
135|
136|</div>
137|
138|## Callbacks
139|
140|Have in mind that if you include a sub-app with `app.add_typer()` **without a name**, the commands will be added to the top level, so **only the top level callback** (if there's any) will be used, the one declared in the main app.
141|
142|If you **want to use a callback** for a sub-app, you need to include the sub-app **with a name**, which creates a sub-command grouping the commands in that sub-app. 🤓
143|
144|In the example above, if the `users` sub-app had a callback, it would be used. But if the `version` sub-app had a callback, it would not be used, because the `version` sub-app was included without a name.
--- END FILE: docs/tutorial/one-file-per-command.md ---

1|# Commands
2|
3|We have seen how to create a CLI program with possibly several *CLI options* and *CLI arguments*.
4|
5|But **Typer** allows you to create CLI programs with several commands (also known as subcommands).
6|
7|For example, the program `git` has several commands.
8|
9|One command of `git` is `git push`. And `git push` in turn takes its own *CLI arguments* and *CLI options*.
10|
11|For example:
12|
13|<div class="termy">
14|
15|```console
16|// The push command with no parameters
17|$ git push
18|
19|---> 100%
20|
21|// The push command with one CLI option --set-upstream and 2 CLI arguments
22|$ git push --set-upstream origin master
23|
24|---> 100%
25|```
26|
27|</div>
28|
29|Another command of `git` is `git pull`, it also has some *CLI parameters*.
30|
31|It's like if the same big program `git` had several small programs inside.
32|
33|/// tip
34|
35|A command looks the same as a *CLI argument*, it's just some name without a preceding `--`. But commands have a predefined name, and are used to group different sets of functionalities into the same CLI application.
36|
37|///
38|
39|## Command or subcommand
40|
41|It's common to call a CLI program a "command".
42|
43|But when one of these programs have subcommands, those subcommands are also frequently called just "commands".
44|
45|Have that in mind so you don't get confused.
46|
47|Here I'll use **CLI application** or **program** to refer to the program you are building in Python with Typer, and **command** to refer to one of these "subcommands" of your program.
48|
49|## A CLI application with multiple commands
50|
51|**Typer** allows creating CLI applications with multiple commands/subcommands.
52|
53|Now that you know how to create an explicit `typer.Typer()` application and add one command, let's see how to add multiple commands.
54|
55|Let's say that we have a CLI application to manage users.
56|
57|We'll have a command to `create` users and another command to `delete` them.
58|
59|To begin, let's say it can only create and delete one single predefined user:
60|
61|{* docs_src/commands/index/tutorial002_py310.py hl[6,11] *}
62|
63|Now we have a CLI application with 2 commands, `create` and `delete`:
64|
65|<div class="termy">
66|
67|```console
68|// Check the help
69|$ uv run python main.py --help
70|
71|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...
72|
73|Options:
74|  --install-completion  Install completion for the current shell.
75|  --show-completion     Show completion for the current shell, to copy it or customize the installation.
76|  --help                Show this message and exit.
77|
78|Commands:
79|  create
80|  delete
81|
82|// Test them
83|$ uv run python main.py create
84|
85|Creating user: Hiro Hamada
86|
87|$ uv run python main.py delete
88|
89|Deleting user: Hiro Hamada
90|
91|// Now we have 2 commands! 🎉
92|```
93|
94|</div>
95|
96|Notice that the help text now shows the 2 commands: `create` and `delete`.
97|
98|/// tip
99|
100|By default, the names of the commands are generated from the function name.
101|
102|///
103|
104|## Show the help message if no command is given
105|
106|By default, we need to specify `--help` to get the command's help page.
107|
108|However, by setting `no_args_is_help=True` when defining the `typer.Typer()` application, the help function will be shown whenever no argument is given:
109|
110|{* docs_src/commands/index/tutorial003_py310.py hl[3] *}
111|
112|Now we can run this:
113|
114|<div class="termy">
115|
116|```console
117|// Check the help without having to type --help
118|$ uv run python main.py
119|
120|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...
121|
122|Options:
123|  --install-completion  Install completion for the current shell.
124|  --show-completion     Show completion for the current shell, to copy it or customize the installation.
125|  --help                Show this message and exit.
126|
127|Commands:
128|  create
129|  delete
130|```
131|
132|</div>
133|
134|
135|## Sorting of the commands
136|
137|Note that by design, **Typer** shows the commands in the order they've been declared.
138|
139|So, if we take our original example, with `create` and `delete` commands, and reverse the order in the Python file:
140|
141|{* docs_src/commands/index/tutorial004_py310.py hl[7,12] *}
142|
143|Then we will see the `delete` command first in the help output:
144|
145|<div class="termy">
146|
147|```console
148|// Check the help
149|$ uv run python main.py --help
150|
151|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...
152|
153|Options:
154|  --install-completion  Install completion for the current shell.
155|  --show-completion     Show completion for the current shell, to copy it or customize the installation.
156|  --help                Show this message and exit.
157|
158|Commands:
159|  delete
160|  create
161|```
162|
163|</div>
164|
165|## Decorator Technical Details
166|
167|When you use `@app.command()` the function under the decorator is registered in the **Typer** application and is then used later by the application.
168|
169|But Typer doesn't modify that function itself, the function is left as is.
170|
171|That means that if your function is simple enough that you could create it without using `typer.Option()` or `typer.Argument()`, you could use the same function for a **Typer** application and a **FastAPI** application putting both decorators on top, or similar tricks.

1|# Alternatives, Inspiration and Comparisons
2|
3|What inspired **Typer**, how it compares to other alternatives and what it learned from them.
4|
5|## Intro
6|
7|**Typer** wouldn't exist if not for the previous work of others.
8|
9|There have been many tools created before that have helped inspire its creation.
10|
11|## Previous tools
12|
13|### [`argparse`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/argparse.html)
14|
15|`argparse` is the Python standard library's module to write CLIs.
16|
17|It provides a better alternative than reading the *CLI Parameters* as a `list` of `str` and parsing everything by hand.
18|
19|/// tip | Inspired **Typer** to
20|
21|Provide a better development experience than just reading *CLI Parameters* by hand.
22|
23|///
24|
25|### [Hug](https://hugapi.github.io/hug/)
26|
27|Hug is a library to create APIs and CLIs, it uses parameters in functions to declare the required data.
28|
29|It inspired a lot of the ideas in **FastAPI** and **Typer**.
30|
31|/// tip | Inspired **Typer** to
32|
33|Use function parameters to declare *CLI arguments* and *CLI options* as it simplifies a lot the development experience.
34|
35|///
36|
37|### [Plac](https://plac.readthedocs.io/en/latest/)
38|
39|Plac is another library to create CLIs using parameters in functions, similar to Hug.
40|
41|/// tip | Inspired **Typer** to
42|
43|Provide a simple way to use a function as a command line app, without having to create a complete app, with `typer.run(some_function)`.
44|
45|///
46|
47|### [Pydantic](https://pydantic-docs.helpmanual.io/)
48|
49|Pydantic is a library to handle data validation using standard modern Python type annotations.
50|
51|It powers **FastAPI** underneath.
52|
53|It is not used by **Typer**, but it inspired a lot of the design (through **FastAPI**).
54|
55|/// tip | Inspired **Typer** to
56|
57|Use standard Python type annotations to declare types instead of library-specific types or classes and use them for data validation and documentation.
58|
59|///
60|
61|### [Click](https://click.palletsprojects.com)
62|
63|Click is one of the most widely used libraries to create CLIs in Python.
64|
65|It's a very powerful tool and there are many CLIs built with it. It is what powers **Typer** underneath.
66|
67|It also uses functions with parameters for *CLI arguments* and *CLI options*, but the declaration of the specific *CLI arguments*, *CLI options*, types, etc, is done in decorators on top of the function. This requires some code repetition (e.g. a *CLI Option* name `--verbose` and a variable name `verbose`) and synchronization between two places related to the same information (the decorator and the parameter function).
68|
69|It uses decorators on top of functions to modify the actual value of those functions, converting them to instances of a specific class. This is a clever trick, but code editors can't provide great support for autocompletion that way.
70|
71|It was built with some great ideas and design using the features available in the language at the time (Python 2.x).
72|
73|/// tip | **Typer** builds on top of Click functionality
74|
75|It has <abbr title="included Click's source code internally, instead of installing it as a third party package">vendored</abbr> Click version 8.3.1 and adds a layer on top of it.
76|
77|Typer aims to make the code simpler and easier to use, with autocompletion everywhere, etc, while still providing many of the powerful features of Click underneath.
78|
79|As someone pointed out: <em>["Nice to see it is built on Click but adds the type stuff. Me gusta!"](https://twitter.com/fishnets88/status/1210126833745838080)</em>
80|
81|///
82|
83|### [`click-completion`](https://github.com/click-contrib/click-completion)
84|
85|`click-completion` is a plug-in for Click. It was created to extend completion support for shells when Click only had support for Bash completion.
86|
87|Previous versions of **Typer** had deep integrations with `click-completion` and used it as an optional dependency. But now all the completion logic is implemented internally in **Typer** itself, the internal logic was heavily inspired and using some parts of `click-completion`.
88|
89|And now **Typer** improved it to have new features, tests, some bug fixes (for issues in plain `click-completion` and Click), and better support for shells, including modern versions of PowerShell (e.g. the default versions that come with Windows 10).
90|
91|/// tip | Inspired **Typer** to
92|
93|Provide auto completion for all the shells.
94|
95|///
96|
97|### [FastAPI](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/)
98|
99|I created **FastAPI** to provide an easy way to build APIs with autocompletion for everything in the code (and some other [features](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/features/)).
100|
101|**Typer** is the "FastAPI of CLIs".
102|
103|It uses the same design and usage of FastAPI as much as possible. So, if you have used FastAPI, you know how to use Typer.
--- END FILE: docs/alternatives.md ---

1|# Vendored Click
2|
3|/// note
4|
5|This is historical information, if you are just learning Typer from scratch, you don't need to read it. ☕️
6|
7|///
8|
9|Typer used to depend on [Click](https://click.palletsprojects.com/), a popular tool for building CLIs in Python, as an external dependency.
10|
11|Since version 0.26.0, Typer has vendored Click (included Click's source code internally, instead of installing it as a third party package) and has unified the code interactions between Typer and the embedded Click source code for easier maintainability in the future.
12|
13|Note that some Click functionality will not be available anymore in the future, as we continue to improve and extend Typer's codebase.
14|
15|## Breaking Changes
16|
17|Typer used to support extracting the internal Click app from a Typer app to use and modify it with any Click functionality. For example, to add Click-specific plug-ins.
18|
19|The same way, it supported adding Click-specific types to override the default Typer ones.
20|
21|Using Click directly was an edge case feature that was not commonly used, and it is no longer supported. If your app depended specifically on this, you will need to either migrate it to use plain Typer, or migrate it to use Click directly instead of Typer.
22|
23|## Codebase Compatibility Improvements
24|
25|Because Typer used to depend on Click, any new features or changes in newer Click versions could break compatibility in Typer.
26|
27|The Click team has always been very helpful and supportive with Typer. But still, this dependency interaction would cause extra effort and burden for both the Typer team and the Click team.
28|
29|Now that Typer continues evolving, starting from a fixed copy of Click's source code, any changes in Click's codebase will not affect Typer.
30|
31|The Typer team will not need to make sure there are workarounds for changes in new versions of Click, and the Click team will not need to consider additional edge cases caused by Typer.
32|
33|## Compatibility Improvements for Your Apps
34|
35|The fact that Typer depended on Click caused an additional ongoing issue that could happen from time to time to user projects.
36|
37|Many packages come with a CLI, some of them could use Click, some could use Typer.
38|
39|Some of these packages could require a recent version of Click that Typer still didn't support, but as all these package dependencies would belong to the same project, there would be conflicts.
40|
41|In these cases, the package that depended on the newer version of Click would require installing it, but the other package that used Typer would break. Or if there were version pins, some combinations of packages would not be installable together.
42|
43|Across different versions of Click through time, there were many changes needed in Typer to make it all compatible with multiple versions of Click at the same time.
44|
45|Now that Typer and Click are decoupled, a package could depend on a newer version of Click, while another package that uses Typer would continue working as normally, as that Typer version would bundle anything necessary from Click's source code to work.
46|
47|## Future Improvements
48|
49|Both the Click team and the Typer team have future improvements planned, not having to coordinate with each other for compatibility will simplify the work of both teams.
50|
51|In some cases feature ideas could overlap, and could have caused incompatibilities. Now this won't be a problem as each team can focus on each project independently.
52|
53|## Typer Changes
54|
55|After vendoring Click, Typer will reduce, simplify and refactor parts of the vendored Click code that are not necessary for Typer, or that could be done in a different way to facilitate future improvements in Typer.
56|
57|Then Typer will gradually introduce new features and improvements that have been planned for a while but were too difficult to implement before this.
58|
59|## User Focus
60|
61|These decisions are all carefully planned and based on real world use cases extracted from the official Typer developer survey, including the tradeoff between the potential breaking changes for some use cases and the planned future features and improvements that will be enabled.
62|
63|## Thank You Click
64|
65|Click has been the foundation building block of Typer and most CLI's in Python (through Typer or directly with Click).
66|
67|We wouldn't be here without Click, and we are very grateful for all the work that the Click team has done.
68|
69|Thank you Click! 🙇
--- END FILE: docs/tutorial/click.md ---

1|# Typer Callback
2|
3|When you create an `app = typer.Typer()` it works as a group of commands.
4|
5|And you can create multiple commands with it.
6|
7|Each of those commands can have their own *CLI parameters*.
8|
9|But as those *CLI parameters* are handled by each of those commands, they don't allow us to create *CLI parameters* for the main CLI application itself.
10|
11|But we can use `@app.callback()` for that.
12|
13|It's very similar to `@app.command()`, but it declares the *CLI parameters* for the main CLI application (before the commands):
14|
15|{* docs_src/commands/callback/tutorial001_py310.py hl[25,26,27,28,29,30,31,32] *}
16|
17|Here we create a `callback` with a `--verbose` *CLI option*.
18|
19|/// tip
20|
21|After getting the `--verbose` flag, we modify a global `state`, and we use it in the other commands.
22|
23|There are other ways to achieve the same, but this will suffice for this example.
24|
25|///
26|
27|And as we added a docstring to the callback function, by default it will be extracted and used as the help text.
28|
29|Check it:
30|
31|<div class="termy">
32|
33|```console
34|// Check the help
35|$ uv run python main.py --help
36|
37|// Notice the main help text, extracted from the callback function: "Manage users in the awesome CLI app."
38|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...
39|
40|  Manage users in the awesome CLI app.
41|
42|Options:
43|  --verbose / --no-verbose  [default: no-verbose]
44|  --install-completion      Install completion for the current shell.
45|  --show-completion         Show completion for the current shell, to copy it or customize the installation.
46|  --help                    Show this message and exit.
47|
48|Commands:
49|  create
50|  delete
51|
52|// Check the new top level CLI option --verbose
53|
54|// Try it normally
55|$ uv run python main.py create Camila
56|
57|Creating user: Camila
58|
59|// And now with --verbose
60|$ uv run python main.py --verbose create Camila
61|
62|Will write verbose output
63|About to create a user
64|Creating user: Camila
65|Just created a user
66|
67|// Notice that --verbose belongs to the callback, it has to go before create or delete ⛔️
68|$ uv run python main.py create --verbose Camila
69|
70|Usage: main.py create [OPTIONS] {username}
71|Try "main.py create --help" for help.
72|
73|Error: No such option: --verbose
74|```
75|
76|</div>
77|
78|## Adding a callback on creation
79|
80|It's also possible to add a callback when creating the `typer.Typer()` app:
81|
82|{* docs_src/commands/callback/tutorial002_py310.py hl[4,5,8] *}
83|
84|That achieves the same as with `@app.callback()`.
85|
86|Check it:
87|
88|<div class="termy">
89|
90|```console
91|$ uv run python main.py create Camila
92|
93|Running a command
94|Creating user: Camila
95|```
96|
97|</div>
98|
99|## Overriding a callback
100|
101|If you added a callback when creating the `typer.Typer()` app, it's possible to override it with `@app.callback()`:
102|
103|{* docs_src/commands/callback/tutorial003_py310.py hl[11,12,13] *}
104|
105|Now `new_callback()` will be the one used.
106|
107|Check it:
108|
109|<div class="termy">
110|
111|```console
112|$ uv run python main.py create Camila
113|
114|// Notice that the message is the one from new_callback()
115|Override callback, running a command
116|Creating user: Camila
117|```
118|
119|</div>
120|
121|## Adding a callback only for documentation
122|
123|You can also add a callback just to add the documentation in the docstring.
124|
125|It can be convenient especially if you have several lines of text, as the indentation will be automatically handled for you:
126|
127|{* docs_src/commands/callback/tutorial004_py310.py hl[8,9,10,11,12,13,14,15,16] *}
128|
129|Now the callback will be used mainly to extract the docstring for the help text.
130|
131|Check it:
132|
133|<div class="termy">
134|
135|```console
136|$ uv run python main.py --help
137|
138|// Notice all the help text extracted from the callback docstring
139|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...
140|
141|  Manage users CLI app.
142|
143|  Use it with the create command.
144|
145|  A new user with the given 'name' will be created.
146|
147|Options:
148|  --install-completion  Install completion for the current shell.
149|  --show-completion     Show completion for the current shell, to copy it or customize the installation.
150|  --help                Show this message and exit.
151|
152|Commands:
153|  create
154|
155|// And it just works as normally
156|$ uv run python main.py create Camila
157|
158|Creating user: Camila
159|```
160|
161|</div>

1|# Add Typer
2|
3|We'll start with the core idea.
4|
5|To add a `typer.Typer()` app inside of another.
6|
7|## Manage items
8|
9|Let's imagine that you are creating a *CLI program* to manage items in some distant land.
10|
11|It could be in an `items.py` file with this:
12|
13|{* docs_src/subcommands/tutorial001_py310/items.py *}
14|
15|And you would use it like:
16|
17|<div class="termy">
18|
19|```console
20|$ uv run python items.py create Wand
21|
22|Creating item: Wand
23|```
24|
25|</div>
26|
27|## Manage users
28|
29|But then you realize that you also have to manage users from your *CLI app*.
30|
31|It could be a file `users.py` with something like:
32|
33|{* docs_src/subcommands/tutorial001_py310/users.py *}
34|
35|And you would use it like:
36|
37|<div class="termy">
38|
39|```console
40|$ uv run python users.py create Camila
41|
42|Creating user: Camila
43|```
44|
45|</div>
46|
47|## Put them together
48|
49|Both parts are similar. In fact, `items.py` and `users.py` both have commands `create` and `delete`.
50|
51|But we need them to be part of the same *CLI program*.
52|
53|In this case, as with `git remote`, we can put them together as subcommands in another `typer.Typer()` *CLI program*.
54|
55|Now create a `main.py` with:
56|
57|{* docs_src/subcommands/tutorial001_py310/main.py hl[3,4,7,8] *}
58|
59|Here's what we do in `main.py`:
60|
61|* Import the other Python modules (the files `users.py` and `items.py`).
62|* Create the main `typer.Typer()` application.
63|* Use `app.add_typer()` to include the `app` from `items.py` and `users.py`, each of those 2 was also created with `typer.Typer()`.
64|* Define a `name` with the command that will be used for each of these "sub-Typers" to group their own commands.
65|
66|And now your *CLI program* has 2 commands:
67|
68|* `users`: with all of the commands (subcommands) in the `app` from `users.py`.
69|* `items` with all the commands (subcommands) in the `app` from `items.py`.
70|
71|Check it:
72|
73|<div class="termy">
74|
75|```console
76|// Check the help
77|$ uv run python main.py --help
78|
79|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...
80|
81|Options:
82|  --install-completion  Install completion for the current shell.
83|  --show-completion     Show completion for the current shell, to copy it or customize the installation.
84|  --help                Show this message and exit.
85|
86|Commands:
87|  users
88|  items
89|```
90|
91|</div>
92|
93|Now you have a *CLI program* with commands `items` and `users`, and they in turn have their own commands (subcommands).
94|
95|Let's check the `items` command:
96|
97|<div class="termy">
98|
99|```console
100|// Check the help for items
101|$ uv run python main.py items --help
102|
103|// It shows its own commands (subcommands): create, delete, sell
104|Usage: main.py items [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...
105|
106|Options:
107|  --help  Show this message and exit.
108|
109|Commands:
110|  create
111|  delete
112|  sell
113|
114|// Try it
115|$ uv run python main.py items create Wand
116|
117|Creating item: Wand
118|
119|$ uv run python main.py items sell Vase
120|
121|Selling item: Vase
122|```
123|
124|</div>
125|
126|/// tip
127|
128|Notice that we are still calling `$ python main.py` but now we are using the command `items`.
129|
130|///
131|
132|And now check the command `users`, with all its subcommands:
133|
134|<div class="termy">
135|
136|```console
137|$ uv run python main.py users --help
138|
139|Usage: main.py users [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...
140|
141|Options:
142|  --help  Show this message and exit.
143|
144|Commands:
145|  create
146|  delete
147|
148|// Try it
149|$ uv run python main.py users create Camila
150|
151|Creating user: Camila
152|```
153|
154|</div>
155|
156|## Recap
157|
158|That's the core idea.
159|
160|You can just create `typer.Typer()` apps and add them inside one another.
161|
162|And you can do that with any levels of commands that you want.
163|
164|Do you need sub-sub-sub-subcommands? Go ahead, create all the `typer.Typer()`s you need and put them together with `app.add_typer()`.
165|
166|In the next sections we'll update this with more features, but you already have the core idea.
167|
168|This way, **Typer** applications are composable, each `typer.Typer()` can be a *CLI app* by itself, but it can also be added as a command group to another Typer app.
--- END FILE: docs/tutorial/subcommands/add-typer.md ---
