1|# Install **Typer**
2|
3|The first step is to set up your project and add **Typer**.
4|
5|Install [`uv`](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/), then create a project and add Typer:
6|
7|<div class="termy">
8|
9|```console
10|$ uv init awesome-project --bare
11|$ cd awesome-project
12|$ uv add typer
13|---> 100%
14|```
15|
16|</div>
17|
18|`uv add` creates the project's virtual environment in `.venv`, adds Typer to `pyproject.toml`, and creates `uv.lock` so the same package versions can be installed later.
19|
20|/// details | What these commands do
21|
22|* `uv init`: create a new Python project.
23|* `awesome-project`: create the project in a new directory with this name.
24|* `--bare`: create only the minimal `pyproject.toml` file, without generating a sample `main.py`, `README.md`, or other files. You will create the application files yourself in the next steps of this tutorial.
25|
26|Then `cd awesome-project` enters the new project directory before adding Typer.
27|
28|`uv` will use a compatible Python version already installed on your system, or download one if needed.
29|
30|When you run `uv add`, it selects compatible versions of Typer and all the packages Typer depends on. It records the exact versions in `uv.lock`, making it possible to install the same package versions later on another computer or when distributing the application.
31|
32|Creating or updating this file is called [**locking** the project dependencies](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/concepts/projects/sync/). `uv` does this automatically when you add a package.
33|
34|///
35|
36|By default, `typer` comes with `rich` and `shellingham`.
37|
38|## Activate the Virtual Environment
39|
40|`uv add typer` installs both the Typer library and the `typer` command in the project's `.venv`.
41|
42|You can normally run project commands with `uv run`. But to configure and use shell completion for the first-class `typer` command, activate the project's virtual environment so that `typer` is available directly in your shell.
43|
44|//// tab | Linux, macOS
45|
46|<div class="termy">
47|
48|```console
49|$ source .venv/bin/activate
50|```
51|
52|</div>
53|
54|////
55|
56|//// tab | Windows PowerShell
57|
58|<div class="termy">
59|
60|```console
61|$ .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
62|```
63|
64|</div>
65|
66|////
67|
68|//// tab | Windows Bash
69|
70|<div class="termy">
71|
72|```console
73|$ source .venv/Scripts/activate
74|```
75|
76|</div>
77|
78|////
79|
80|Enable completion for your current shell with:
81|
82|<div class="termy">
83|
84|```console
85|$ typer --install-completion
86|```
87|
88|</div>
89|
90|Restart your terminal for the new completion configuration to take effect.
91|
92|Activate the project's virtual environment again in each new terminal session where you want to use the `typer` command directly.
93|
94|/// details | Using `pip` instead
95|
96|If you prefer to manage a virtual environment and packages manually, create and activate a virtual environment and then install Typer with `pip install typer`.
97|
98|Read the [Virtual Environments guide](https://tiangolo.com/guides/virtual-environments/) for the detailed steps.
99|
100|///
101|
102|## AI Agent Skills
103|
104|Typer includes an official skill for AI coding agents. It is bundled with the package, so its guidance stays aligned with the version of Typer installed in your project and updates when you update Typer.
105|
106|After installing Typer in your project, you can install the skill with <a href="https://library-skills.io">Library Skills</a>:
107|
108|```bash
109|uvx library-skills
110|```
111|
112|/// note
113|
114|`uvx` is an alias for `uv tool run`. It runs Library Skills in a temporary, isolated environment while Library Skills scans the packages installed in your project.
115|
116|///
117|
118|The skill is compatible with Codex, Claude Code, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Gemini CLI, Pi, OpenCode, and most other coding agents. For Claude Code, select `.claude/skills` when asked where to install the skill.
--- END FILE: docs/tutorial/install.md ---

1|# One or Multiple Commands
2|
3|You might have noticed that if you create a single command, as in the following example:
4|
5|{* docs_src/typer_app/tutorial001_py310.py hl[3,6,12] *}
6|
7|**Typer** is smart enough to create a CLI application with that single function as the main CLI application, not as a command/subcommand:
8|
9|<div class="termy">
10|
11|```console
12|// Without a CLI argument
13|$ uv run python main.py
14|
15|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS] {name}
16|Try "main.py --help" for help.
17|
18|Error: Missing argument 'name'.
19|
20|// With the 'name' CLI argument
21|$ uv run python main.py Camila
22|
23|Hello Camila
24|
25|// Asking for help
26|$ uv run python main.py --help
27|
28|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS] {name}
29|
30|Options:
31|  --install-completion  Install completion for the current shell.
32|  --show-completion     Show completion for the current shell, to copy it or customize the installation.
33|  --help                Show this message and exit.
34|```
35|
36|</div>
37|
38|/// tip
39|
40|Notice that it doesn't show a command `main`, even though the function name is `main`.
41|
42|///
43|
44|But if you add multiple commands, **Typer** will create one *CLI command* for each one of them:
45|
46|{* docs_src/commands/index/tutorial002_py310.py hl[6,11] *}
47|
48|Here we have 2 commands `create` and `delete`:
49|
50|<div class="termy">
51|
52|```console
53|// Check the help
54|$ uv run python main.py --help
55|
56|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...
57|
58|Options:
59|  --install-completion  Install completion for the current shell.
60|  --show-completion     Show completion for the current shell, to copy it or customize the installation.
61|  --help                Show this message and exit.
62|
63|Commands:
64|  create
65|  delete
66|
67|// Test the commands
68|$ uv run python main.py create
69|
70|Creating user: Hiro Hamada
71|
72|$ uv run python main.py delete
73|
74|Deleting user: Hiro Hamada
75|```
76|
77|</div>
78|
79|## One command and one callback
80|
81|If you want to create a CLI app with one single command but you still want it to be a command/subcommand you can just add a callback:
82|
83|{* docs_src/commands/one_or_multiple/tutorial001_py310.py hl[11,12,13] *}
84|
85|And now your CLI program will have a single command.
86|
87|Check it:
88|
89|<div class="termy">
90|
91|```console
92|// Check the help
93|$ uv run python main.py --help
94|
95|// Notice the single command create
96|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...
97|
98|Options:
99|  --install-completion  Install completion for the current shell.
100|  --show-completion     Show completion for the current shell, to copy it or customize the installation.
101|  --help                Show this message and exit.
102|
103|Commands:
104|  create
105|
106|// Try it
107|$ uv run python main.py create
108|
109|Creating user: Hiro Hamada
110|```
111|
112|</div>
113|
114|## Using the callback to document
115|
116|Now that you are using a callback just to have a single command, you might as well use it to add documentation for your app:
117|
118|{* docs_src/commands/one_or_multiple/tutorial002_py310.py hl[11,12,13,14,15,16,17] *}
119|
120|And now the docstring from the callback will be used as the help text:
121|
122|<div class="termy">
123|
124|```console
125|$ uv run python main.py --help
126|
127|// Notice the help text from the docstring
128|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...
129|
130|  Creates a single user Hiro Hamada.
131|
132|  In the next version it will create 5 more users.
133|
134|Options:
135|  --install-completion  Install completion for the current shell.
136|  --show-completion     Show completion for the current shell, to copy it or customize the installation.
137|  --help                Show this message and exit.
138|
139|Commands:
140|  create
141|
142|// And it still works the same, the callback does nothing
143|$ uv run python main.py create
144|
145|Creating user: Hiro Hamada
146|```
147|
148|</div>
--- END FILE: docs/tutorial/commands/one-or-multiple.md ---
--- FILE: docs/contributing.md ---
1|# Development - Contributing
2|
3|First, you might want to see the basic ways to [help Typer and get help](https://typer.tiangolo.com/help-typer/).
4|
5|## Developing
6|
7|To contribute code to the project, please follow the guidelines in [tiangolo.com - Contributing](https://tiangolo.com/open-source/contributing/).
8|
9|## Completion
10|
11|To try and test the completion for different shells and check that they are working you can use a Docker container.
12|
13|There's a `Dockerfile` and a Docker Compose file `compose.yaml` at `./scripts/docker/`.
14|
15|It has installed `bash`, `zsh`, `fish`, and `pwsh` (PowerShell for Linux).
16|
17|It also has installed `nano` and `vim`, so that you can check the modified configuration files for the shells (for example `.bashrc`, `.zshrc`, etc).
18|
19|It also has `uv` installed, so you can install the dependencies and the project quickly.
20|
21|The Docker Compose file mounts the main directory as `/code` inside the container, so you can change things and try them out.
22|
23|Go to the `./scripts/docker/` directory:
24|
25|```console
26|$ cd scripts/docker/
27|```
28|
29|Then run an interactive session with `bash` inside the container:
30|
31|```console
32|$ docker compose run typer bash
33|
34|root@79c4b9b70cbe:/code#
35|```
36|
37|Then inside the container, you can install `typer` with:
38|
39|```console
40|$ uv pip install -r requirements.txt
41|```
42|
43|Then, you can start the shell you want to use, the one where you want to try out completion:
44|
45|* `bash`
46|* `fish`
47|* `pwsh`
48|* `zsh`
49|
50|For example:
51|
52|```console
53|$ zsh
54|```
55|
56|Then install `typer` completion:
57|
58|```console
59|$ typer --install-completion
60|```
61|
62|/// note
63|
64|In `pwsh` you will probably get a warning of:
65|
66|```plaintext
67|Set-ExecutionPolicy: Operation is not supported on this platform.
68|```
69|
70|this is because that configuration is only available in Windows (and needed there), not in PowerShell for Linux.
71|
72|///
73|
74|For completion to take effect, you need to restart the shell. So, exit the current shell:
75|
76|```console
77|$ exit
78|```
79|
80|and start a new shell (for the same shell you installed completion in) again. For example:
81|
82|```console
83|$ zsh
84|```
85|
86|Now you could create a demo file on the same Typer directory in your editor, for example `demo.py`:
87|
88|```python
89|import typer
90|
91|app = typer.Typer()
92|
93|
94|@app.command()
95|def hello():
96|    print("Hello")
97|
98|
99|@app.command()
100|def goodbye():
101|    print("Goodbye")
102|
103|
104|if __name__ == "__main__":
105|    app()
106|```
107|
108|Because the directory is mounted as a volume, you will be able to access the file from inside the container.
109|
110|So, you can try running it with the `typer` command, that will use the installed shell completion:
111|
112|```console
113|$ typer demo.py <TAB>
114|```
115|
116|And you should see the completion working:
117|
118|```console
119|run    -- Run the provided Typer app.
120|utils  -- Extra utility commands for Typer apps.
121|```
122|
123|And the same for the commands in your `demo.py` file:
124|
125|```console
126|$ typer demo.py run <TAB>
127|
128|hello    goodbye
129|```
130|
131|You can also check the configuration file using `nano` or `vim`, for example:
132|
133|```bash
134|nano ~/.zshrc
135|```
136|
137|It will show some content like:
138|
139|```bash
140|fpath+=~/.zfunc; autoload -Uz compinit; compinit
141|
142|
143|zstyle ':completion:*' menu select
144|```
145|
146|If you exit from the container, you can start a new one, you will probably have to install the packages again and install completion again.
147|
148|Using this process, you can test all the shells, with their completions, being able to start from scratch quickly in a fresh container, and verifying that everything works as expected.
--- END FILE: docs/contributing.md ---

1|# Boolean CLI Options
2|
3|We have seen some examples of *CLI options* with `bool`, and how **Typer** creates `--something` and `--no-something` automatically.
4|
5|But we can customize those names.
6|
7|## Only `--force`
8|
9|Let's say that we want a `--force` *CLI option* only, we want to discard `--no-force`.
10|
11|We can do that by specifying the exact name we want:
12|
13|{* docs_src/parameter_types/bool/tutorial001_an_py310.py hl[9] *}
14|
15|Now there's only a `--force` *CLI option*:
16|
17|<div class="termy">
18|
19|```console
20|// Check the help
21|$ uv run python main.py --help
22|
23|// Notice there's only --force, we no longer have --no-force
24|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS]
25|
26|Options:
27|  --force
28|  --help                Show this message and exit.
29|
30|// Try it:
31|$ uv run python main.py
32|
33|Not forcing
34|
35|// Now add --force
36|$ uv run python main.py --force
37|
38|Forcing operation
39|
40|// And --no-force no longer exists ⛔️
41|$ uv run python main.py --no-force
42|
43|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS]
44|Try "main.py --help" for help.
45|
46|Error: No such option: --no-force
47|```
48|
49|</div>
50|
51|## Alternative names
52|
53|Now let's imagine we have a *CLI option* `--accept`.
54|
55|And we want to allow setting `--accept` or the contrary, but `--no-accept` looks ugly.
56|
57|We might want to instead have `--accept` and `--reject`.
58|
59|We can do that by passing a single `str` with the 2 names for the `bool` *CLI option* separated by `/`:
60|
61|{* docs_src/parameter_types/bool/tutorial002_an_py310.py hl[9] *}
62|
63|Check it:
64|
65|<div class="termy">
66|
67|```console
68|// Check the help
69|$ uv run python main.py --help
70|
71|// Notice the --accept / --reject
72|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS]
73|
74|Options:
75|  --accept / --reject
76|  --help                Show this message and exit.
77|
78|// Try it
79|$ uv run python main.py
80|
81|I don't know what you want yet
82|
83|// Now pass --accept
84|$ uv run python main.py --accept
85|
86|Accepting!
87|
88|// And --reject
89|$ uv run python main.py --reject
90|
91|Rejecting!
92|```
93|
94|</div>
95|
96|## Short names
97|
98|The same way, you can declare short versions of the names for these *CLI options*.
99|
100|For example, let's say we want `-f` for `--force` and `-F` for `--no-force`:
101|
102|{* docs_src/parameter_types/bool/tutorial003_an_py310.py hl[9] *}
103|
104|Check it:
105|
106|<div class="termy">
107|
108|```console
109|// Check the help
110|$ uv run python main.py --help
111|
112|// Notice the -f, --force / -F, --no-force
113|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS]
114|
115|Options:
116|  -f, --force / -F, --no-force  [default: no-force]
117|  --help                        Show this message and exit.
118|
119|// Try with the short name -f
120|$ uv run python main.py -f
121|
122|Forcing operation
123|
124|// Try with the short name -F
125|$ uv run python main.py -F
126|
127|Not forcing
128|```
129|
130|</div>
131|
132|## Only names for `False`
133|
134|If you want to (although it might not be a good idea), you can declare only *CLI option* names to set the `False` value.
135|
136|To do that, use a space and a single `/` and pass the negative name after:
137|
138|{* docs_src/parameter_types/bool/tutorial004_an_py310.py hl[9] *}
139|
140|/// tip
141|
142|Have in mind that it's a string with a preceding space and then a `/`.
143|
144|So, it's `" /-S"` not `"/-S"`.
145|
146|///
147|
148|Check it:
149|
150|<div class="termy">
151|
152|```console
153|// Check the help
154|$ uv run python main.py --help
155|
156|// Notice the / -d, --demo
157|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS]
158|
159|Options:
160|   / -d, --demo         [default: True]
161|  --help                Show this message and exit.
162|
163|// Try it
164|$ uv run python main.py
165|
166|Running in production
167|
168|// Now pass --demo
169|$ uv run python main.py --demo
170|
171|Running demo
172|
173|// And the short version
174|$ uv run python main.py -d
175|
176|Running demo
177|```
178|
179|</div>
--- END FILE: docs/tutorial/parameter-types/bool.md ---
--- FILE: docs/tutorial/parameter-types/enum.md ---
1|# Enum - Choices
2|
3|To define a *CLI parameter* that can take a value from a predefined set of values you can use a standard Python [`enum.Enum`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/enum.html):
4|
5|{* docs_src/parameter_types/enum/tutorial001_py310.py hl[1,6:9,16:17] *}
6|
7|/// tip
8|
9|Notice that the function parameter `network` will be an `Enum`, not a `str`.
10|
11|To get the `str` value in your function's code use `network.value`.
12|
13|///
14|
15|Check it:
16|
17|<div class="termy">
18|
19|```console
20|$ uv run python main.py --help
21|
22|// Notice the predefined values <simple|conv|lstm>
23|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS]
24|
25|Options:
26|  --network <simple|conv|lstm>  [default: simple]
27|  --help                        Show this message and exit.
28|
29|// Try it
30|$ uv run python main.py --network conv
31|
32|Training neural network of type: conv
33|
34|// Invalid value
35|$ uv run python main.py --network capsule
36|
37|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS]
38|Try "main.py --help" for help.
39|
40|Error: Invalid value for '--network': 'capsule' is not one of 'simple', 'conv', 'lstm'.
41|
42|// Note that enums are case sensitive by default
43|$ uv run python main.py --network CONV
44|
45|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS]
46|Try "main.py --help" for help.
47|
48|Error: Invalid value for '--network': 'CONV' is not one of 'simple', 'conv', 'lstm'.
49|```
50|
51|</div>
52|
53|### Case insensitive Enum choices
54|
55|You can make an `Enum` (choice) *CLI parameter* be case-insensitive with the `case_sensitive` parameter:
56|
57|{* docs_src/parameter_types/enum/tutorial002_an_py310.py hl[19] *}
58|
59|And then the values of the `Enum` will be checked no matter if lower case, upper case, or a mix:
60|
61|<div class="termy">
62|
63|```console
64|// Notice the upper case CONV
65|$ uv run python main.py --network CONV
66|
67|Training neural network of type: conv
68|
69|// A mix also works
70|$ uv run python main.py --network LsTm
71|
72|Training neural network of type: lstm
73|```
74|
75|</div>
76|
77|### List of Enum values
78|
79|A *CLI parameter* can also take a list of `Enum` values:
80|
81|{* docs_src/parameter_types/enum/tutorial003_an_py310.py hl[17] *}
82|
83|This works just like any other parameter value taking a list of things:
84|
85|<div class="termy">
86|
87|```console
88|$ uv run python main.py --help
89|
90|// Notice the default values being shown
91|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS]
92|
93|Options:
94|  --groceries <Eggs|Bacon|Cheese>         [default: Eggs, Cheese]
95|  --help                                  Show this message and exit.
96|
97|// Try it with the default values
98|$ uv run python main.py
99|
100|Buying groceries: Eggs, Cheese
101|
102|// Try it with a single value
103|$ uv run python main.py --groceries "Eggs"
104|
105|Buying groceries: Eggs
106|
107|// Try it with multiple values
108|$ uv run python main.py --groceries "Eggs" --groceries "Bacon"
109|
110|Buying groceries: Eggs, Bacon
111|```
112|
113|</div>
114|
115|### Literal choices
116|
117|You can also use `Literal` to represent a set of possible predefined choices, without having to use an `Enum`:
118|
119|{* docs_src/parameter_types/enum/tutorial004_an_py310.py hl[10] *}
120|
121|<div class="termy">
122|
123|```console
124|$ uv run python main.py --help
125|
126|// Notice the predefined values <simple|conv|lstm>
127|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS]
128|
129|Options:
130|  --network <simple|conv|lstm>  [default: simple]
131|  --help                        Show this message and exit.
132|
133|// Try it
134|$ uv run python main.py --network conv
135|
136|Training neural network of type: conv
137|
138|// Invalid value
139|$ uv run python main.py --network capsule
140|
141|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS]
142|Try "main.py --help" for help.
143|
144|Error: Invalid value for '--network': 'capsule' is not one of 'simple', 'conv', 'lstm'.
145|```
146|
147|</div>
--- END FILE: docs/tutorial/parameter-types/enum.md ---
--- FILE: docs/tutorial/options/version.md ---
1|# Version CLI Option, `is_eager`
2|
3|You could use a callback to implement a `--version` *CLI option*.
4|
5|It would show the version of your CLI program and then it would terminate it. Even before any other *CLI parameter* is processed.
6|
7|## First version of `--version`
8|
9|Let's see a first version of how it could look like:
10|
11|{* docs_src/options/version/tutorial001_an_py310.py hl[10:13,19:21] *}
12|
13|/// tip
14|
15|Notice that we don't have to get the `typer.Context` and check for `ctx.resilient_parsing` for completion to work, because we only print and modify the program when `--version` is passed, otherwise, nothing is printed or changed from the callback.
16|
17|///
18|
19|If the `--version` *CLI option* is passed, we get a value `True` in the callback.
20|
21|Then we can print the version and raise `typer.Exit()` to make sure the program is terminated before anything else is executed.
22|
23|We also declare the explicit *CLI option* name `--version`, because we don't want an automatic `--no-version`, it would look awkward.
24|
25|Check it:
26|
27|<div class="termy">
28|
29|```console
30|$ uv run python main.py --help
31|
32|// We get a --version, and don't get an awkward --no-version 🎉
33|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS]
34|
35|Options:
36|  --version
37|  --name <str>          [default: World]
38|  --help                Show this message and exit.
39|
40|
41|// We can call it normally
42|$ uv run python main.py --name Camila
43|
44|Hello Camila
45|
46|// And we can get the version
47|$ uv run python main.py --version
48|
49|Awesome CLI Version: 0.1.0
50|
51|// Because we exit in the callback, we don't get a "Hello World" message after the version 🚀
52|```
53|
54|</div>
55|
56|## Previous parameters and `is_eager`
57|
58|But now let's say that the `--name` *CLI option* that we declared before `--version` is required, and it has a callback that could exit the program:
59|
60|{* docs_src/options/version/tutorial002_an_py310.py hl[16:19,25:27] *}
61|
62|Then our CLI program could not work as expected in some cases as it is *right now*, because if we use `--version` after `--name` then the callback for `--name` will be processed before and we can get its error:
63|
64|<div class="termy">
65|
66|```console
67|$ uv run python main.py --name Rick --version
68|
69|Only Camila is allowed
70|Aborted!
71|```
72|
73|</div>
74|
75|/// tip
76|
77|We don't have to check for `ctx.resilient_parsing` in the `name_callback()` for completion to work, because we are not using `typer.echo()`, instead we are raising a `typer.BadParameter`.
78|
79|///
80|
81|/// note | Technical Details
82|
83|`typer.BadParameter` prints the error to "standard error", not to "standard output", and because the completion system only reads from "standard output", it won't break completion.
84|
85|///
86|
87|/// note
88|
89|If you need a refresher about what is "standard output" and "standard error" check the section in [Printing and Colors: "Standard Output" and "Standard Error"](../printing.md#standard-output-and-standard-error).
90|
91|///
92|
93|### Fix with `is_eager`
94|
95|For those cases, we can mark a *CLI parameter* (a *CLI option* or *CLI argument*) with `is_eager=True`.
96|
97|That will tell **Typer** that it should process this *CLI parameter* before the others:
98|
99|{* docs_src/options/version/tutorial003_an_py310.py hl[25:28] *}
100|
101|Check it:
102|
103|<div class="termy">
104|
105|```console
106|$ uv run python main.py --name Rick --version
107|
108|// Now we only get the version, and the name is not used
109|Awesome CLI Version: 0.1.0
110|```
111|
112|</div>

--- FILE: docs/tutorial/typer-app.md ---
1|# Typer App
2|
3|## Explicit application
4|
5|So far, you have seen how to create a single function and then pass that function to `typer.run()`.
6|
7|For example:
8|
9|{* docs_src/first_steps/tutorial002_py310.py hl[9] *}
10|
11|But that is actually a shortcut. Under the hood, **Typer** converts that to a CLI application with `typer.Typer()` and executes it. All that inside of `typer.run()`.
12|
13|There's also a more explicit way to achieve the same:
14|
15|{* docs_src/typer_app/tutorial001_py310.py hl[3,6,12] *}
16|
17|When you use `typer.run()`, **Typer** is doing more or less the same as above, it will:
18|
19|* Create a new `typer.Typer()` "application".
20|* Create a new "`command`" with your function.
21|* Call the same "application" as if it was a function with "`app()`".
22|
23|/// note | `@decorator` Info
24|
25|That `@something` syntax in Python is called a "decorator".
26|
27|You put it on top of a function. Like a pretty decorative hat (I guess that's where the term came from).
28|
29|A "decorator" takes the function below and does something with it.
30|
31|In our case, this decorator tells **Typer** that the function below is a "`command`".
32|You will learn more about commands later in the section [commands](./commands/index.md).
33|
34|///
35|
36|Both ways, with `typer.run()` and creating the explicit application, achieve almost the same.
37|
38|/// tip
39|
40|If your use case is solved with just `typer.run()`, that's fine, you don't have to create the explicit `app` and use `@app.command()`, etc.
41|
42|You might want to do that later when your app needs extra features, but if it doesn't need them yet, that's fine.
43|
44|///
45|
46|If you run the second example, with the explicit `app`, it works exactly the same:
47|
48|<div class="termy">
49|
50|```console
51|// Without a CLI argument
52|$ uv run python main.py
53|
54|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS] {name}
55|Try "main.py --help" for help.
56|
57|Error: Missing argument 'name'.
58|
59|// With the 'name' CLI argument
60|$ uv run python main.py Camila
61|
62|Hello Camila
63|
64|// Asking for help
65|$ uv run python main.py  --help
66|
67|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS] {name}
68|
69|Arguments:
70|  name  [required]
71|
72|Options:
73|  --install-completion  Install completion for the current shell.
74|  --show-completion     Show completion for the current shell, to copy it or customize the installation.
75|  --help                Show this message and exit.
76|```
77|
78|</div>
79|
80|## CLI application completion
81|
82|There's a little detail that is worth noting here.
83|
84|Now the help shows two new *CLI options*:
85|
86|* `--install-completion`
87|* `--show-completion`
88|
89|To get shell/tab completion, it's necessary to build a package that you and your users can install and **call directly**.
90|
91|So instead of running a Python script like:
92|
93|<div class="termy">
94|
95|```console
96|$ uv run python main.py
97|
98|✨ Some magic here ✨
99|```
100|
101|</div>
102|
103|...It would be called like:
104|
105|<div class="termy">
106|
107|```console
108|$ magic-app
109|
110|✨ Some magic here ✨
111|```
112|
113|</div>
114|
115|Having a standalone program like that allows setting up shell/tab completion.
116|
117|The first step to be able to create an installable package like that is to use an explicit `typer.Typer()` app.
118|
119|Later you can learn all the process to create a standalone CLI application and [Build a Package](./package.md).
120|
121|But for now, it's just good to know that you are on that path. 😎
--- END FILE: docs/tutorial/typer-app.md ---

1|# Path
2|
3|You can declare a *CLI parameter* to be a standard Python [`pathlib.Path`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/pathlib.html#basic-use).
4|
5|This is what you would do for directory paths, file paths, etc:
6|
7|{* docs_src/parameter_types/path/tutorial001_an_py310.py hl[1,10] *}
8|
9|And again, as you receive a standard Python `Path` object the same as the type annotation, your editor will give you autocompletion for all its attributes and methods.
10|
11|Check it:
12|
13|<div class="termy">
14|
15|```console
16|// No config
17|$ uv run python main.py
18|
19|Aborted.
20|No config file
21|
22|// Pass a config that doesn't exist
23|$ uv run python main.py --config config.txt
24|
25|The config doesn't exist
26|
27|// Now create a quick config
28|$ echo "some settings" > config.txt
29|
30|// And try again
31|$ uv run python main.py --config config.txt
32|
33|Config file contents: some settings
34|
35|// And with a directory
36|$ uv run python main.py --config ./
37|
38|Config is a directory, will use all its config files
39|```
40|
41|</div>
42|
43|## Path validations
44|
45|You can perform several validations for `Path` *CLI parameters*:
46|
47|* `exists`: if set to true, the file or directory needs to exist for this value to be valid. If this is not required and a file does indeed not exist, then all further checks are silently skipped.
48|* `file_okay`: controls if a file is a possible value.
49|* `dir_okay`: controls if a directory is a possible value.
50|* `writable`: if true, a writable check is performed.
51|* `readable`: if true, a readable check is performed.
52|* `resolve_path`: if this is true, then the path is fully resolved before the value is passed onwards. This means that it’s absolute and <abbr title="symbolic links, also known as shortcuts. Links in a file system that point to other location. For example, some applications when installed create symlinks in the desktop to launch them.">symlinks</abbr> are resolved.
53|
54|/// note | Technical Details
55|
56|It will not expand a tilde-prefix (something with `~`, like `~/Documents/`), as this is supposed to be done by the shell only.
57|
58|///
59|
60|For example:
61|
62|{* docs_src/parameter_types/path/tutorial002_an_py310.py hl[14:19] *}
63|
64|Check it:
65|
66|<div class="termy">
67|
68|```console
69|$ uv run python main.py --config config.txt
70|
71|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS]
72|Try "main.py --help" for help.
73|
74|Error: Invalid value for '--config': File 'config.txt' does not exist.
75|
76|// Now create a quick config
77|$ echo "some settings" > config.txt
78|
79|// And try again
80|$ uv run python main.py --config config.txt
81|
82|Config file contents: some settings
83|
84|// And with a directory
85|$ uv run python main.py --config ./
86|
87|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS]
88|Try "main.py --help" for help.
89|
90|Error: Invalid value for '--config': File './' is a directory.
91|```
92|
93|</div>
94|
95|### Advanced `Path` configurations
96|
97|/// warning | Advanced Details
98|
99|You probably won't need these configurations at first, you may want to skip it.
100|
101|They are used for more advanced use cases.
102|
103|///
104|
105|* `allow_dash`: If this is set to True, a single dash to indicate standard streams is permitted.
106|* `path_type`: optionally a string type that should be used to represent the path. The default is `None` which means the return value will be either bytes or unicode depending on what makes most sense given the input data.
--- END FILE: docs/tutorial/parameter-types/path.md ---
--- FILE: docs/tutorial/commands/context.md ---
1|# Using the Context
2|
3|When you create a **Typer** application it always has a special, hidden object underneath called the "Context".
4|
5|But you can access the context by declaring a function parameter of type `typer.Context`.
6|
7|You might have read it in [CLI Option Callback and Context](../options/callback-and-context.md).
8|
9|The same way, in commands or in the main `Typer` callback you can access the context by declaring a function parameter of type `typer.Context`.
10|
11|## Getting the context
12|
13|For example, let's say that you want to execute some logic in a `Typer` callback depending on the subcommand that is being called.
14|
15|You can get the name of the subcommand from the context:
16|
17|{* docs_src/commands/context/tutorial001_py310.py hl[17,21] *}
18|
19|Check it:
20|
21|<div class="termy">
22|
23|```console
24|$ uv run python main.py create Camila
25|
26|// We get the message from the callback
27|About to execute command: create
28|Creating user: Camila
29|
30|$ uv run python main.py delete Camila
31|
32|// We get the message from the callback, this time with delete
33|About to execute command: delete
34|Deleting user: Camila
35|```
36|
37|</div>
38|
39|## Executable callback
40|
41|By default, the callback is only executed right before executing a command.
42|
43|And if no command is provided, the help message is shown.
44|
45|But we could make it run even without a subcommand with `invoke_without_command=True`:
46|
47|{* docs_src/commands/context/tutorial002_py310.py hl[16] *}
48|
49|Check it:
50|
51|<div class="termy">
52|
53|```console
54|$ uv run python main.py
55|
56|// The callback is executed, we don't get the default help message
57|Initializing database
58|
59|// Try with a command
60|$ uv run python main.py create Camila
61|
62|// The callback is still executed
63|Initializing database
64|Creating user: Camila
65|```
66|
67|</div>
68|
69|## Exclusive executable callback
70|
71|We might not want the callback to be executed if there's already other command that will be executed.
72|
73|For that, we can get the `typer.Context` and check if there's an invoked command in `ctx.invoked_subcommand`.
74|
75|If it's `None`, it means that we are not calling a subcommand but the main program (the callback) directly:
76|
77|{* docs_src/commands/context/tutorial003_py310.py hl[17,21] *}
78|
79|Check it:
80|
81|<div class="termy">
82|
83|```console
84|$ uv run python main.py
85|
86|// The callback is executed
87|Initializing database
88|
89|// Check it with a subcommand
90|$ uv run python main.py create Camila
91|
92|// This time the callback is not executed
93|Creating user: Camila
94|```
95|
96|</div>
97|
98|## Configuring the context
99|
100|You can pass configurations for the context when creating a command or callback.
101|
102|For example, you could keep additional *CLI parameters* not declared in your CLI program with `ignore_unknown_options` and `allow_extra_args`.
103|
104|Then you can access those extra raw *CLI parameters* as a `list` of `str` in `ctx.args`:
105|
106|{* docs_src/commands/context/tutorial004_py310.py hl[7,9,10] *}
107|
108|<div class="termy">
109|
110|```console
111|$ uv run python main.py --name Camila --city Berlin
112|
113|Got extra arg: --name
114|Got extra arg: Camila
115|Got extra arg: --city
116|Got extra arg: Berlin
117|```
118|
119|</div>
120|
121|/// tip
122|
123|Notice that it saves all the extra *CLI parameters* as a raw `list` of `str`, including the *CLI option* names and values, everything together.
124|
125|///
--- END FILE: docs/tutorial/commands/context.md ---
--- FILE: docs/tutorial/parameter-types/number.md ---
1|# Number
2|
3|You can define numeric validations with `max` and `min` values for `int` and `float` *CLI parameters*:
4|
5|{* docs_src/parameter_types/number/tutorial001_an_py310.py hl[10:12] *}
6|
7|*CLI arguments* and *CLI options* can both use these validations.
8|
9|You can specify `min`, `max` or both.
10|
11|Check it:
12|
13|<div class="termy">
14|
15|```console
16|$ uv run python main.py --help
17|
18|// Notice the extra range information in the help text for --age and --score
19|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS] {ID}
20|
21|Arguments:
22|  ID  [required]
23|
24|Options:
25|  --age <int range>      [default: 20; x>=18]
26|  --score <float range>  [default: 0; x<=100]
27|  --help                 Show this message and exit.
28|
29|// Pass all the CLI parameters
30|$ uv run python main.py 5 --age 20 --score 90
31|
32|ID is 5
33|--age is 20
34|--score is 90.0
35|
36|// Pass an invalid ID
37|$ uv run python main.py 1002
38|
39|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS] {ID}
40|Try "main.py --help" for help.
41|
42|Error: Invalid value for 'ID': 1002 is not in the range 0<=x<=1000.
43|
44|// Pass an invalid age
45|$ uv run python main.py 5 --age 15
46|
47|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS] {ID}
48|Try "main.py --help" for help.
49|
50|Error: Invalid value for '--age': 15 is not in the range x>=18.
51|
52|// Pass an invalid score
53|$ uv run python main.py 5 --age 20 --score 100.5
54|
55|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS] {ID}
56|Try "main.py --help" for help.
57|
58|Error: Invalid value for '--score': 100.5 is not in the range x<=100.
59|
60|// But as we didn't specify a minimum score, this is accepted
61|$ uv run python main.py 5 --age 20 --score -5
62|
63|ID is 5
64|--age is 20
65|--score is -5.0
66|```
67|
68|</div>
69|
70|## Clamping numbers
71|
72|You might want to, instead of showing an error, use the closest minimum or maximum valid values.
73|
74|You can do it with the `clamp` parameter:
75|
76|{* docs_src/parameter_types/number/tutorial002_an_py310.py hl[10:12] *}
77|
78|And then, when you pass data that is out of the valid range, it will be "clamped", the closest valid value will be used:
79|
80|<div class="termy">
81|
82|```console
83|// ID doesn't have clamp, so it shows an error
84|$ uv run python main.py 1002
85|
86|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS] {ID}
87|Try "main.py --help" for help.
88|
89|Error: Invalid value for 'ID': 1002 is not in the range 0<=x<=1000.
90|
91|// But --rank and --score use clamp
92|$ uv run python main.py 5 --rank 11 --score -5
93|
94|ID is 5
95|--rank is 10
96|--score is 0
97|```
98|
99|</div>
100|
101|## Counter *CLI options*
102|
103|You can make a *CLI option* work as a counter with the `count` parameter:
104|
105|{* docs_src/parameter_types/number/tutorial003_an_py310.py hl[9] *}
106|
107|It means that the *CLI option* will be like a boolean flag, e.g. `--verbose`.
108|
109|And the value you receive in the function will be the amount of times that `--verbose` was added:
110|
111|<div class="termy">
112|
113|```console
114|// Check it
115|$ uv run python main.py
116|
117|Verbose level is 0
118|
119|// Now use one --verbose
120|$ uv run python main.py --verbose
121|
122|Verbose level is 1
123|
124|// Now 3 --verbose
125|$ uv run python main.py --verbose --verbose --verbose
126|
127|Verbose level is 3
128|
129|// And with the short name
130|$ uv run python main.py -v
131|
132|Verbose level is 1
133|
134|// And with the short name 3 times
135|$ uv run python main.py -v -v -v
136|
137|Verbose level is 3
138|
139|// As short names can be put together, this also works
140|$ uv run python main.py -vvv
141|
142|Verbose level is 3
143|```
144|
145|</div>
--- END FILE: docs/tutorial/parameter-types/number.md ---
--- FILE: docs/features.md ---
1|# Features
2|
3|## Design based on **FastAPI**
4|
5|<a href="https://fastapi.tiangolo.com"><img src="https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/img/logo-margin/logo-teal.png" style="width: 20%;"></a>
6|
7|**Typer** is [FastAPI](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com)'s little sibling.
8|
9|It follows the same design and ideas. If you know **FastAPI**, you already know **Typer**... more or less.
10|
11|## Just Modern Python
12|
13|It's all based on standard **Python type** declarations. No new syntax to learn. Just standard modern Python.
14|
15|If you need a 2 minute refresher of how to use Python types (even if you don't use FastAPI or Typer), check the FastAPI tutorial section: [Python types intro](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/python-types/).
16|
17|You will also see a 20 seconds refresher on the section [Tutorial - User Guide: First Steps](tutorial/first-steps.md).
18|
19|## Editor support
20|
21|**Typer** was designed to be easy and intuitive to use, to ensure the best development experience. With autocompletion everywhere.
22|
23|You will rarely need to come back to the docs.
24|
25|Here's how your editor might help you:
26|
27|* in [Visual Studio Code](https://code.visualstudio.com/):
28|
29|![editor support](img/vscode-completion.png)
30|
31|* in [PyCharm](https://www.jetbrains.com/pycharm/):
32|
33|![editor support](img/pycharm-completion.png)
34|
35|You will get completion for everything. That's something no other CLI library provides right now.
36|
37|No more guessing what type was that variable, if it could be `None`, etc.
38|
39|### Short
40|
41|It has sensible **defaults** for everything, with optional configurations everywhere. All the parameters can be fine-tuned to do what you need, customize the help, callbacks per parameter, make them required or not, etc.
42|
43|But by default, it all **"just works"**.
44|
45|## User friendly CLI apps
46|
47|The resulting CLI apps created with **Typer** have the nice features of many "pro" command line programs you probably already love.
48|
49|* Automatic help options for the main CLI program and all its subcommands.
50|* Automatic command and subcommand structure handling (you will see more about subcommands in the Tutorial - User Guide).
51|* Automatic completion for the CLI app in all operating systems, in all the shells (Bash, Zsh, Fish, PowerShell), so that the final user of your app can just hit <kbd>TAB</kbd> and get the available options or subcommands. *
52|
53|/// note | * Auto completion
54|
55|Auto completion works when you create a package (installable with `pip`). Or when using the `typer` command.
56|
57|**Typer** uses `shellingham` to auto-detect the current shell when installing completion.
58|
59|**Typer** will automatically create 2 *CLI options*:
60|
61|* `--install-completion`: Install completion for the current shell.
62|* `--show-completion`: Show completion for the current shell, to copy it or customize the installation.
63|
64|///
65|
66|## Tested
67|
68|* 100% <abbr title="The amount of code that is automatically tested">test coverage</abbr>.
69|* 100% <abbr title="Python type annotations, with this your editor and external tools can give you better support">type annotated</abbr> code base.
70|* Used in production applications.
--- END FILE: docs/features.md ---

1|# CLI Arguments with Environment Variables
2|
3|You can also configure a *CLI argument* to read a value from an environment variable if it is not provided in the command line as a *CLI argument*.
4|
5|An **environment variable** (also known as an **env var**) is a value that lives outside of your Python code, in the operating system, and can be read by your application and other programs.
6|
7|/// tip
8|
9|Read the [Environment Variables guide](https://tiangolo.com/guides/environment-variables/) for a detailed, cross-platform explanation.
10|
11|///
12|
13|To do that, use the `envvar` parameter for `typer.Argument()`:
14|
15|{* docs_src/arguments/envvar/tutorial001_an_py310.py hl[9] *}
16|
17|In this case, the *CLI argument* `name` will have a default value of `"World"`, but will also read any value passed to the environment variable `AWESOME_NAME` if no value is provided in the command line:
18|
19|<div class="termy">
20|
21|```console
22|// Check the help
23|$ uv run python main.py --help
24|
25|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS] [name]
26|
27|Arguments:
28|  name  [env var: AWESOME_NAME; default: World]
29|
30|Options:
31|  --help                Show this message and exit.
32|
33|// Call it without a CLI argument
34|$ uv run python main.py
35|
36|Hello Mr. World
37|
38|// Now pass a value for the CLI argument
39|$ uv run python main.py Czernobog
40|
41|Hello Mr. Czernobog
42|
43|// And now use the environment variable
44|$ AWESOME_NAME=Wednesday uv run python main.py
45|
46|Hello Mr. Wednesday
47|
48|// CLI arguments take precedence over env vars
49|$ AWESOME_NAME=Wednesday uv run python main.py Czernobog
50|
51|Hello Mr. Czernobog
52|```
53|
54|</div>
55|
56|/// tip | Windows PowerShell
57|
58|In PowerShell, set the environment variable first and then run the command:
59|
60|```console
61|$ $Env:AWESOME_NAME = "Wednesday"
62|$ uv run python main.py
63|```
64|
65|///
66|
67|## Multiple environment variables
68|
69|You are not restricted to a single environment variable, you can declare a list of environment variables that could be used to get a value if it was not passed in the command line:
70|
71|{* docs_src/arguments/envvar/tutorial002_an_py310.py hl[10] *}
72|
73|Check it:
74|
75|<div class="termy">
76|
77|```console
78|// Check the help
79|$ uv run python main.py --help
80|
81|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS] [name]
82|
83|Arguments:
84|  name  [env var: AWESOME_NAME, GOD_NAME; default: World]
85|
86|Options:
87|  --help                Show this message and exit.
88|
89|// Try the first env var
90|$ AWESOME_NAME=Wednesday uv run python main.py
91|
92|Hello Mr. Wednesday
93|
94|// Try the second env var
95|$ GOD_NAME=Anubis uv run python main.py
96|
97|Hello Mr. Anubis
98|```
99|
100|</div>
101|
102|## Hide an env var from the help text
103|
104|By default, environment variables used will be shown in the help text, but you can disable them with `show_envvar=False`:
105|
106|{* docs_src/arguments/envvar/tutorial003_an_py310.py hl[11] *}
107|
108|Check it:
109|
110|<div class="termy">
111|
112|```console
113|//Check the help
114|$ uv run python main.py --help
115|
116|// It won't show the env var
117|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS] [name]
118|
119|Arguments:
120|  name  [default: World]
121|
122|Options:
123|  --help                Show this message and exit.
124|
125|// But it will still be able to use it
126|$ AWESOME_NAME=Wednesday uv run python main.py
127|
128|Hello Mr. Wednesday
129|```
130|
131|</div>
--- END FILE: docs/tutorial/arguments/envvar.md ---
--- FILE: docs/tutorial/terminating.md ---
1|# Terminating
2|
3|There are some cases where you might want to terminate a command at some point, and stop all subsequent execution.
4|
5|It could be that your code determined that the program completed successfully, or it could be an operation aborted.
6|
7|## `Exit` a CLI program
8|
9|You can normally just let the code of your CLI program finish its execution, but in some scenarios, you might want to terminate at some point in the middle of it. And prevent any subsequent code to run.
10|
11|This doesn't have to mean that there's an error, just that nothing else needs to be executed.
12|
13|In that case, you can raise a `typer.Exit()` exception:
14|
15|{* docs_src/terminating/tutorial001_py310.py hl[9] *}
16|
17|There are several things to see in this example.
18|
19|* The CLI program is the function `main()`, not the others. This is the one that takes a *CLI argument*.
20|* The function `maybe_create_user()` can terminate the program by raising `typer.Exit()`.
21|* If the program is terminated by `maybe_create_user()` then `send_new_user_notification()` will never execute inside of `main()`.
22|
23|Check it:
24|
25|<div class="termy">
26|
27|```console
28|$ uv run python main.py Camila
29|
30|User created: Camila
31|Notification sent for new user: Camila
32|
33|// Try with an existing user
34|$ uv run python main.py rick
35|
36|The user already exists
37|
38|// Notice that the notification code was never run, the second message is not printed
39|```
40|
41|</div>
42|
43|/// tip
44|
45|Even though you are raising an exception, it doesn't necessarily mean there's an error.
46|
47|This is done with an exception because it works as an "error" and stops all execution.
48|
49|But then **Typer** catches it and just terminates the program normally.
50|
51|///
52|
53|## Exit with an error
54|
55|`typer.Exit()` takes an optional `code` parameter. By default, `code` is `0`, meaning there was no error.
56|
57|You can pass a `code` with a number other than `0` to tell the terminal that there was an error in the execution of the program:
58|
59|{* docs_src/terminating/tutorial002_py310.py hl[10] *}
60|
61|Check it:
62|
63|<div class="termy">
64|
65|```console
66|$ uv run python main.py Camila
67|
68|New user created: Camila
69|
70|// Print the result code of the last program executed
71|$ echo $?
72|
73|0
74|
75|// Now make it exit with an error
76|$ uv run python main.py root
77|
78|The root user is reserved
79|
80|// Print the result code of the last program executed
81|$ echo $?
82|
83|1
84|
85|// 1 means there was an error, 0 means no errors.
86|```
87|
88|</div>
89|
90|/// tip
91|
92|The error code might be used by other programs (for example a Bash script) that execute your CLI program.
93|
94|///
95|
96|## Abort
97|
98|There's a special exception that you can use to "abort" a program.
99|
100|It works more or less the same as `typer.Exit()` but will print `"Aborted!"` to the screen and can be useful in certain cases later to make it explicit that the execution was aborted:
101|
102|{* docs_src/terminating/tutorial003_py310.py hl[10] *}
103|
104|Check it:
105|
106|<div class="termy">
107|
108|```console
109|$ uv run python main.py Camila
110|
111|New user created: Camila
112|
113|// Now make it exit with an error
114|$ uv run python main.py root
115|
116|The root user is reserved
117|Aborted!
118|```
119|
120|</div>
--- END FILE: docs/tutorial/terminating.md ---

1|# Help
2|
3|Would you like to help Typer or get help about Typer?
4|
5|There are very simple ways to help and get help.
6|
7|## Subscribe to the newsletter
8|
9|You can subscribe to the (infrequent) [**FastAPI and friends** newsletter](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/newsletter/) to stay updated about:
10|
11|* News about FastAPI and friends, including Typer 🚀
12|* Guides 📝
13|* Features ✨
14|* Breaking changes 🚨
15|* Tips and tricks ✅
16|
17|## Follow FastAPI online
18|
19|You can follow **FastAPI** online in several places:
20|
21|* [@fastapi on **X / Twitter**](https://x.com/fastapi)
22|* [@fastapi.tiangolo.com on **Bluesky**](https://bsky.app/profile/fastapi.tiangolo.com)
23|* [FastAPI on **LinkedIn**](https://www.linkedin.com/company/fastapi/)
24|
25|## Star **Typer** in GitHub
26|
27|You can "star" Typer in GitHub (clicking the star button at the top right): [https://github.com/fastapi/typer](https://github.com/fastapi/typer). ⭐️
28|
29|By adding a star, other users will be able to find it more easily and see that it has been already useful for others.
30|
31|## Watch the GitHub repository for releases
32|
33|You can "watch" Typer in GitHub (clicking the "watch" button at the top right): [https://github.com/fastapi/typer](https://github.com/fastapi/typer). 👀
34|
35|There you can select "Releases only".
36|
37|By doing it, you will receive notifications (in your email) whenever there's a new release (a new version) of **Typer** with bug fixes and new features.
38|
39|## Follow the author
40|
41|You can follow [me (Sebastián Ramírez / `tiangolo`)](https://tiangolo.com), the author in a few places, to hear when I have news to share about FastAPI and friends:
42|
43|* [@tiangolo on **GitHub**](https://github.com/tiangolo).
44|* [@tiangolo on **X (Twitter)**](https://x.com/tiangolo)
45|* [@tiangolo.com on **Bluesky**](https://bsky.app/profile/tiangolo.com)
46|* [@tiangolo on **LinkedIn**](https://www.linkedin.com/in/tiangolo/).
47|
48|## Ask Questions
49|
50|You can [create a new question](https://github.com/fastapi/typer/discussions/new?category=questions) in the GitHub repository, for example to:
51|
52|* Ask a **question** or ask about a **problem**.
53|* Suggest a new **feature**.
54|
55|## Join the Chat
56|
57|Join the 👥 [FastAPI and Friends Discord chat server](https://discord.gg/VQjSZaeJmf) 👥 and hang out with others in the community. There's a `#typer` channel.
58|
59|/// tip
60|
61|For questions, ask them in [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/fastapi/typer/discussions/new?category=questions), there's a much better chance you will receive help there.
62|
63|Use the chat only for other general conversations.
64|
65|///
66|
67|### Don't use the Chat for Questions
68|
69|Keep in mind that as chats allow more "free conversation", it's easy to ask questions that are too general and more difficult to answer, so, you might not receive answers.
70|
71|In GitHub, the template will guide you to write the right question so that you can more easily get a good answer, or even solve the problem yourself even before asking.
72|
73|Conversations in the chat systems are also not as easily searchable as in GitHub, they get lost.
--- END FILE: docs/help-typer.md ---

1|# Sub-Typer Callback Override
2|
3|When creating a **Typer** app you can define a callback function, it always executes and defines the *CLI arguments* and *CLI options* that go before a command.
4|
5|When adding a Typer app inside of another, the sub-Typer can also have its own callback.
6|
7|It can handle any *CLI parameters* that go before its own commands and execute any extra code:
8|
9|{* docs_src/subcommands/callback_override/tutorial001_py310.py hl[9,10,11] *}
10|
11|In this case it doesn't define any *CLI parameters*, it just writes a message.
12|
13|Check it:
14|
15|<div class="termy">
16|
17|```console
18|$ uv run python main.py users create Camila
19|
20|// Notice the first message is not created by the command function but by the callback
21|Running a users command
22|Creating user: Camila
23|```
24|
25|</div>
26|
27|## Add a callback on creation
28|
29|It's also possible to add a callback when creating the `typer.Typer()` app that will be added to another Typer app:
30|
31|{* docs_src/subcommands/callback_override/tutorial002_py310.py hl[6,7,10] *}
32|
33|This achieves exactly the same as above, it's just another place to add the callback.
34|
35|Check it:
36|
37|<div class="termy">
38|
39|```console
40|$ uv run python main.py users create Camila
41|
42|Running a users command
43|Creating user: Camila
44|```
45|
46|</div>
47|
48|## Overriding the callback on creation
49|
50|If a callback was added when creating the `typer.Typer()` app, it's possible to override it with a new one using `@app.callback()`.
51|
52|This is the same information you saw on the section about [Commands - Typer Callback](../commands/callback.md), and it applies the same for sub-Typer apps:
53|
54|{* docs_src/subcommands/callback_override/tutorial003_py310.py hl[6,7,10,14,15,16] *}
55|
56|Here we had defined a callback when creating the `typer.Typer()` sub-app, but then we override it with a new callback with the function `user_callback()`.
57|
58|As `@app.callback()` takes precedence over `typer.Typer(callback=some_function)`, now our CLI app will use this new callback.
59|
60|Check it:
61|
62|<div class="termy">
63|
64|```console
65|$ uv run python main.py users create Camila
66|
67|// Notice the message from the new callback
68|Callback override, running users command
69|Creating user: Camila
70|```
71|
72|</div>
73|
74|## Overriding the callback when adding a sub-Typer
75|
76|Lastly, you can override the callback defined anywhere else when adding a sub-Typer with `app.add_typer()` using the `callback` parameter.
77|
78|This has the highest priority:
79|
80|{* docs_src/subcommands/callback_override/tutorial004_py310.py hl[13,14,17] *}
81|
82|Notice that the precedence goes to `app.add_typer()` and is not affected by the order of execution. There's another callback defined below, but the one from `app.add_typer()` wins.
83|
84|Now when you use the CLI program it will use the new callback function `callback_for_add_typer()`.
85|
86|Check it:
87|
88|<div class="termy">
89|
90|```console
91|$ uv run python users create Camila
92|
93|// Notice the message from the callback added in add_typer()
94|I have the high land! Running users command
95|Creating user: Camila
96|```
97|
98|</div>
--- END FILE: docs/tutorial/subcommands/callback-override.md ---

1|# SubCommands in a Single File
2|
3|In some cases, it's possible that your application code needs to live on a single file.
4|
5|You can still use the same ideas:
6|
7|{* docs_src/subcommands/tutorial002_py310/main.py *}
8|
9|There are several things to notice here...
10|
11|## Apps at the top
12|
13|First, you can create `typer.Typer()` objects and add them to another one at the top.
14|
15|It doesn't have to be done after creating the subcommands:
16|
17|{* docs_src/subcommands/tutorial002_py310/main.py hl[4,5,6,7] *}
18|
19|You can add the commands (subcommands) to each `typer.Typer()` app later and it will still work.
20|
21|## Function names
22|
23|As you now have subcommands like `create` for `users` and for `items`, you can no longer call the functions with just the name, like `def create()`, because they would overwrite each other.
24|
25|So we use longer names:
26|
27|{* docs_src/subcommands/tutorial002_py310/main.py hl[11,16,21,26,31] *}
28|
29|## Command name
30|
31|We are naming the functions with longer names so that they don't overwrite each other.
32|
33|But we still want the subcommands to be `create`, `delete`, etc.
34|
35|To call them like:
36|
37|<div class="termy">
38|
39|```console
40|// We want this ✔️
41|$ uv run python main.py items create
42|```
43|
44|</div>
45|
46|instead of:
47|
48|<div class="termy">
49|
50|```console
51|// We don't want this ⛔️
52|$ uv run python main.py items items-create
53|```
54|
55|</div>
56|
57|So we pass the name we want to use for each subcommand as the function argument to the decorator:
58|
59|{* docs_src/subcommands/tutorial002_py310/main.py hl[10,15,20,25,30] *}
60|
61|## Check it
62|
63|It still works the same:
64|
65|
66|<div class="termy">
67|
68|```console
69|// Check the help
70|$ uv run python main.py --help
71|
72|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...
73|
74|Options:
75|  --install-completion  Install completion for the current shell.
76|  --show-completion     Show completion for the current shell, to copy it or
77|                        customize the installation.
78|  --help                Show this message and exit.
79|
80|Commands:
81|  items
82|  users
83|```
84|
85|</div>
86|
87|Check the `items` command:
88|
89|
90|<div class="termy">
91|
92|```console
93|// Check the help for items
94|$ uv run python main.py items --help
95|
96|// It shows its own commands (subcommands): create, delete, sell
97|Usage: main.py items [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...
98|
99|Options:
100|  --help  Show this message and exit.
101|
102|Commands:
103|  create
104|  delete
105|  sell
106|
107|// Try it
108|$ uv run python main.py items create Wand
109|
110|Creating item: Wand
111|
112|$ uv run python main.py items sell Vase
113|
114|Selling item: Vase
115|```
116|
117|</div>
118|
119|And the same for the `users` command:
120|
121|
122|<div class="termy">
123|
124|```console
125|$ uv run python main.py users --help
126|
127|Usage: main.py users [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...
128|
129|Options:
130|  --help  Show this message and exit.
131|
132|Commands:
133|  create
134|  delete
135|
136|// Try it
137|$ uv run python main.py users create Camila
138|
139|Creating user: Camila
140|```
141|
142|</div>

1|# CLI Arguments with Default
2|
3|We can also use the same `typer.Argument()` to set a default value.
4|
5|That way the *CLI argument* will be optional *and also* have a default value.
6|
7|## An optional *CLI argument* with a default
8|
9|We can also use `typer.Argument()` to make a *CLI argument* have a default value other than `None`:
10|
11|{* docs_src/arguments/default/tutorial001_an_py310.py hl[9] *}
12|
13|/// tip
14|
15|Because now the value will be a `str` passed by the user or the default value of `"Wade Wilson"` which is also a `str`, we know the value will never be `None`, so we don't have to (and shouldn't) use `Optional[str]`.
16|
17|Have in mind that the `Optional[something]` tells Python that a value "could be `None`". But the use of `Optional` doesn't affect Typer in any way, e.g. it doesn't tell Typer if a value is required or not.
18|
19|///
20|
21|Check it:
22|
23|<div class="termy">
24|
25|```console
26|// Check the help
27|$ uv run python main.py --help
28|
29|// Notice the [default: Wade Wilson] ✨
30|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS] [name]
31|
32|Arguments:
33|  name  [default: Wade Wilson]
34|
35|Options:
36|  --help                Show this message and exit.
37|
38|// With no optional CLI argument
39|$ uv run python main.py
40|
41|Hello Wade Wilson
42|
43|// With one CLI argument
44|$ uv run python main.py Camila
45|
46|Hello Camila
47|```
48|
49|</div>
50|
51|## Dynamic default value
52|
53|And we can even make the default value be dynamically generated by passing a function as the `default_factory` argument:
54|
55|{* docs_src/arguments/default/tutorial002_an_py310.py hl[9:10,14] *}
56|
57|In this case, we created the function `get_name` that will just return a random `str` each time.
58|
59|And we pass it as the first function argument to `typer.Argument()`.
60|
61|/// tip
62|
63|The word "factory" in `default_factory` is just a fancy way of saying "function that will create the default value".
64|
65|///
66|
67|Check it:
68|
69|<div class="termy">
70|
71|```console
72|// Check the help
73|$ uv run python main.py --help
74|
75|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS] [name]
76|
77|Arguments:
78|  name  [default: (dynamic)]
79|
80|Options:
81|  --help                Show this message and exit.
82|
83|// Try it several times, it will use a random default each time
84|$ uv run python main.py
85|
86|Hello Deadpool
87|
88|$ uv run python main.py
89|
90|Hello Hiro
91|
92|$ uv run python main.py
93|
94|Hello Rick
95|
96|// Now pass a value for the CLI argument
97|$ uv run python main.py Camila
98|
99|Hello Camila
100|```
101|
102|</div>

--- FILE: docs/tutorial/index.md ---
1|# Learn
2|
3|Learn how to use **Typer** in this step-by-step **Tutorial** - **User Guide**.
4|
5|It covers everything you need to know from the **simplest scripts** to **complex CLI applications**.
6|
7|You could consider this a **book**, a **course**, the **official** and recommended way to learn **Typer**. 😎
8|
9|## Python Types
10|
11|If you need a refresher about how to use Python type hints, check the first part of [FastAPI's Python types intro](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/python-types/).
12|
13|You can also check the [mypy cheat sheet](https://mypy.readthedocs.io/en/latest/cheat_sheet_py3.html).
14|
15|In short (very short), you can declare a function with parameters like:
16|
17|```Python
18|from typing import Optional
19|
20|
21|def type_example(name: str, formal: bool = False, intro: Optional[str] = None):
22|    pass
23|```
24|
25|And your editor (and **Typer**) will know that:
26|
27|* `name` is of type `str` and is a required parameter.
28|* `formal` is a `bool` and is by default `False`.
29|* `intro` is an optional `str`, by default is `None`.
30|
31|These type hints are what give you autocomplete in your editor and several other features.
32|
33|**Typer** is based on these type hints.
34|
35|## About this Tutorial
36|
37|This tutorial shows you how to use **Typer** with all its features, step by step.
38|
39|Each section gradually builds on the previous ones, but it's structured to separate topics, so that you can go directly to any specific one to solve your specific CLI needs.
40|
41|It is also built to work as a future reference so you can come back and see exactly what you need.
42|
43|## Run the Code
44|
45|All the code blocks can be copied and used directly (they are tested Python files).
46|
47|To run any of the examples, copy the code to a file `main.py`, and run it:
48|
49|<div class="termy">
50|
51|```console
52|$ uv run python main.py
53|
54|✨ The magic happens here ✨
55|```
56|
57|</div>
58|
59|It is **HIGHLY encouraged** that you write or copy the code, edit it and run it locally.
60|
61|Using it in your editor is what really shows you the benefits of **Typer**, seeing how little code you have to write, all the **inline errors**, **autocompletion**, etc.
62|
63|And running the examples is what will really help you **understand** what is going on.
64|
65|You can learn a lot more by **running some examples** and **playing around** with them than by reading all the docs here.
--- END FILE: docs/tutorial/index.md ---
--- FILE: docs/tutorial/parameter-types/datetime.md ---
1|# DateTime
2|
3|You can specify a *CLI parameter* as a Python [`datetime`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/datetime.html).
4|
5|Your function will receive a standard Python `datetime` object, and again, your editor will give you completion, etc.
6|
7|{* docs_src/parameter_types/datetime/tutorial001_py310.py hl[1,9,10,11] *}
8|
9|Typer will accept any string from the following formats:
10|
11|* `%Y-%m-%d`
12|* `%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S`
13|* `%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S`
14|
15|Check it:
16|
17|<div class="termy">
18|
19|```console
20|$ uv run python main.py --help
21|
22|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS] {birth}:<%Y-%m-%d|%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S|%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S>
23|
24|Arguments:
25|  birth:<%Y-%m-%d|%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S|%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S> [required]
26|
27|Options:
28|  --help                Show this message and exit.
29|
30|// Pass a datetime
31|$ uv run python main.py 1956-01-31T10:00:00
32|
33|Interesting day to be born: 1956-01-31 10:00:00
34|Birth hour: 10
35|
36|// An invalid date
37|$ uv run python main.py july-19-1989
38|
39|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS] {birth}:<%Y-%m-%d|%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S|%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S>
40|Try 'main.py --help' for help.
41|
42|Error: Invalid value for 'birth': 'july-19-1989' does not match the formats '%Y-%m-%d', '%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S', '%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S'.
43|```
44|
45|</div>
46|
47|## Custom date format
48|
49|You can also customize the formats received for the `datetime` with the `formats` parameter.
50|
51|`formats` receives a list of strings with the date formats that would be passed to [datetime.strptime()](https://docs.python.org/3/library/datetime.html#datetime.datetime.strptime).
52|
53|For example, let's imagine that you want to accept an ISO formatted datetime, but for some strange reason, you also want to accept a format with:
54|
55|* first the month
56|* then the day
57|* then the year
58|* separated with "`/`"
59|
60|...It's a crazy example, but let's say you also needed that strange format:
61|
62|{* docs_src/parameter_types/datetime/tutorial002_an_py310.py hl[14] *}
63|
64|/// tip
65|
66|Notice the last string in `formats`: `"%m/%d/%Y"`.
67|
68|///
69|
70|Check it:
71|
72|<div class="termy">
73|
74|```console
75|// ISO dates work
76|$ uv run python main.py 1969-10-29
77|
78|Launch will be at: 1969-10-29 00:00:00
79|
80|// But the strange custom format also works
81|$ uv run python main.py 10/29/1969
82|
83|Launch will be at: 1969-10-29 00:00:00
84|```
85|
86|</div>
--- END FILE: docs/tutorial/parameter-types/datetime.md ---

2|

14|    * `username`: a *CLI argument*.
15|    * `--force`: a *CLI option*, if not provided, it's prompted.
16|* `delete-all`:
17|    * `--force`: a *CLI option*, if not provided, it's prompted.
18|* `init`:

22|

28|

35|  create
36|  delete
37|  delete-all
38|  init
39|```
40|
41|</div>
42|

50|
51|<div class="termy">
52|
53|```console
54|// Check the command create
55|$ uv run python main.py create Camila
56|
57|Creating user: Camila
58|
59|// Now test the command delete

61|
62|# Are you sure you want to delete the user? [y/n]: $ y

1|# Required CLI Options
2|
3|We said before that *by default*:
4|
5|* *CLI options* are **optional**
6|* *CLI arguments* are **required**
7|
8|Well, that's how they work *by default*, and that's the convention in many CLI programs and systems.
9|
10|But if you really want, you can change that.
11|
12|To make a *CLI option* required, you can put `typer.Option()` inside of `Annotated` and leave the parameter without a default value.
13|
14|Let's make `--lastname` a required *CLI option*:
15|
16|{* docs_src/options/required/tutorial001_an_py310.py hl[9] *}
17|
18|The same way as with `typer.Argument()`, the old style of using the function parameter default value is also supported, in that case you would just not pass anything to the `default` parameter.
19|
20|{* docs_src/options/required/tutorial001_py310.py hl[7] *}
21|
22|Or you can explicitly pass `...` to `typer.Option(default=...)`:
23|
24|{* docs_src/options/required/tutorial002_py310.py hl[7] *}
25|
26|/// note
27|
28|If you hadn't seen that `...` before: it is a special single value, it is [part of Python and is called "Ellipsis"](https://docs.python.org/3/library/constants.html#Ellipsis).
29|
30|///
31|
32|That will tell **Typer** that it's still a *CLI option*, but it doesn't have a default value, and it's required.
33|
34|/// tip
35|
36|Again, prefer to use the `Annotated` version if possible. That way your code will mean the same in standard Python and in **Typer**.
37|
38|///
39|
40|And test it:
41|
42|<div class="termy">
43|
44|```console
45|// Pass the 'name' CLI argument
46|$ uv run python main.py Camila
47|
48|// We didn't pass the now required --lastname CLI option
49|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS] {name}
50|Try "main.py --help" for help.
51|
52|Error: Missing option '--lastname'.
53|
54|// Now update it to pass the required --lastname CLI option
55|$ uv run python main.py Camila --lastname Gutiérrez
56|
57|Hello Camila Gutiérrez
58|
59|// And if you check the help
60|$ uv run python main.py --help
61|
62|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS] {name}
63|
64|Arguments:
65|  name  [required]
66|
67|Options:
68|  --lastname <str>      [required]
69|  --help                Show this message and exit.
70|
71|// It now tells you that --lastname is required 🎉
72|```
73|
74|</div>
--- END FILE: docs/tutorial/options/required.md ---

1|# CLI Option Prompt
2|
3|It's also possible to, instead of just showing an error, ask for the missing value with `prompt=True`:
4|
5|{* docs_src/options/prompt/tutorial001_an_py310.py hl[9] *}
6|
7|And then your program will ask the user for it in the terminal:
8|
9|<div class="termy">
10|
11|```console
12|// Call it with the 'name' CLI argument
13|$ uv run python main.py Camila
14|
15|// It asks for the missing CLI option --lastname

23|## Customize the prompt
24|
25|You can also set a custom prompt, passing the string that you want to use instead of just `True`:
26|
27|{* docs_src/options/prompt/tutorial002_an_py310.py hl[11] *}
28|
29|And then your program will ask for it using with your custom prompt:
30|
31|<div class="termy">
32|
33|```console
34|// Call it with the 'name' CLI argument
35|$ uv run python main.py Camila
36|
37|// It uses the custom prompt
38|# Please tell me your last name: $ Gutiérrez

44|
45|## Confirmation prompt
46|
47|In some cases you could want to prompt for something and then ask the user to confirm it by typing it twice.
48|
49|You can do it passing the parameter `confirmation_prompt=True`.
50|
51|Let's say it's a CLI app to delete a project:
52|
53|{* docs_src/options/prompt/tutorial003_an_py310.py hl[10] *}
54|
55|And it will prompt the user for a value and then for the confirmation:
56|
57|<div class="termy">
58|
59|```console

63|# Project name: $ Old Project
64|# Repeat for confirmation: $ Old Project
65|

69|$ uv run python main.py

--- FILE: docs/tutorial/multiple-values/options-with-multiple-values.md ---
1|# CLI Options with Multiple Values
2|
3|You can also declare a *CLI option* that takes several values of different types.
4|
5|You can set the number of values and types to anything you want, but it has to be a fixed number of values.
6|
7|For this, use the standard Python `tuple`:
8|
9|{* docs_src/multiple_values/options_with_multiple_values/tutorial001_an_py310.py hl[9] *}
10|
11|Each of the internal types defines the type of each value in the tuple.
12|
13|So:
14|
15|```Python
16|user: tuple[str, int, bool]
17|```
18|
19|means that the parameter `user` is a tuple of 3 values.
20|
21|* The first value is a `str`.
22|* The second value is an `int`.
23|* The third value is a `bool`.
24|
25|Later we do:
26|
27|```Python
28|username, coins, is_wizard = user
29|```
30|
31|If you hadn't seen that, it means that `user` is a tuple with 3 values, and we are assigning each of the values to a new variable:
32|
33|* The first value in the tuple `user` (a `str`) goes to the variable `username`.
34|* The second value in the tuple `user` (an `int`) goes to the variable `coins`.
35|* The third value in the tuple `user` (a `bool`) goes to the variable `is_wizard`.
36|
37|So, this:
38|
39|```Python
40|username, coins, is_wizard = user
41|```
42|
43|is equivalent to this:
44|
45|```Python
46|username = user[0]
47|coins = user[1]
48|is_wizard = user[2]
49|```
50|
51|## Check it
52|
53|Now let's see how this works in the terminal:
54|
55|<div class="termy">
56|
57|```console
58|// check the help
59|$ uv run python main.py --help
60|
61|// Notice the <str int boolean>
62|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS]
63|
64|Options:
65|  --user <str int boolean>...
66|  --help                       Show this message and exit.
67|
68|// Now try it
69|$ uv run python main.py --user Camila 50 yes
70|
71|The username Camila has 50 coins
72|And this user is a wizard!
73|
74|// With other values
75|$ uv run python main.py --user Morty 3 no
76|
77|The username Morty has 3 coins
78|
79|// Try with invalid values (not enough)
80|$ uv run python main.py --user Camila 50
81|
82|Error: Option '--user' requires 3 arguments
83|```
84|
85|</div>
--- END FILE: docs/tutorial/multiple-values/options-with-multiple-values.md ---
--- FILE: docs/tutorial/parameter-types/index.md ---
1|# CLI Parameter Types
2|
3|You can use several data types for the *CLI options* and *CLI arguments*, and you can add data validation requirements too.
4|
5|## Data conversion
6|
7|When you declare a *CLI parameter* with some type **Typer** will convert the data received in the command line to that data type.
8|
9|For example:
10|
11|{* docs_src/parameter_types/index/tutorial001_py310.py hl[7] *}
12|
13|In this example, the value received for the *CLI argument* `name` will be treated as `str`.
14|
15|The value for the *CLI option* `--age` will be converted to an `int` and `--height-meters` will be converted to a `float`.
16|
17|And as `female` is a `bool` *CLI option*, **Typer** will convert it to a "flag" `--female` and the counterpart `--no-female`.
18|
19|And here's how it looks like:
20|
21|<div class="termy">
22|
23|```console
24|$ uv run python main.py --help
25|
26|// Notice how --age is an 'int' (integer) and --height-meters is a 'float'
27|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS] {name}
28|
29|Arguments:
30|  name  [required]
31|
32|Options:
33|  --age <int>               [default: 20]
34|  --height-meters <float>   [default: 1.89]
35|  --female / --no-female    [default: female]
36|  --help                    Show this message and exit.
37|
38|// Call it with CLI parameters
39|$ uv run python main.py Camila --age 15 --height-meters 1.70 --female
40|
41|// All the data has the correct Python type
42|name is Camila, of type: class 'str'
43|--age is 15, of type: class 'int'
44|--height-meters is 1.7, of type: class 'float'
45|--female is True, of type: class 'bool'
46|
47|// And if you pass an incorrect type
48|$ uv run python main.py Camila --age 15.3
49|
50|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS] {name}
51|Try "main.py --help" for help.
52|
53|Error: Invalid value for '--age': '15.3' is not a valid int.
54|
55|// Because 15.3 is not an integer (it's a float)
56|```
57|
58|</div>
59|
60|## Watch next
61|
62|See more about specific types and validations in the next sections...

1|# CLI Arguments with Multiple Values
2|
3|*CLI arguments* can also receive multiple values.
4|
5|You can define the type of a *CLI argument* using `list`.
6|
7|{* docs_src/multiple_values/arguments_with_multiple_values/tutorial001_py310.py hl[9] *}
8|
9|And then you can pass it as many *CLI arguments* of that type as you want:
10|
11|<div class="termy">
12|
13|```console
14|$ uv run python main.py ./index.md ./first-steps.md woohoo!
15|
16|This file exists: index.md
17|woohoo!
18|This file exists: first-steps.md
19|woohoo!
20|```
21|
22|</div>
23|
24|/// tip
25|
26|We also declared a final *CLI argument* `celebration`, and it's correctly used even if we pass an arbitrary number of `files` first.
27|
28|///
29|
30|/// note
31|
32|A `list` can only be used in the last command (if there are subcommands), as this will take anything to the right and assume it's part of the expected *CLI arguments*.
33|
34|///
35|
36|## *CLI arguments* with tuples
37|
38|If you want a specific number of values and types, you can use a tuple, and it can even have default values:
39|
40|{* docs_src/multiple_values/arguments_with_multiple_values/tutorial002_an_py310.py hl[10:12] *}
41|
42|Check it:
43|
44|<div class="termy">
45|
46|```console
47|// Check the help
48|$ uv run python main.py --help
49|
50|Usage: main.py [OPTIONS] [names]...
51|
52|Arguments:
53|  names...  Select 3 characters to play with  [default: Harry, Hermione, Ron]
54|
55|Options:
56|  --help                Show this message and exit.
57|
58|// Use it with its defaults
59|$ uv run python main.py
60|
61|Hello Harry
62|Hello Hermione
63|Hello Ron
64|
65|// If you pass an invalid number of arguments you will get an error
66|$ uv run python main.py Draco Hagrid
67|
68|Error: Argument 'names' takes 3 values
69|
70|// And if you pass the exact number of values it will work correctly
71|$ uv run python main.py Draco Hagrid Dobby
72|
73|Hello Draco
74|Hello Hagrid
75|Hello Dobby
76|```
77|
78|</div>
--- END FILE: docs/tutorial/multiple-values/arguments-with-multiple-values.md ---

1|# Ask with Prompt
2|
3|When you need to ask the user for info interactively you should normally use [*CLI Option*s with Prompt](options/prompt.md), because they allow using the CLI program in a non-interactive way (for example, a Bash script could use it).
4|
5|But if you absolutely need to ask for interactive information without using a *CLI option*, you can use `typer.prompt()`:
6|
7|{* docs_src/prompt/tutorial001_py310.py hl[8] *}
8|
9|Check it:
10|
11|<div class="termy">
12|
13|```console
14|$ uv run python main.py
15|
16|# What's your name?:$ Camila
17|
18|Hello Camila
19|```
20|
21|</div>
22|
23|## Confirm
24|
25|There's also an alternative to ask for confirmation. Again, if possible, you should use a [*CLI Option* with a confirmation prompt](options/prompt.md):
26|
27|{* docs_src/prompt/tutorial002_py310.py hl[8] *}
28|
29|Check it:
30|
31|<div class="termy">
32|
33|```console
34|$ uv run python main.py
35|
36|# Are you sure you want to delete it? [y/N]:$ y
37|
38|Deleting it!
39|
40|// This time cancel it
41|$ uv run python main.py
42|
43|# Are you sure you want to delete it? [y/N]:$ n
44|
45|Not deleting
46|Aborted!
47|```

49|</div>

51|## Confirm or abort
52|

60|$ uv run python main.py
61|
62|# Are you sure you want to delete it? [y/N]:$ y
63|
64|Deleting it!
65|
66|// This time cancel it
67|$ uv run python main.py
68|
69|# Are you sure you want to delete it? [y/N]:$ n
70|
71|Aborted!
72|```
73|
74|</div>
75|
76|## Prompt with Rich
77|
78|You can use Rich to prompt the user for input:
79|
80|{* docs_src/prompt/tutorial004_py310.py hl[2,9] *}

84|<div class="termy">
85|

88|

91|Hello Morty
